articles.title: Kilmar Ábrego García, target of Trump’s immigration crackdown, lands in Spain after ‘leaving happy’
articles.summary: Ábrego García chooses to depart from US after previously being deported to El Salvador due to ‘administrative error’

blocks.text: Kilmar Ábrego García, the Salvadorian national whose mistaken deportation turned him into a symbol of Donald Trump’s mass deportation efforts, has landed in Spain.

Ábrego García arrived in Madrid on Wednesday after leaving the United States of his own volition. Prior to his departure, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents met him at the airport and removed his ankle monitor, according to We Are Casa, a Maryland-based advocacy group.
The interaction, the group noted, was “a powerful symbol that ends a chapter marked by illegal deportation, imprisonment, abuse at Cecot, retaliatory prosecution, and government surveillance”.
As he made his way through the Madrid airport, Ábrego García did not speak to reporters, instead raising his fist in the air as he climbed into a waiting van.
In a statement provided by We Are Casa, he described his departure from the US as proof that justice was still capable of prevailing over the most powerful government in the world.

“In this case, despite everything they tried to say, every obstacle they put in my way, and every attempt to shame me, justice prevailed under this administration in a way that many people never thought was possible,” he said. “I am leaving happy. I am leaving with my freedom.”
On Wednesday, Ábrego García spoke to reporters by video call from Spain. “The government does not decide where my story continues,” he said. “My family and I will decide our future.”
Ábrego García became a lightning rod in the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in 2025 after he was deported to El Salvador in what an official later called an “administrative error”.

The 31-year-old had been living in the US since 2019, after a judge ruled that he could not be deported to El Salvador due to the dangers posed by a gang that had threatened his family. The judge allowed him to live and work in the US under ICE supervision, but he was not given residency status.

Married to an American woman, the Maryland resident was part of a group of more than 200 people sent by the US to Cecot, a notorious anti-terrorism mega-prison, in violation of the US immigration judge’s 2019 order.

Amid public outcry, he was returned to the US after a decision by the supreme court. Since then, Ábrego García has been fighting government efforts to deport him for a second time to a series of African countries proposed by Department of Homeland Security officials.
On Wednesday, his lawyer, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, said the Trump administration had wanted to deport Ábrego García “handcuffed, on an ICE flight bound for Liberia” on Tuesday.

“And what happened? He walked out a free man, without any restrictions, without shackles on his feet. He left for the country of his choosing, and he did so on a commercial flight, alongside everyone else,” Sandoval-Moshenberg added.
He described it as a “complete victory”, adding: “Instead of flying ICE Air, he flew United Airlines. Instead of being in shackles, he was in economy plus.”

He said Ábrego García had negotiated a deal with federal authorities in which they had agreed to allow him to leave the country, removing obstacles such as the ankle monitor and taking him off the no-fly list, as long as he left by 24 November. The Department of Homeland Security said on Tuesday Ábrego García had “self-deported” to Spain.

Sandoval-Moshenberg described Ábrego García’s departure from the US as temporary, saying that he would decide where to settle for the next two years as he waited out the remainder of the Trump administration.

“Mr Ábrego García has many options to return to the United States as the husband of a US citizen spouse and the father of a US citizen child,” he said. “We don’t expect that to happen under this administration, which we know will never give him a fair shake, but we expect that the next administration will prioritise reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland.”

On Wednesday, Ábrego García’s lawyer, Chris Newman, said his client had landed in Spain as a tourist and that he had no plans to meet with any politicians while in Spain. “I can confirm that he’s coming here with the intention of staying for just a few days and that he already has tickets, one could say, for his next appointment,” he told Spanish media.

His departure this week was celebrated by many who had sought to push back against the Trump administration’s pursuit of Ábrego García. “A year and a half ago, the Trump administration wanted to leave Kilmar to rot in a Salvadoran gulag,” said Chris Van Hollen, the Maryland senator who visited Abrego Garcia at Cecot, in a statement.
“Today, he is traveling to a country of his choice, a free man – unharmed and with dignity.”

articles.title: US Army says controlled blast of explosives in Iowa was 'huge success'
articles.summary: Despite widespread concern from residents ahead of the blast, officials say that lead readings in the area so far have been promising.

blocks.text: Despite widespread concern from residents of Middletown, Iowa ahead of the blast, officials have said that lead readings in the area so far have been promising.
"The Army's controlled, mitigated detonation exceeded all expectations and was a HUGE success," Adam Telle, acting secretary of the US Army, wrote on social media.
"We are watching EPA's [Environmental Protection Agency] MASSIVE sensor array throughout the area closely, and there are no readings so far above 0.0," he added.

The explosives had been in storage for around 20 years, and degraded as part of a process known as recrystallisation - this made them more responsive to accidental detonation from friction or other movement.
No level of lead exposure is considered safe, with children and pregnant women particularly vulnerable to its harmful effects.
Middletown Mayor Rodney Johnson told the BBC he felt "relieved" and "vindicated" after the detonation.
He watched the blast from his job at a manufacturing plant eight miles (12km) away from the blast - and monitored a camera at his two-bedroom home just one mile from the detonation site.
"We did not feel anything. We did not see anything," Johnson said.
Some eight miles (12km) away from Middletown, Sandy Mabeus closed the windows and the garage at her home, brought their outdoor cat inside and hunkered down earlier today.
The family watched three separate live streams on iPads and televisions of the explosion as it happened.
"We did not feel or hear a thing here," she told the BBC, adding that she checked the videos to confirm it had actually happened.
"The waiting and wondering has not been a good thing for anybody in the area," she said. "Hopefully they had a very good result and we can just get on with things."
There is also caution from some quarters.
Iowa's incoming Governor-elect Rob Sand said there was "more testing to do" and called for "immediate transparency" to explain why the lead-up was "so chaotic and unclear".
Sand said that any Iowans who have been impacted in any way "must be taken care of fully, right away".
Cameron Hamilton, administrator of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), said there would be additional resources and testing in the coming days and weeks.
In recent weeks, the army scheduled and rescheduled their detonation ahead of colder winter temperatures.

It also warned locals of "potential exposure to toxic lead dust", which led to some panic. They instituted measures including an optional evacuation zone and a shelter-in-place advisory ahead of the detonation.
The army faced pushback from residents and politicians alike and there were legal challenges to prevent the detonation from going ahead on environmental and health grounds.
But on Monday, the appeals court overturned a decision to halt the blast. It said that - while these concerns were valid - the risk from an unplanned explosion was greater.

articles.title: Ministers can’t control gas prices, but they can attack other energy costs more ruthlessly
articles.summary:
Louise Haigh talked the right talk at the CBI this week, but greater ambition and tighter timelines are needed

Shocked by

blocks.text: Shocked by average annual energy bills at £2,166 for the first three months of next year? Here’s worse news. It is currently possible, and perhaps even likely, that the regulator, Ofgem, will set the price cap at £2,000-plus in every quarter of 2027.

Predictions for bills are less certain the further out one looks, it should be said. Gas prices, the overwhelming culprit in the £443 hike in the cap announced on Wednesday, can always fall – and might do so if calm returns to the strait of Hormuz.

But EDF’s outlook for next year currently reads: £2,254 for the second quarter, which will include about £100 extra in the “network costs” line in bills that includes paying for the upgrade of the electricity grid – demonstrating that gas prices are not the only story on a medium and long-term horizon. Then £2,078 in the quarter starting in July and £2,035 from October.

To repeat, projections can change, albeit an increasing slice of the electricity side comprises fixed costs, such as those network charges, that are nailed down in advance. The point, though, is that no one – certainly not government ministers – can claim to be surprised if this crisis lasts a while.

There are two points to make. First, the government no longer has an excuse to dodge the vexed question of a “social tariff” for energy – a scheme to give financial support to struggling households on a properly targeted basis.

The aim would be to get off today’s rickety practice of the chancellor giving 11th-hour handouts without a meaningful effort to ensure the money goes where it is most needed. This time it was £100 for council tax payers in lower bands – an inadequate proxy for poorer households or energy hardship.

The misnamed energy independence bill would give the government powers to do the necessary data-sharing work to design a proper social tariff. It’s time to hurry up with a job that has been talked about since the energy crisis of 2022 that followed Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Next winter should serve as a hard deadline to get a workable social tariff in place.

The second point is this. Even as the government under Andy Burnham has emphasised cheaper energy as a new priority, its specific target is not terribly ambitious. It is to lower UK energy costs to bring them in line with other European countries within 10 years.
after newsletter promotion

The goal is more credible than Keir Starmer’s empty (or cynical) promise of “£300 off bills” in the life of this parliament. But a decade to get in line with European averages? That is not speedy. Energy costs are, by a distance, the most pressing concern for UK industry. Yes, there are discounts for a limited number of heavy users, but how is wider “re-industrialisation” meant to happen if the UK remains uncompetitive on energy for another nine years?

A more encouraging way to look at things is that the government’s emerging new thinking on energy is bolder than a 10-year timeframe would suggest. The speech at the CBI this week by Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, offered three clear lines of attack: take more costs off bills and into general taxation; accelerate electrification and grid connections and get “wasted wind” costs under control; and go after the excess profits earned not only by gas plants at moments of high system stress but also by clean power generators with revenue arrangements tied to gas prices.

All are worthwhile strategies, but in combination they ought to be capable of delivering something better than European norms sometime around 2036. If not, the Treasury’s new “cost control framework” on energy levies will have to be sweated harder.

Being charitable, one might say the loose “within 10 years” phraseology was used because every government goal at the moment is framed within Burnham’s yet-to-be-unveiled 10-year plan. One hopes so, because the war on energy costs is more urgent for businesses and households alike.

There is nothing the government can do about wholesale gas prices, of course. But the necessary transition to clean power can be pursued with far more ruthlessness on costs. The 10-year plan, when it finally arrives, should also set a few five-year targets.

articles.title: North Korea expels Swiss diplomat in sanctions row
articles.summary: Swiss officials said relations would be kept through North Korea's embassy in Bern, and its own embassy in Beijing.

blocks.text: North Korea has ordered Switzerland's diplomatic representative to leave the country within 48 hours and called for the office to close amid a row over sanctions.
It said the move was in response to Switzerland's decision to place sanctions on the Songdowon international children's camp. State media described this as "a blatant hostile act".
That camp is at the centre of claims that it was involved in transferring children from Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine.
North Korea's foreign ministry said "any act of violating the sovereign rights" of the country and the interests of its citizens "can never be welcomed".
Switzerland is one of the few Western nations to maintain dialogue with Pyongyang.
Swiss authorities said relations between the two countries would be maintained through the North Korean embassy in Bern, and the Swiss embassy in Beijing.
The diplomatic rebuke comes weeks after Swiss foreign minister Ignazio Cassis made a rare visit to North Korea, where he officially reopened the office and discussed normalising relations.
Diplomatic links with North Korea were first established in 1974 and Switzerland opened a co-operation office in Pyongyang in 1997.

articles.title: Treasury raises spending concerns in proposed support for youth unemployment
articles.summary:
Chancellor wants system laid out in Alan Milburn’s review to break even at an earlier date, sources say

The Treasury has raised concerns about the level of spending on support proposed in…
articles.byline: Rowena Mason, Jessica Elgot and Kiran Stacey

blocks.text: The Treasury has raised concerns about the level of spending on support proposed in Alan Milburn’s review into youth unemployment, amid pressure for the welfare bill to start reducing more quickly.
Whitehall sources have told the Guardian that the chancellor, John Healey, is not happy with the level of spending required under the proposals and wants the system to break even at an earlier date.

The government has promised to back the report’s overall vision to create an entirely new welfare system for young people under 25, including spending cuts next year to help pay for his proposals for additional help and support for those out of work to get them into education or employment.

But ministers have privately admitted that the multibillion-pound costs of Milburn’s support package may be unaffordable, given that they must be met from existing budgets. “Obviously there is trepidation about the upfront costs,” one said.

A second minister said it was clearly Healey’s intention to find ways to reduce the costs of delivering the support package, citing the political necessity of seeing the overall welfare bill begin to come down faster.
At least two options are under cross-government consideration – one of which is initially less generous upfront support than suggested by Milburn’s report.

A second option is to use the planned changes for over-25s to cut disability payments for a wide group of people, with as many as one in six at risk of losing them altogether. The over-25s are also likely to be given a less generous offer of support and training than younger people.
Milburn’s plan would see the government spend £5.8bn a year by the end of the decade on getting young people into work.

Nearly £2bn of that would provide advice to get into training, education or work, while another £2bn would be spent on creating more vocational training courses and apprenticeships, and a further £1bn would go to companies to incentivise them to hire young workers.

That spending would be increased over time, starting with £500m next year, which Milburn has promised will be found from existing budgets. The Department for Work and Pensions, Department of Health and Social Care and Department for Education are now looking for ways to deliver those.
The longer-term spending, however, is not guaranteed, and will be decided for certain in next year’s spending review.
after newsletter promotion

Officials are also drawing up plans to redesign the personal independence payment (Pip) system for older adults in England and Wales after the work and pensions minister, Stephen Timms, deemed it “no longer fit for purpose”.

While ministers are keen to extend the Milburn principle that disability benefits should be focused on getting people into work, they are understood to have accepted the central proposal in the Timms report not to scrap Pip altogether.
Instead they are designing a new assessment system for 90% of claimants over 25, which will involve some people receiving more, some receiving less and many losing their benefits altogether.

Timms recommended that no one who is deemed not to incur extra costs as a result of their disability should receive Pip – a number that the Resolution Foundation calculated could be as high as one in six claimants, or more than 600,000 over-25s.

Officials are now working on the details not only of how the new assessments should work, but also whether they should be applied to existing claimants. They are also drawing up transitional arrangements that would apply to people coming off Pip after they are 25 and any existing claimant who is affected by the changes.

The relatively non-specific nature of Timms’s recommendations mean there is scope to design systems that save very different amounts of money, government sources say. Downing Street officials say Andy Burnham is keen to start cutting the welfare bill as soon as possible.

The prime minister faces pressure from the Conservatives to reduce the overall cost of working-age benefits. He has said this is his plan, but he has pushed back against the idea of what he called “crude cuts”, saying these often just created costs elsewhere.

articles.title: UK food inflation could hit 5% next year, Bank of England says
articles.summary:
Sharp rise expected as cost pressures mount, with experts factoring in coming energy price cap hike and potential impact of El Niño

Food price inflation in the UK could hit 5% next year, the…

blocks.text: Food price inflation in the UK could hit 5% next year, the Bank of England has said, despite rising less sharply than feared since the onset of the Iran war.

The deputy governor Clare Lombardelli told MPs on the cross-party Treasury select committee: “Food price inflation is coming in under what we expected [it] to be, and in fact under what the industry expected it to be.”

But she said the Bank expected food price inflation to rise sharply from the current level of about 1.3%. “We think that … it will go up to 3 to 5% in the middle of next year. I mean, obviously that’s quite uncertain, but that pressure is there,” Lombardelli said.
Lombardelli was being questioned by MPs alongside other members of the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC).
The MPC raised interest rates by a quarter-point to 4% at its last meeting earlier this month to tackle above-target inflation, and suggested further action could be necessary.
Andrew Bailey, the Bank’s governor, said the MPC was also monitoring the potential impact of this year’s unusually large El Niño weather event on future food prices.
“There is uncertainty around this. You know, we still don’t know what the impact of this El Niño effect is going to be, for instance, because it will take time for it to manifest,” he said.
Surging oil and gas prices have pushed up the annual rate of inflation, which hit 3.6% last month, with the cost of petrol and diesel up by more than 33% over the past year.

blocks.caption: The cost of petrol and diesel has gone up by more than a third over the past year. Photograph: Andy Rain/EPA

blocks.text: But so far there have been fewer knock-on effects beyond energy prices. Food inflation has fallen well short of the peak above 17% seen in 2023, when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine exacerbated the supply squeeze as the global economy emerged from the Covid-19 pandemic.
Catherine Mann, an external member of the MPC who voted for a half-point increase this month, pointed to fierce competition in the food retail sector as a reason price rises had been constrained.
“We all go shopping ourselves. I can say that Aldi price match in my stores is apparent. Now, it wasn’t apparent four years ago. So that’s, I think, important,” she said.
Oil prices have fallen sharply since the Democratic party’s sweep in the US midterms brought hopes of an end to the Iran conflict, and as alternative sources of supply start to come onstream.
Bailey said if these lower prices continued, they would moderate the Bank’s predictions for UK inflation – which it had expected to peak at almost 5% next year.

“The prices are volatile … if these current prices were to stay what they are, the peak of inflation mechanically would be lower,” he said. However, Bailey and other MPC members underlined that some inflationary pressure for next year is already baked in – pointing to the 26% rise in the price cap for household energy bills due in January as an example.

The two-hour hearing underlined the divisions within the committee. The more dovish Swati Dhingra suggesting she saw this month’s rate rise as a one-off “insurance” measure, while Mann said she feared the MPC had undermined public confidence by failing to move more aggressively.

blocks.caption: The Bank of England’s monetary policy committee will hold its next rate-setting meeting on 17 December. Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PA

blocks.text: Dhingra compared the muted impact of rocketing oil and gas prices this year on the wider economy with the effects of the surge in 2022 after Russia invaded Ukraine.
At a similar point in that year, the prices of 70% of goods included in the consumer price index had risen, she said – but just 20% of prices have reacted so far this year.
But Mann pointed out that inflation had now been consistently above the Bank’s 2% target for five years.

“If we let inflation expectations drift away from 2% in the longer term, then monetary policy is going to have to work harder, meaning a higher rate for longer,” she said, adding: “The optimal response is to hike more and sooner.” The MPC’s next rate-setting meeting is on 17 December.

articles.title: Montreal mayor walks back 'clumsy' Kraft Dinner comment after major tax hike
articles.summary: A day after the City of Montreal unveiled a budget that featured a property tax average increase of 9.8 per cent — about three times the inflation rate — the mayor is once again on the defensive.

image.caption: Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada, seen here in a photo from Nov. 21, 2025, says her comments were meant to illustrate that the city had to make some tough choices. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Montreal
A day after the City of Montreal unveiled a budget that featured a property tax average increase of 9.8 per cent — about three times the inflation rate — the mayor is once again on the defensive.
Day after unveiling budget with huge tax increase, mayor once again on the defensive
This time, it's over comments she made about Kraft Dinner.
The property tax increase unveiled on Tuesday was the talk of city hall, as it meant that Montreal homeowners will need to spend an average of $515 more on taxes.
Soraya Martinez Ferrada has insisted the tax increase is necessary to get the city's finances in order and to catch up on much-needed infrastructure work.
During an interview with local media outlet Urbania, the mayor talked about the city's financial struggles and made a comment that has sparked lots of social media backlash.
"We're going through every service to see what we can save. It's like when you make your personal budget: if you know you'll have less money one year, then, you have to make choices," she said.
"Sometimes, you'll have to eat a little more Kraft Dinner because we can't afford filet mignon."

items: Montreal's 'unprecedented' tax hike key to tackling 'infrastructure crisis,' mayor says
Montreal's tax hike is making headlines, but here are other takeaways from the budget

blocks.text: Many comments online suggested the mayor and the city should've found alternative solutions to the city's financial problems instead of imposing such a hefty tax on residents.
In an Instagram story posted on Wednesday, the mayor acknowledged her comments were "clumsy."
"What I wanted to say is the city will have to make choices: Build new parks or fill potholes. I'm going to focus on filling potholes."

A large chunk of the 9.8 per cent average property tax increase will generate money for a new infrastructure fund that will help the city make more cash payments for maintenance and repair work, rather than relying on credit.
This increase means Martinez Ferrada has broken her campaign promise about limiting tax increases to the rate of inflation.
She was sworn in as mayor in November 2025 and this is her administration's second budget.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Antoni Nerestant has been with CBC Montreal since 2015. He's worked as a video journalist, a sports reporter and a web writer, covering everything from Quebec provincial politics to the 2022 Beijing Olympics.
With files from Radio-Canada

articles.title: Peter Magyar meets Volodymyr Zelenskyy: Hungary and Ukraine make a fresh start after the icy relations of the Viktor Orban era
articles.summary: After years of frosty and hostile relations under Hungary's Kremlin-friendly former PM Viktor Orban, his successor, Peter Magyar, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy seek to reset their…

image.caption: Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar (left, pictured here with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy) said his visit to Ukraine marked the beginning of a new chapter in the relationship between Kyiv and BudapestImage: Genya Savilov/AFP

blocks.text: The location and the gesture were carefully chosen: Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stood side by side, laid flowers and bowed their heads at the military cemetery in the center of the Ukrainian city of Uzhhorod.
One of those buried there is an ethnic Hungarian who was one of the first soldiers killed in Russia's full-scale war of aggression against Ukraine.

Magyar intentionally chose not to begin his first visit to Ukraine as prime minister at a government building. Instead, his Tuesday afternoon visit began at a place where he could demonstrate his solidarity with Ukraine more clearly than anywhere else.

Uzhhorod, known as Ungvar in Hungarian, is the capital of Ukraine's Transcarpathia region, which is home to around 80,000 members of Ukraine's Hungarian minority. Thousands of ethnic Hungarians are fighting Russian occupying forces on the front lines.
For Hungary, where ethnic Hungarian minorities in neighboring countries traditionally play an important role, the war is therefore closer to home than it is for other European countries.

Magyar described his visit to Ukraine as a "historic day" in a Facebook post. Before the ceremony at the cemetery in Uzhhorod, he said: "I bring with me the solidarity of the Hungarian people. We stand with Ukraine against the Russian aggressor."
Zelenskyy responded on X, saying "We appreciate this gesture of respect toward those who sacrificed their lives for Ukraine's independence."
From low point to fresh start
The meeting between Magyar and Zelenskyy marked a turning point in Hungary's approach to Ukraine.

The two leaders repeatedly shook hands throughout the day. Such scenes would have been unthinkable just a few months ago. The propaganda of Magyar's pro-Russian predecessor, Viktor Orban, portrayed Ukraine as a "mafia state" and "lawless country" on an almost daily basis.
Under Orban, relations between Hungary and Ukraine reached a historic low.

Now the two countries are seeking a political reset, which is important not only for Hungary and Ukraine but for Europe as a whole. After all, Orban's repeated obstruction of support for Ukraine drove the EU to the brink of despair.
Closer economic cooperation
During talks in Uzhhorod, the two leaders also agreed to closer economic cooperation.

blocks.caption: Hungary's Prime Minister Peter Magyar (left) and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy laid wreaths and flowers at a ceremony commemorating the Ukrainian defenders who fell during the Russian invasionImage: Janos Nemes/MTI/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The talks centered on Hungarian diesel supplies to Ukraine, greater use of Ukrainian gas storage facilities by Hungarian companies, and joint infrastructure projects, including the opening of new border crossings and a direct rail link between Budapest and Kyiv.
Nevertheless, no formal agreements were signed on Tuesday.
At a subsequent news conference, journalists asked questions about sensitive issues between the two countries: minority rights, Ukraine's EU integration and a new EU loan for Ukraine.
Throughout the day, the two men were visibly keen to avoid any discord.

Magyar, for example, described his angry outburst over Ukraine's "Carpathian Eight" initiative in parliament in late September as a "misunderstanding" and suggested that Hungary might, after all, take part.
Zelenskyy's cautious replies to journalists suggest that he knows his country's path to EU membership also runs through Budapest.
A fresh — but not always smooth — start
One of Magyar's statements on Tuesday was key: "We've finally put a stop to this completely unnecessary and inexplicable political escalation."
Even before taking office in early May 2026, Magyar had promised to reset relations with Ukraine. But the process has not been entirely smooth.

blocks.caption: Posters belonging to Viktor Orban's Fidesz party portrayed Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Peter Magyar and Ursula von der Leyen as a risk and Fidesz as 'the better choice' in the run-up to the parliamentary election in AprilImage: Martin Fejer/estost.net/EST&OST/IMAGO

blocks.text: In many respects — but certainly not all — Magyar is distancing himself from his predecessor. He has made no bones of the fact that he sees Russia as the aggressor, but he rejects both arms deliveries to Ukraine and even the transit of weapons across Hungarian territory.

Magyar previously accused Ukraine of treating ethnic Hungarians as second-class citizens — a claim that is not borne out by the facts. He pressed for greater minority rights and for a time blocked the opening of negotiating chapters in Ukraine's EU accession talks.
Magyar also departed from diplomatic convention by choosing the location of his meeting with Zelenskyy in Ukraine: Indeed, it was Magyar who invited Zelenskyy to Transcarpathia.
Hungarian attitudes to Ukraine
Magyar's sometimes confrontational tone toward Ukraine can also be explained by the need to avoid appearing too pro-Ukrainian to the Hungarian public.

According to a November 2026 poll conducted by the think tank Globsec, 33% of Hungarians would now support their country providing military aid to Ukraine. Although this is much more than during Orban's time in office, many Hungarians remain skeptical of Ukraine.
That's why Olena Halushka, a Ukrainian political scientist at the International Centre for Ukrainian Victory (ICUV), sees some aspects of Magyar's visit as a concession to public opinion in Hungary.

blocks.caption: A monument to members of the military killed during Russia's war in Ukraine in the city of Berehove, the political and cultural center of Ukraine's Hungarian minorityImage: Hanna Sokolova-Stekh/DW

blocks.text: "Magyar has taken over a deeply polarized country," she told DW's Ukrainian Service. "A visit to Transcarpathia is more of a step for the Hungarian population than for Ukraine."

Ukraine accommodated not only Magyar's choice of location but also Hungary's demands for better protection of minority rights, which were set out in a 10-point plan in June. That's because EU integration is one of the country's top political priorities.

After planned restrictions on the use of minority languages were withdrawn in late 2023, Ukraine's parliament in early October passed a law on minority language rights that in some respects goes even further than European standards.
Hungary subsequently dropped its obstruction of the opening of negotiating clusters for Ukraine's EU accession.
'Historic' meeting

Laszlo Zubanics, chairman of the Hungarian Democratic Federation in Ukraine (UMDSZ, one of two Hungarian political parties in Transcarpathia), told DW that the Magyar-Zelenskyy meeting was "historic."

He particularly welcomed the fact that Ukraine will probably implement practical improvements in the protection of minority rights "not only by the end of 2027, but much sooner, within just a few months."

blocks.caption: Laszlo Zubanics welcomed the fact that Ukraine is likely to implement practical improvements in the protection of minority rights 'within just a few months'Image: Hanna Sokolova-Stekh/DW

blocks.text: A Hungarian diplomat who spoke to DW on condition of anonymity also called the meeting "historic," adding that after the Orban government's anti-Ukrainian policies, trust now needs to be rebuilt, and that personal meetings between the two leaders play an important role in that process.
The diplomat went on to say that Hungary not only wants to ensure that the rights of the Hungarian minority are protected, it also has a strong interest in being involved in Ukraine's reconstruction.
Overall, the diplomat concluded, both sides are very keen to expand economic cooperation.
A path forward

Hungarian political scientist Daniel Hegedus of the Institute for European Politics (IEP) in Berlin told DW that while the meeting was a "symbolic milestone," it will be important to see "how the two political leaders capitalize on the symbolic political capital generated by this meeting."
No observers have suggested that this is the grand finale of reconciliation between Hungary and Ukraine.

Nevertheless, Tuesday's reset sends an important signal to Europe, namely that if the political will is there, a deep gulf that has existed for years can be transformed into a set of diverging interests that can be addressed through negotiations.
Or, as Zelenskyy put it, now there are "all the opportunities to build hopefully constructive relations."
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Despite new powers, industry minister hasn't forced telecoms to remove Huawei equipment
articles.summary: Despite legislating new powers last spring to force telecommunications companies to remove products considered a security risk, the minister of industry hasn't used them — and the Conservative…

image.caption: Minister of Industry Mélanie Joly is seen on Tuesday. Asked when the minister will use new powers to force the removal of high-risk telecommunications equipment, Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada said orders 'will be made in due course, in consultation with affected parties.' (Just

blocks.text: Politics·New

Despite legislating new powers last spring to force telecommunications companies to remove products considered a security risk, the minister of industry hasn't used them — and the Conservative Opposition is asking why.
Chinese tech giant convicted in U.S. this week of conspiring to steal trade secrets

Bill C-8 received royal assent in June, enabling the federal government to restrict or ban equipment or services that could put Canada's telecommunications system at risk of "interference, manipulation, disruption or degradation"
Although no companies were named in the bill, it was a successor to a Trudeau-era bill targeting Chinese companies Huawei and ZTE.
On Tuesday, Huawei was convicted of 10 U.S. charges, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets.

items: Carney secures another China trade deal — but at what cost?
How Canada's expanded trade deal with China affects different sectors

blocks.text: For years, Huawei hasn't been allowed to sell equipment to U.S. telecommunications carriers due to security concerns. All of Canada's Five Eyes allies have banned Huawei's 5G equipment.
While Canada has committed to cracking down on companies still using the equipment, it hasn't used its enforcement mechanisms to do so.

A 2022 policy statement named Huawei and ZTE as at risk of being "compelled to comply with extrajudicial directions from foreign governments." The statement includes deadlines to stop using — and rip out — the equipment.
The next deadline — Dec. 31, 2027 — prohibits all 4G equipment and managed services from Huawei and ZTE. The deadline to remove 5G equipment was in 2024.
CBC News reported in 2024 that all major telecommunications companies except Telus Corp. were co-operating with the policy directive.

Telus did not respond to a request for comment about its compliance with the policy. But the company told the Globe and Mail last year that it doesn't consider its equipment subject to the 2024 deadline.
Conservatives point to relations with China
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly now has the ability to compel any companies not in compliance to remove the gear.

"It was well understood at the time that Huawei and ZTE were indeed high-risk firms. And the minister has not exercised that power yet," said Conservative industry critic Adam Chambers in an interview on Tuesday.

"The government has now seemingly had a change of position with respect to engagement on Beijing, and I think Canadians deserve to know if that is the reason for which the minister has not yet used that power."

U.S. prosecutors had originally also brought criminal charges against Huawei's chief financial officer, Meng Wanzhou, accusing her of misleading HSBC bank about the company's business dealings in Iran.
Meng was arrested in Canada in 2018, which led to a diplomatic crisis involving the U.S., Canada and China.
The Huawei executive ultimately was allowed to return to China in 2021 in a prisoner swap that freed two Canadians held by China. As part of the deal, the U.S. dropped its case against Meng.

items: If Quebecor buys Telus, less competition could mean higher cellphone bills, experts say

blocks.text: The company was acquitted on two additional counts, including the most serious: engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy.
In a statement posted online, Huawei said the acquittal on the racketeering charge "confirms these allegations lack factual basis and vindicates our consistent position over the past eight years."
Joly's department said that the government of Canada is "fully committed to protecting the security and reliability of Canadian networks."
"Orders under the Telecommunications Act will be made in due course, in consultation with affected parties," reads a statement from Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED).
Huawei Technologies is one of the biggest suppliers of gear for telecommunications networks in the world. U.S. authorities have long claimed the company poses national security risks.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kate McKenna is a senior reporter with CBC’s parliamentary bureau in Ottawa, where she covers federal politics. She previously worked for CBC’s The Fifth Estate and in the Halifax, Montreal and Charlottetown newsrooms. Her investigative and breaking news coverage has won five RTDNA awards. She is the author of No Choice: The 30-Year Fight for Abortion on Prince Edward Island.
With files from The Associated Press

articles.title: Canadian intern and suspected NATO spy to await trial under electronic monitoring
articles.summary: Biwei Zhang, the 33-year-old computer scientist accused of spying on NATO, will be under electronic monitoring while awaiting trial, a Belgian court ruled on Wednesday.
articles.byline: Aloysius Wong, Idil Mussa, Albert Leung

image.caption: 33-year-old computer scientist Biwei Zhang will continue her pretrial detention under electronic monitoring, a Belgian court decided today. Zhang was arrested in July amid allegations of spying on NATO's military headquarters, where she was working as an intern. (Reuters, Catina Zhang/Facebook)

blocks.text: Canada·Breaking
Biwei Zhang, the 33-year-old computer scientist accused of spying on NATO, will be under electronic monitoring while awaiting trial, a Belgian court ruled on Wednesday.
Belgian federal prosecutor's office considering launching appeal
· CBC News
· Posted: Nov 25, 2026 1:30 PM EST | Last Updated: 30 minutes ago
The Canadian intern accused of spying on NATO on behalf of China will continue her pretrial detention under electronic monitoring, a Belgian court decided Wednesday.
Belgian prosecutors are considering lodging an appeal against the decision, the federal prosecutor's office said in a press release.
The prosecutors did not immediately clarify whether there were other conditions placed on the suspect.

Biwei Zhang, 33, was an intern at NATO's Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe (SHAPE) when she was arrested in July and charged with "spying on behalf of a third country and of being a member of a criminal organization."

Zhang — who is also known by the names Claire and Catina — has a background in computer science and economics and previously worked for Canadian federal agencies including StatsCan and the Canadian Space Agency.
The allegations against Zhang have not been tested in court.
Neither Zhang nor her lawyer have responded to past CBC News requests for comment.

articles.title: Major League Baseball sues players' union, asking court to declare lockout legal
articles.summary: Major League Baseball sued its players' association in federal court on Wednesday in New York, asking that its contemplated lockout next week be declared legal and trying to head off any attempt for…

image.caption: MLB team owners have proposed a salary cap for the first time since 1994, when players fought off the proposal with a 7 1/2-month strike that led to the first cancellation of the World Series in 90 years. (Karen Warren/Associated Press/File)

blocks.text: MLB

Major League Baseball sued its players' association in federal court on Wednesday in New York, asking that its contemplated lockout next week be declared legal and trying to head off any attempt for the union to decertify and challenge the work stoppage with an antitrust case.
5-year labour contract expires at 11:59 p.m. on Dec. 1
· The Associated Press
· Posted: Nov 25, 2026 1:27 PM EST | Last Updated: 30 minutes ago

In a 38-page complaint filed in U.S. District Court in Manhattan, MLB and the corporate entities owning its 30 teams sued the Major League Baseball Players Association and the eight players on the union's executive subcommittee, including record-setting pitcher Tarik Skubal.

"MLB brings this action to keep the dispute over the next collective bargaining agreement ('CBA') at the bargaining table, where federal law says it belongs," the lawsuit suit. "MLB has a reasonable and imminent fear that the Union will attempt to use the threat of antitrust liability to derail the collective bargaining process altogether in favor of antitrust litigation."

Baseball's five-year labour contract expires at 11:59 p.m. Dec. 1 and owners are expected to immediately impose a lockout, which would be the sport's 10th work stoppage since 1972. Team owners have proposed a salary cap for the first time since 1994, when players fought off the proposal with a 7 1/2-month strike that led to the first cancellation of the World Series in 90 years.

Owners asked for a declaratory judgment determining a lockout doesn't violate antitrust laws and doesn't amount to an unreasonable restraint of trade. They asked for a ruling that the federal courts lack jurisdiction to enjoin a lockout and for an order that the players be defined as a legal class, which if granted could block individual lawsuits.

"The lawsuit filed today by MLB is completely frivolous," the union said in a statement. "We will respond appropriately, but MLB's decision to run to court in the middle of negotiations rather than bargain in good faith is incredibly disappointing."

Among the lawyers representing MLB are former Solicitor General Paul D. Clement and Keker, Van Nest & Peters, which worked on behalf of the union in litigation against government seizure of drug tests.

articles.title: EU nationals will pay higher tuition fees than UK students, Burnham indicates
articles.summary:
Asked by Kemi Badenoch to rule out equal rate for UK and EU students, PM says proposal ‘will not be put on the table’

European students will have to pay higher fees than their domestic…

blocks.text: European students will have to pay higher fees than their domestic equivalents at UK universities under a still-to-be-finalised part of the new deal with the EU, Andy Burnham has indicated.

The issue of fees paid by EU nationals studying at British universities is the main element of the arrangement hailed by Burnham in Brussels on Friday that has not been agreed, with both sides giving an extra six months to reach a solution.

Since Brexit, EU students – aside from Irish nationals and those with settled status in the UK – are treated as overseas entrants, so pay tuition fees which can exceed £30,000 a year, rather than a home student rate capped at £9,790.

The EU has been pushing for a lower rate, as part of the reset deal agreed at Friday’s summit in Brussels, which also included plans for looser checks on food and drink, emissions trading and a mutual exchange scheme for young people.
There have also been reports that Brussels has pushed for EU students to pay the domestic rate, while an annual charge of about £12,000 was suggested as a possible compromise.
Asked by Kemi Badenoch at prime minister’s questions to rule out an equal rate between UK and EU students, Burnham indicated that this was requested by the EU but it would not be granted.

“In relation to the deal, the right honourable lady is referring to the European negotiating position, which is not the British negotiating position,” he told her. “That has not been put on the table, and it will not be put on the table.”
Burnham’s official spokesperson said: “Both sides have agreed to negotiate a reciprocal agreement, and any deal would have to be in our national interest.”
Higher overseas fees are an important source of income for most UK universities, and dropping them significantly for EU students could cost the sector hundreds of millions of pounds a year.
Burnham said the deal on tuition fees with the EU was “not done” when asked by the leader of the opposition if the government would compensate universities.

blocks.caption: Badenoch was asked if her party would ‘stand against a deal that will remove mountains of paperwork from British businesses and British exporters’. Photograph: House of Commons/PA

blocks.text: He reiterated the UK’s position that the implementation of the deals agreed on Friday would not be dependent on an agreement about tuition fees, something EU officials took a different view of on Friday.

Burnham said Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, referred to the tuition fees talks as being “a separate piece of paper” to the main deal at the summit, meaning they were not linked.

He also said the Conservative party had to be clear on whether it opposed the plans: “Will it stand against a deal that will remove mountains of paperwork from British businesses and British exporters? A deal that the vast majority of Britain’s major supermarkets support because, they say, it can bring down pressure on the weekly shop? The Conservatives were once the party that opposed the imposition of red tape; they are now the red tape Tories.”

articles.title: UN sacked Palestinian staff on back of unproven Israeli allegations, tribunal rules
articles.summary:
Judgment casts doubt on evidence linking aid workers to Hamas and says humanitarian efforts in Gaza were damaged

A UN tribunal has cast doubt on the evidence used to justify the sacking of…

blocks.text: A UN tribunal has cast doubt on the evidence used to justify the sacking of Palestinian UN aid workers in 2024, saying it was based “almost entirely” on unproven assertions from the Israeli government and had damaged humanitarian operations in Gaza.

The judgment, seen by the Guardian, raises fresh questions about the decision by the UN Relief and Works Agency (Unrwa), the main humanitarian organisation working in Gaza, to sack members of staff. It was taken on the basis of Israeli allegations of involvement in the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023.

The nine workers had their contracts terminated in January 2024 “in the interests of the agency” and were told in termination letters that the allegations against them were “very serious and credible”. The dismissals were confirmed after a UN investigation found they might have been involved in the 7 October attacks.

The decision, which was taken by former Unrwa commissioner general Philippe Lazzarini after consultation with the UN secretary general, António Guterres, was apparently made in the hope that appeasing Israel and its allies would allow humanitarian work to continue in Gaza.

blocks.caption: Philippe Lazzarini, a former UN aid chief, took the decision to dismiss the nine Palestinian staff. Photograph: Heiko Junge/Reuters

blocks.text: Critics warned at the time that the decision, on the basis of allegations rather than evidence, compromised the UN’s integrity and had the opposite effect, giving credence to unproven allegations.
The dismissals failed to prevent the Biden administration ordering a pause in funding, a measure that was echoed temporarily by other backers, leading to a financial shortfall of $450m (£340m).

“I have always said on the record that the Israeli allegations against Unrwa were the mother of all lies,” said Chris Gunness, a former Unrwa spokesperson “Sacking the workers without any evidence confirmed their guilt unfairly in the minds of journalists, led 16 top donors to abandon Unrwa and produced the worst financial crisis in the agency’s history, from which it may never recover.”
The Unrwa dispute tribunal that ruled in favour of one of its sacked workers, Abu Awad, described the Israeli allegations as unsupported and of “limited evidentiary value and reliability”.

The tribunal also found that an internal UN investigation had not interviewed the 19 staff members initially accused by Israel of involvement in the 7 October attacks because of “safety and security” concerns.
“The allegations against the applicant and the other staff members, it seems, are therefore based almost entirely on information in Israel’s possession,” the tribunal said.

It cast doubt on intercepted mobile phone conversations and messages offered by Israel as evidence, noting that one case had involved mistaken identity based on a cloned sim card, a common phenomenon in Gaza.

It also said that voice recognition claims made by Israel were dubious and some transcripts of conversations were found by UN investigators not to support claims that they proved links to Hamas or the 7 October attacks.

The allegation against Awad was that he was a “platoon commander” in Hamas’s military wing, the Al-Qassam Brigades, a claim he rejected. He was not alleged to have physically taken part in the 7 October attack and witness statements to the tribunal said he was on an Unrwa staff bus as normal.

blocks.caption: Israeli soldiers on patrol by the Unrwa headquarters in Gaza City in 2024. Many countries paused funding for the UN agency after Israel made allegations against some of its Palestinian staff. Photograph: Dylan Martinez/Reuters

blocks.text: The specific allegation against Awad was that he “had been instructed in a telephone call intercepted by Israeli intelligence to monitor the events of 7 October 2023, while simultaneously receiving Hamas intelligence updates related to the attacks”.
The tribunal said the Israeli security services had failed to clarify who was alleged to have made the call to Awad and in what way the mobile phone that received the call was associated with him.

Unrwa did not respond to a request for comment. Asked by the tribunal to provide evidence underpinning the dismissal of the workers, the agency cited the Israeli government as well as a report in the Times of Israel and another on the website UN Watch, a pro-Israel pressure group that has campaigned against Unrwa.

In its ruling, the tribunal said Unrwa’s claim that the cited sources had informed the decision to dismiss the workers was “open to some doubt” because all the supporting documents it had submitted were produced after the disputed decision was made on 26 January 2024.

Lazzarini, a Swiss humanitarian expert who left the commissioner general post in March, did not respond to a request for comment. In February 2024, he admitted his decision to sack the workers represented “reverse due process” in that the investigation followed the dismissal.

“My judgment, based on this going public, true or untrue, was I need to take the swiftest and boldest decision to show that as an agency we take this allegation seriously,” he said, adding that “the ability of the entire agency to continue to operate and deliver critical humanitarian assistance was at stake”.

The tribunal said it could not decide on the allegations against Awad but ruled that Unrwa had failed to produce evidence supporting its decision to sack him. It awarded him a year’s pay and $5,000 for “moral damages”.

In the wake of its allegations against the sacked workers, Israel claimed that Unrwa was heavily infiltrated by Hamas and its parliament voted in 2024 to ban the agency from operating in Israel or in the occupied Palestinian territories.

The international court of justice stated in October 2025, however, that “Israel has not substantiated its allegations that a significant part of Unrwa’s employees are members of Hamas … or other terrorist factions”.

articles.title: Remember when NASA slammed a spacecraft into an asteroid? We now have close-up images of the aftermath
articles.summary: Four years after NASA slammed a spacecraft into an asteroid to see if it could successfully alter its orbit around a larger companion, the European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft has arrived to see…

image.caption: This Hera Asteroid Framing Camera image shows Dimorphos in orbit around Didymos, with the crater caused by the 2022 DART impact clearly visible. The impact appears to have flattened one side of Dimorphos, leaving a crater that seems as wide as the impacted face of the asteroid and some weird structu

blocks.text: Science·New

Four years after NASA slammed a spacecraft into an asteroid to see if it could successfully alter its orbit around a larger companion, the European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft has arrived to see just how well that went.
'It's hard to describe in words all the excitement to finally see what happened,' says Hera mission scientist
In 2021, NASA embarked on an ambitious mission: Sending a spacecraft to slam into one of two asteroids in a double-asteroid system to test whether the impact could change its orbit.
Why? To see if the technology could be used to redirect any potentially hazardous asteroid that was on a collision course with Earth. (Don’t panic: There’s no known asteroid on a collision course.)

The binary asteroid system consists of Didymos and its smaller moonlet, Dimorphos, which orbit a common centre of mass. The mission was to slam into the moonlet to see if it would change its orbit around Didymos.

Fast forward to September 2022, and the Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) did just that. It shortened Dimorphos's orbit around Didymos by roughly 33 minutes. NASA had anticipated a change of roughly 10 minutes.
While telescopes on Earth revealed the aftermath, another mission — the European Space Agency’s (ESA) Hera — was planned to take a closer look.
Now, ESA has released close-up images and videos of the pair four years after DART.
Looking closely at the images and video, there is a noticeable flattening on Dimorphos compared to pre-impact.

“But now where that rounded face was, now, well, it's a big crater … that is almost as large as the body itself, which is really, really spectacular,” said Sabina Raducan, planetary scientist with the International Space Science Institute and part of the Hera mission.
“It's hard to describe in words all the excitement to finally see what happened.”
A big surprise
But there was more for Hera to discover.

“Every space mission has surprises. But there was a particularly big one in store for Hera,” said Naomi Murdoch, planetary scientist with ISAE-SUPAERO at the Université de Toulouse, and part of the Hera science team.
“Hera has observed hundreds of boulders moving around these two asteroids and ranging in size from tens of centimetres to metre-sized,” she said.
The image produced by 11 long-exposure images look like fireflies are swarming around the pair of asteroids.

This is a composite image combining 11 long-exposure Hyperscout H images, centred on the Didymos asteroid. The dot trails correspond to hundreds of boulders of differing sizes in motion around the Didymos-Dimorphos system. The two asteroids have been subtracted from the image for improved visualisation of the boulders. These images were acquired on 6 November with an approximate distance of 29.9 km from the asteroids. (European Space Agency)
But it’s not clear from where they originated. Was it a result of the 2022 impact, or were they there before, as part of Didymos?

“We're still really trying to characterize them,” Murdoch said. “So, understanding with lots of imaging what their sizes are and how exactly they're moving in the space around the asteroids. So right now, we're not entirely sure where they came from.”
Hera has been orbiting the dual asteroid system for the past three weeks. There are still six months left in its mission. And scientists are eager to discover more.

Comparing images of the Didymos system before and after the 2022 impact of NASA's DART mission with the smaller Dimorphos moonlet. The left-side image is a view from the DART spacecraft shortly before impact. The right-side image is a view from Hera, aiming to match the previous mission's view angle as closely as possible. Dimorphos appears entirely transformed, with its once-rounded face flattened into a crater that seems as wide as the impacted face of the asteroid and some weird structures inside it, including an apparent cigar-shaped structure at its centre. (NASA/Johns Hopkins APL/European Space Agency)
For example, Didymos looks like a giant walnut, with a pronounced ridge across the 700-metre wide asteroid.

“The central ridge is a very spectacular feature of this asteroid. What we know is that the asteroid is rotating very fast, and we think that what happens when asteroids rotate fast is that the material on the surface actually flows down from the higher latitudes, down towards the equatorial region,” Murdoch explained.

items: NASA's asteroid deflection test for planetary defence even more successful than we thought
NASA's planetary defence test successfully shifts asteroid orbit

blocks.text: Another interesting thing is that, since the impact, Dimorphos is now tumbling as it orbits.
“Before the DART impact, Dimorphos was more like our own moon. So it was always showing the same face to Didymos,” Raducan said. “It was behaving quite nicely. Now it's very chaotic.”
More successful than anticipated
Not only did DART change Dimorphos’s orbit around Didymos, but it turns out it also changed the pair’s orbit around the sun.

In March, a study published in the journal Science Advances, reported that the impact changed its 770-day orbital period around the sun by a fraction of a second. A fraction of a second may not seem like much, but it marks the first time in history that a human-made object has changed the orbit of an object around the sun.
NASA slams spacecraft into asteroid to test planetary defence

Over the next six months, Hera will continue to collect data about the binary asteroid system to see what else may have changed. It will deploy two CubeSats (miniature satellites), to further explore both the mineral make-up of Dimorphos as well as the first radar sounding within an asteroid.
After that, the pair will descend to the asteroid’s surface. And when Hera’s mission is completed, it too will descend to the surface.

For now, astronomers are excited to see what the next six months will tell them about this little pairing, and specifically, if an asteroid re-direct mission is a viable solution to keeping Earth safe.

“We learned that from DART, that we can send a spacecraft there, we can hit it, and now from Hera, we can see this effect,” Raducan said. “We know that we can deflect it. The next question that we would need to answer as we get more data is to see how much this deflection, how efficient this deflection actually was.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Based in Toronto, Nicole covers all things science for CBC News. As an amateur astronomer, Nicole can be found looking up at the night sky appreciating the marvels of our universe. She is the editor of the Journal of the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada and the author of several books. In 2021, she won the Kavli Science Journalism Award from the American Association for the Advancement of Science for a Quirks and Quarks audio special on the history and future of Black people in science. You can send her story ideas at nicole.mortillaro@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Rodrigo Duterte camp: Link to alleged crimes against humanity "untenable"
articles.summary: In its major 77-page pre-trial brief released on November 25, Duterte"s defense team questioned the Office of the Prosecutor"s evidence that links Duterte to the allegations of murder and alleged…
articles.byline: ANDY PEÑAFUERTE III, JAY-VEE MARASIGAN PANGAN

blocks.text: Published November 26, 2026 2:05am

PRAGUE, Czech Republic – Roughly four days before the International Criminal Court (ICC) opens its trial of Rodrigo Duterte, his camp has reiterated its position: the allegation of crimes against humanity charged to the former president is “untenable”.

In its major 77-page pre-trial brief released on November 25, Duterte’s defense team questioned the Office of the Prosecutor’s evidence that links Duterte to the allegations of murder and alleged murder during the charged period.

"The link between Mr. Duterte and the alleged crimes is untenable," according to the document. "The Prosecution places weight on the speeches of Mr. Duterte, but that rhetoric, situated in its proper context, establishes neither criminal intent nor the requisite nexus to the charges. Furthermore, the term neutralisation did not mean to kill a suspect."

Saying that the defense “does not intend to raise a positive defense,” lead counsel Peter Haynes emphasized that Duterte’s camp will instead “show that the crimes alleged do not constitute crimes against humanity”.

Haynes refuted the prosecution’s charges, saying that even if it could prove beyond reasonable doubt the 56 incidents it linked to Duterte, their evidence “cannot establish the contextual elements” of crimes against humanity.

“There was no widespread or systematic attack against the civilian population of the Philippines. There was no State or organisational policy to murder. This is not a crimes against humanity case and, as such, does not belong before this Court.”

Duterte’s defense also told Trial Chamber III that it “is not contesting the existence of unlawful killings by police” during Duterte’s drug war, but argued the killings “undoubtedly occurred”, but “they were not crimes against humanity."

Haynes argued that the drug war killings “have been prosecuted and continue to be prosecuted as ordinary murders” in the Philippines, which he said has a “functioning criminal justice system” as well as “functioning domestic mechanisms for accountability – including criminal accountability."
He also asserted that the ICC case against Duterte “organically emerged from an impartial investigation into incriminating and exonerating circumstances.”

“There is something obscene and perverse about a process which removes accountability processes from a national system entirely equipped to deal with them, and instead rewards the direct perpetrators with impunity for the crimes, all to build an “international” case against an 81-year old man, whose cognitive impairment has been acknowledged by court-appointed doctors, one of whom was transparent that Mr Duterte doesn’t remember things from one meeting to the next,” Haynes stated in the brief.
The defense’s pre-trial brief, originally submitted to Trial Chamber III on November 20, is released with redactions.

The filing comes as Presiding Judge Joanna Korner, Judge Keebong Paek, and Judge Nicolas Guillou are hearing and deciding on a multitude of evidentiary and procedural arguments from the defense, the prosecution, the Common Legal Representatives of Victims, and the ICC Registry.

With less than a week before Duterte’s trial begins, information on which prosecution witness testimony should be admitted in court, the in-court security measures to protect witnesses and victims, and other logistical courtroom concerns remains scarce.

Duterte’s trial for charges against humanity begins on Monday, November 30. The ICC Public Affairs Unit said the trial may take months, as the first block of presentations will focus on the prosecution presenting its witnesses and evidence. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Spain: Canary Islands witness 1-day migration record
articles.summary: The arrival of over 2,000 migrants to the islands comes as Spain holds elections this weekend. The president of the Canary Islands said the archipelago is facing "unprecedented migration pressure."

image.caption: The migrants travel on rickety wooden boats known in Spanish as 'cayucos'Image: Antonio Sempere/AFP

blocks.text: The Spanish Canary Islands witnessed a one-day migration record on Tuesday, with over 2,100 people arriving to the region in over 24 hours.
Most of the migrants landed on the the island of El Hierro, according to Spanish authorities.
'The Canaries can't take it anymore,' regional leader says

"The Canaries can't take it anymore. We're experiencing an unprecedented migration pressure," President of the Canary Islands Fernando Clavijo wrote on X. He requested an urgent meeting with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to discuss an immediate EU response.
Around 100 minors arrived on Tuesday, with a baby also born during the trip from Africa to the islands.

The Canaries, a tourist destination whose shortest gap with northwest Africa is around 100 kilometers (around 62 miles), tends to see more migrant arrivals in the fall when the waters are calmer. The waters become rougher in the winter due to storms and swells.

Earlier this month, nearly 1,600 migrants from West Africa were saved and taken to the Canary Islands in a previous record. Over 26,000 migrants came to the Canaries this year so far — with half of that figure in November alone.
Spain's Canary Islands see record migrant rescues
The route from Africa to the Canaries is one of the deadliest in the world for migrants.

Boats taking off for the islands sometimes drift out to open sea, with the migrants onboard facing starvation, dehydration and lack of medical care. Human smugglers frequently organize the trips and abuse the migrants.
Migration major topic as Spain holds snap vote Sunday
The spike in migration to the Canaries comes as Spain will hold a snap election on Sunday.
Migration, along with housing, will be one of the topics at the forefront of voters' minds when they cast their ballots.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who belongs to the center-left Socialist Party, has faced backlash from the opposition regarding his tolerant attitude towards migration. The Spanish government earlier this year enacted a plan to legalize up to 500,000 undocumented migrants.
Moroccan migrants refuse to leave Ceuta

In late July, over 80,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into the Spanish North African enclave of Ceuta, triggering a crisis for the Sanchez government. Countries such as Germany and Italy tightened or extended border controls due to the influx of migrants into Ceuta.

The far-right Vox party, which could receive its best-ever result in upcoming election, has called for Sanchez and his ministers to be prosecuted for treason over the Ceuta crisis. The conservative Popular Party could form a coalition government with Vox after the election.

blocks.text: Published November 26, 2026 1:38am
A longtime lotto player won the P21.69-million jackpot in the Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office’s (PCSO) Lotto 6/42 draw on October 29, 2026, after placing a Lucky Pick bet.
The winner claimed his prize of P21,694,699.03 at the PCSO main office in Mandaluyong City on November 3.
He correctly matched the winning combination 34-15-19-37-25-38.

The winner, a father currently renting a house with his children, recalled discovering his win only when he returned to the lotto outlet the following day to place another bet. Upon seeing the winning numbers posted, his knees began to tremble as he realized he had hit the jackpot.
Still in disbelief, he managed to remain composed, saying the reality of his life-changing win only sank in when he arrived home.
He said he plans to use his newfound fortune to improve their living conditions and start a business that would provide them with a more stable future.
The PCSO reminded jackpot winners to immediately sign the back of their winning tickets and claim their prizes within one year from the date of the draw.
Under the Tax Reform for Acceleration and Inclusion (TRAIN) Law, lotto winnings exceeding P10,000 are subject to a 20% final tax.
Proceeds from lotto ticket sales help fund its various charitable programs, including medical assistance, health services, and other initiatives for Filipinos in need.
The lotto 6/42 draws are held every Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday at 9:00 p.m., and are broadcast live on IBC-13, D8TV, and the PCSO Games Online Hub Facebook page.

articles.title: Trump open to pardoning Jensen Huang if needed: ‘It’s always an option’
articles.summary:
The president’s comments came after pressuring Nvidia’s board to reinstall Huang as CEO despite lawmakers’ concerns over national security

Donald Trump

blocks.text: Donald Trump said on Tuesday he would be open to pardoning Jensen Huang, the recently reinstalled Nvidia CEO, for potential crimes but didn’t think it would be necessary.
“It’s always an option, I guess,” the US president told the New York Post in an interview. “But I don’t think it’ll be necessary.”

Trump’s comments came after he intervened in Nvidia’s leadership drama and put pressure on the tech company’s board to reinstall Huang as the CEO despite other lawmakers’ concerns over whether Huang posed a national security risk for having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Huang is expected to testify to congressional committees in the coming weeks about Nvidia’s chip exports, Huang’s alleged affair and the US government’s role in having Nvidia reinstate Huang as CEO.

“I think I want [Huang] to just tell the truth, and I mean, his lawyers are going to have to advise him, but I’ve always found him to be 100% aboveboard, and you know, a very smart person,” Trump told the New York Post.
Huang has not been formally accused of any crime, and Todd Blanche, the US attorney general, told reporters on Tuesday that no evidence indicated Huang committed a crime.

“To the extent that … the Department of Justice had information that he was committing crimes or something like this, that is, that’s just not, that’s something that I would have certainly told the president had it been true,” Blanche said.
At the same time, Blanche did not confirm whether the justice department had conducted a thorough investigation into Huang, instead saying law enforcement agents “looked into” the situation.
Yet days earlier, Trump told CNBC that his administration had done “a pretty good investigation” to exonerate Huang.
But lawmakers from both sides of the aisle have questions about the US government’s determination

John Curtis, a Republican who sits on the Senate commerce committee, wrote on X: “Nvidia’s board says it relied on input from senior U.S. officials to conclude that bringing Jensen Huang back posed no national security risk. I have some questions. Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board? And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?”

Pete Ricketts, a Republican who sits on the Senate foreign relations committee, wrote on X on Monday, “Nvidia’s decision today doesn’t excuse Jensen Huang from testifying before Congress. It also doesn’t absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips.”
John Kennedy, a Republican on the Senate banking committee, told Fox News that he wanted to know more about Huang’s alleged affair for national security purposes.
“I got no interest; it’s not my place if Mr Huang wants to be a feral, if he wants to cheat on Mrs Huang. It is my interest, though, if he was having sex with a Chinese spy,” Kennedy said.

“The Trump Administration needs to explain what ‘input’ was given and by which senior officials to support Huang’s reinstatement,” Elizabeth Warren, top Democrat on the Senate banking committee, wrote on X on Monday.

Elissa Slotkin, a Democrat on the Senate homeland security committee, raised concerns about whether Trump “knew about the potential compromise with the alleged Chinese spy influencing Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang” and “did nothing about it”.

articles.title: Edmonton to host 2028 Grey Cup
articles.summary: The Edmonton Elks and the Canadian Football League announced that the 2028 Grey Cup will be held in Edmonton. The last time Commonwealth Stadium hosted a Grey Cup was in 2018, when the Calgary…

image.caption: A file photo of Commonwealth Stadium in Edmonton, on Tuesday, June 1, 2021. (Jason Franson/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Edmonton·Breaking

The Edmonton Elks and the Canadian Football League announced that the 2028 Grey Cup will be held in Edmonton. The last time Commonwealth Stadium hosted a Grey Cup was in 2018, when the Calgary Stampeders beat the Ottawa Redblacks 27-16.
Commonwealth Stadium last hosted the Grey Cup in 2018
The 2028 Grey Cup is coming to Edmonton.
The Edmonton Elks, the winners of this year's championship, and the Canadian Football League made the announcement Wednesday in Edmonton.
The 115th Grey Cup game will be played at Commonwealth Stadium.
The last time Commonwealth Stadium hosted the Grey Cup was in 2018, when the Calgary Stampeders beat the Ottawa Redblacks 27-16.

While Edmonton has won 15 Grey Cups, none of them have been won at Commonwealth Stadium. Their closest opportunity was in 2002, when the team lost 25-16 to the Montreal Alouettes in front of a spillover crowd of 62,531.
The announcement comes just over a week after the Elks won the 113th Grey Cup game in Calgary, securing the club's 15th championship in franchise history and its first Grey Cup win in 11 years.
Saskatchewan is set to host the 2027 Grey Cup game at Mosaic Stadium in Regina.

articles.title: US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China
articles.summary: The new levies would hit many of America's biggest trading partners, including China and the EU.

blocks.text: The US has announced a fresh raft of tariffs as President Donald Trump pushes ahead with his signature trade policy.
The new taxes charged on imports to America are set to hit many of the country's biggest trading partners - China, the European Union and 12 other jurisdictions.

The move follows the White House's investigation into the trade practices of other countries in March after the US Supreme Court ruled Trump's previously announced Liberation Day tariffs were illegal.
China is facing the highest rate of up to 40%, followed by Vietnam at up to 35% and then others facing either 20% or 25%.
The new duties are not expected to take effect until next year.
Tariffs are taxes levied on imported goods. The amount is typically calculated as a percentage of the good's value and paid to the government by businesses importing the products from abroad.
Some of these rates will be effectively reduced because of caps on tariffs Trump has agreed to. Individual countries also face different levies.
The proposed tariffs will affect China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the latest tariffs issued would "level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy".

He claimed that many of America's trading partners had "for decades" adopted industrial strategies which included "targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression" as well as "other market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favor while eroding America's manufacturing base".
But economists have warned tariffs can fuel inflation and push prices up for consumers if businesses pass on higher costs, as well as dampen global trade.
Trump has repeatedly threatened or imposed tariffs during his second term, arguing they will boost US manufacturing and create jobs.
Despite a poor result for the Republican party in the midterm elections, the president has continued to press on with his flagship trade policy.
Trump is also seeking to cut the US trade deficit - the gap between the value of goods it buys from other countries and those it sells to them.

However, Stephen Brown, chief North America economist for Capital Economics, said the latest tariff announcement was "not as alarming as it looks", due to the taxes "essentially replacing" previously announced tariffs made in the summer.

"The increase in the effective tariff rate looks set to be a touch lower than we've been assuming for our forecasts, although the new tariffs will still provide a marginal boost to prices," he said in a note.
"The key message is that the additional tariff burden is likely to be small, especially as various goods... are also not subject to these new tariffs."
The announcement is likely to increase tensions between the US and China, the world's two biggest economies, who remain locked in a trade dispute and the AI race.
The two countries have also been embroiled in a tit-for-tat tariffs war, which is currently on hold.
Despite last week's meeting between Trump and China's President Xi Jinping, the two sides made no announcement on the trade war truce, which is set to expire on 10 January.
The European Commission rejected the new US tariffs, saying it would investigate the US's reasons for bringing them in. It pointed out that tariffs are limited to the 15% previously agreed.
