articles.title: US stocks fall further as fears over AI intensify
articles.summary: All three main US indexes were down in early trading, with the tech-dominated Nasdaq down almost 4%.

blocks.text: Big technology firms connected to AI continued to see share prices fall on Wednesday, with stock in Nvidia and Anthropic dropping sharply in early trading.
All three main US stock market indices were down, with the tech-dominated Nasdaq shedding almost 4%.
The declines come amid concerns over the level and sustainability of AI investment which has rattled investors in recent weeks.
Shares in other major tech firms, including Amazon, Tesla and SpaceX, Micrsoft and Meta were also down.
The US government also announced a raft of new tariffs on countries and trading partners on Wednesday as part of President Donald Trump's flagship trade policy.

The value of big tech companies have sheltered the US economy from global economic shocks, including tariffs, but share prices in recent weeks have been volatile in response to the US midterm elections and other events in the AI industry.
The resignation and subsequent reinstatement of Nvidia boss Jensen Huang after revelations of his extra marital affairs has seen the market value of the world's premier AI chipmaker fluctuate wildly.
Given Nvidia's position as both supplier and financier of many other firms involved in the AI rollout, its rocky fortnight has had a wider impact.
Investors have taken fright at Democrat gains in the US midterm elections, with many having campaigned for tougher regulation of AI firms and even a moratorium on the development of new data centres.
Questions also remain about whether the huge sums being invested in AI will eventually pay off.

"It seems that these companies are trying to one-up each other on the amount of money that they're spending but you have to show that it's worth it, and that's where Wall Street is saying I don't know," said Todd Schoenberger, chief investment officer at CrossCheck Management.

Despite concerns, investment in AI is expected to exceed $1 trillion in 2026, according to investment bank Goldman Sachs, which said the technology will remain the "dominant driver of business investment growth" next year.
Nvidia's share price was down 8% in early trading on Wednesday, extending Tuesday's slide as the boost from Huang's return eased.
Shares in Anthropic continued to trade below the $83 they debuted at last week, while Amazon shares fell by more than 5%.
The declines come ahead of the US stock market closing for Thanksgiving on Thursday before opening for a shortened session on Friday.

articles.title: €561 Billion and Still Not Enough: Germany's 2027 Budget Exposes a Coalition on the Brink
articles.summary: The budget for 2027 has reached new highs, and pension funds, defense spending and a weak economy are increasing the pressure. At the same time, tensions are mounting within the government.

image.caption: The Bundestag is debating the 2027 federal budget this weekImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: At first glance, everything seems to be business as usual. Lawmakers in the Bundestag, the lower house of parliament, are holding four days of final debates on how much money the federal government may spend in the coming year, and on what. These follow a familiar pattern: The government pats itself on the back, while the opposition voices criticism. But anyone listening more closely will notice that there are doubts even in the ranks of the coalition parties, the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), their Bavarian allies, the Christian Social Union (CSU), and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD).

"As a country, we are in a difficult situation geopolitically, technologically, and demographically, and next year's budget is an accurate reflection of that," Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) acknowledged on Wednesday in the Bundestag.

"If we don't change course, in a few years we'll find ourselves in a situation where all federal revenue will have to be spent on social programs, interest payments, and defense," he reflected on Wednesday during a four-hour debate focused on government policy as a whole, rather than the individual budgets of the ministries.
€200 billion in new borrowing: Germany's not so frugal budget

This government has now been in office for about 20 months. Back in early 2025, expectations were enormous. Merz had promised to bring the budget back in line with the debt brake enshrined in the constitution, which stipulates that the government can spend only as much as it collects.

Yet for 2027, spending — at just under €561 billion ($614 billion) — will be higher than ever before, and tax revenues are nowhere near sufficient to cover this, meaning Germany is looking at a record debt totaling €210 billion.

The largest opposition party, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) calculated that the government will incur €401,000 in new debt every minute next year. In the Bundestag, AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla called it a "debt orgy" that will paralyze the country. Merz will "go down in history as the chancellor who led Germany to bankruptcy," he exclaimed.
Record spending and record debt

Germany's debt has only ever been higher in the COVID-19 pandemic. The current pressures are obvious: The economy is struggling, the population aging, and Russia's war against Ukraine is about to enter its sixth year.
Merz accused of 'blackmail' over Ukraine funding

The defense budget is now by far the highest in the history of the Federal Republic, with €109 billion allocated for 2027, an increase of €27 billion on last year. Added to this is the multi-year, debt-financed special military fund, intended to modernize the armed forces, bringing the total defense budget to €139 billion.
Defense spending rises to historic levels

The AfD and the socialist Left Party have sharply criticized this. Left Party parliamentary leader Heidi Reichinnek accused the government of pursuing "militarization and boundless rearmament on the one hand, and brutal social cuts and an orgy of budget cuts on the other."

The AfD's Chrupalla said that the temporary reduction in the electricity tax, pushed through at the last minute, would save the average family a mere €100 a year, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy "walks out of the chancellery here in Berlin with a check for €200 million after just one afternoon." "Whose chancellor are you, Mr. Merz?" he asked.

The opposition Greens did not agree. While they also criticized the budget as "unserious," Green Party Bundestag member Britta Haßelmann described the AfD's stance on Ukraine as shameful. She rejected the idea that money was being wasted on Ukraine, saying that supporting Ukraine bolstered security for Germany and Europe.
Aid to Ukraine: Still a central controversy

The chancellor shares this view. "You can't say it often enough, either to the far right or the far left: Russia knows exactly what it wants. And Russia wants more than just Ukraine," Merz said. Russia is escalating tensions in the Baltic region, in Poland, in the Black Sea, and in space. Moscow is also seeking escalation in Germany, even at the cost of lives. "That is why we must show Russia its limits," he said.

But it is becoming increasingly difficult for the government to justify the high spending on Ukraine. Germany's pension and health care costs are only getting bigger: By far the largest single budget item is that of the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs, which is growing to over €200 billion, even with cuts to unemployment benefits.
Social spending growing faster than revenue

Work is currently underway on a reform of the pension system — something that many see as urgent, as the workforce born in the 1960s, when more than a million children were born in Germany every year, is on brink of retiring. Birth rates nearly halved by the mid-1970s and declined even further afterward. For now, so-called "boomers" still make up one-third of the current workforce — but soon they will be drawing pensions.

Even now, Germany's pensions cannot be financed solely with contributions on wages and salaries. In 2025, just over €420 billion in pensions were paid out, with the government contributing €127 billion of that amount. By 2027, the government aims to save €3 billion on this figure, which is likely to further increase pension contributions.
Pension reform becomes a test for the coalition

The coalition parties are stuck in a row over how to reform the pension system. Chancellor Merz insisted in the Bundestag that the coalition was solving the country's fundamental problems, but he warned that in future, tax revenues "will no longer be enough to afford everything we have become all too accustomed to," he said. "All of us here will have to give up some of the ideas we cherish."

The SPD, on the other hand, is counting on increasing federal revenue. SPD parliamentary leader Matthias Miersch emphasized in the Bundestag that large fortunes and inheritances must contribute more to "public costs."

That, he said, must also apply to large companies. Currently, heirs to family-owned businesses often pay significantly less in taxes than heirs to real estate or financial assets, because they can be exempted from inheritance tax if they continue to run the business. This is intended to protect them from having to pay taxes in the event of a breakup or sale of the company.
SPD calls for higher taxes on fortunes

According to Miersch, the government must now think about taxing the wealthy more. "For us, this issue is by no means off the table; on the contrary, we are putting it on the agenda," he said. The government's revenue situation is "an issue we need to discuss."

All in all, the outlook for 2027 is strained — and not just financially. The political differences between the CDU/CSU and the SPD are likely to make working together even more difficult. Conflict is inevitable, especially with several state elections scheduled for the spring.

The chancellor knows this and tried to appear confident that better collaboration was possible: "We must seek compromise in our joint decision-making, represented by these — admittedly quite different — coalition partners," he said.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Lacson alleges House push to remove 'Anti-Epal' clause from 2027 budget
articles.summary: Senator Panfilo Lacson on Wednesday floated that certain members of the House of Representatives are seeking to have the provision barring politicians from the distribution of financial assistance…

blocks.text: Published November 26, 2026 12:02am

Senator Panfilo Lacson on Wednesday floated that certain members of the House of Representatives are seeking to have the provision barring politicians from the distribution of financial assistance removed from the 2027 national budget.

This was raised amid the Senate plenary deliberations on the proposed P253.34 billion budget of the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) and its attached agencies for the next fiscal year.
During the session, Lacson asked budget sponsor Senator Risa Hontiveros if the DSWD has full control over the disbursement of the Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situation (AICS).
Hontiveros, who was taking answers from DSWD Secretary Rex Gatchalian, said the agency is maintaining that it has full control over the decision-making in the AICS program.
“I’m sorry, but I don’t believe that. That's why some congressmen are pushing for the AICS,” Lacson said.
“Actually, meron tayong parang I think forthcoming na bicam. Ito ‘yung sa Bawal Epal, gusto nila tanggalin ‘yung provision eh, sa Bawal Epal. They want to retain that, na merong epal,” he added.

(Actually, I believe there’s a bicameral conference coming up. This is regarding the Anti-Epal provision. They want to remove that provision. They want to retain that there is indeed an epal among them.)

The word “epal” is Filipino slang for someone who wants attention or wants to be noticed, especially in a way that’s inappropriate or self-serving. In politics, it usually refers to officials who take credit for government projects to boost their public image or electoral appeal.
In the 2026 General Appropriations Act (GAA), a so-called "anti-epal" special provision was included, preventing politicians from using government programs, projects, or funds to promote themselves.
Guarantee letters

During the budget deliberations, Lacson likewise questioned a provision in the House version of the 2027 budget bill which he said would allow the settlement of unpaid claims from guarantee letters issued in 2024.
He pointed out that the P34.269 billion allocation for the AICS program under the 2024 GAA had already been fully obligated.
“Ang sinasabi po rito, ‘yung guarantee letters issued in 2024, babayaran sa GAA in 2027. Parang nag-issue ng tseke na walang pondo ng 2024. Popondohan ng GAA ng 2027,” Lacson said.

(It seems that guarantee letters issued in 2024 will be paid for through the GAA in 2027. It’s like saying checks were issued in 2024 without any funds to back them. The 2027 GAA will be the one to pay for it.)

Lacson was referring to Special Provision No. 2 in the House General Appropriations Bill (HGAB), where the DSWD’s proposed budget provides for a “Protective Services Program for Individuals and Families in Difficult Circumstances.”

Under the special provision, the amount appropriated for such “shall likewise be used for the payment of arrears to accredited and/or partner service providers arising from the issuance of guarantee letter in fiscal year 2024, subject to the availability of funds and compliance with applicable budgeting, accounting, and auditing laws, rules and regulations.”
Hontiveros admitted that such information was shocking, but said there were service providers that belatedly filed money claims and submitted supporting documents.
“Kaya ngayon lamang ni-request and special provision na ito sa fiscal year 2027,” she said.
(That’s why this special provision is being requested only now for fiscal year 2027.) —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Philippines misses crown bids in Miss Universe, Miss International
articles.summary: It is a sad day for the Philippines as the delegates of the country in the Miss Universe and Miss International pageants failed to bag the crown.

blocks.text: November 26, 2026 | 12:00am
MANILA, Philippines — It is a sad day for the Philippines as the delegates of the country in the Miss Universe and Miss International pageants failed to bag the crown.
Miss Universe candidate Bea Millan-Windorski was 3rd runner-up while Miss International bet Katrina Anne Johnson made it to the Top 20.
Home court candidate Jennifer Barreto of Puerto Rico won the Miss Universe crown after three hours of competition.
Barreto bested 115 queens with Melissa Núñez of Dominican Republic as 1st runner-up and Clara Vegas of Venezuela as 2nd runner-up.
Bea entered the Top 30 as one of two Asians, along with Kaziah Liz Mejo of India, to make the first cut.
Several Asian delegates were not able to compete this year due to franchise or licensing disputes or withdrawal due to various reasons.
Her flawless pasarela was worthy enough to earn her spot in the Top 12, making her the only Asian candidate still gunning for the crown.
Bea looked ethereal during the evening gown competition with her gown in the color of the “Pearl of the Orient” designed by Anthony Ramirez.
This earned her a spot in the Top 5 and was asked during the Q&A portion: “After 75 years, how will you convince doubters that the Miss Universe pageant is still relevant?”
Bea stressed the need to pass on the wisdom that she learned from the past generation to the future of the world.

“And I would use their wisdom to guide the present so that we could build the kind of future that we all deserve. I would use my experience in the international arena to work with the United Nations to continue my work advocating for climate displaced communities and vulnerable places all around the world,” she added.
In the Final Q&A, Bea emphasized the need for world leaders to listen when asked: “What does the world need most from its leaders right now?”

“As someone who has been an environmentalist my whole life, I wish that our leaders would listen to nature and realize that they have much to learn. I volunteered with sea turtles for the past 10 years and while we’ve often heard of the crab mentality or tearing one another down, the turtle mentality is the opposite,” the beauty queen said.

“The strongest sea turtle hatchlings actually stay behind in the nest to help their weaker brothers and sisters out and into the sea. I wish that our world leaders would embrace the same mentality and realize that when one rises, we all rise,” she added.
After Georgia Waddington of New Zealand was called as 4th runner-up, Bea was called next, giving the Philippines a second consecutive year in the runners-up circle.
Last year, the Philippines’ Ahtisa Manalo also ended her journey as 3rd runner-up, with Mexico’s Fátima Bosch winning the crown.
Bea was aiming to be the Philippines’ fifth Miss Universe titleholder after Catriona Gray (2018), Pia Wurtzbach (2015), Margie Moran (1973) and Gloria Diaz (1969).
In a Facebook post after the pageant ceremony, Windorski said she fought for the country until the very end.
Meanwhile, Johnson has ended her journey in the Miss International 2026 competition in the Top 20, out of more than 70 contestants overall at the competition in Tokyo.
Katrina was at the top of her game with her blue skirt sportswear, which replaces the swimsuit round.
The Filipina queen looked angelic in her white and gold gown and made it to the semifinals, entering the Top 20.
Unfortunately, Katrina failed to enter the Top 10 and the Sustainable Development Goals speech round.
Katrina continued the semifinal streak of the Philippines after Myrna Esguerra was 4th runner-up.
She was aiming for the country’s seventh Miss International crown which was last won in 2016 by Kylie Versoza.

articles.title: Romualdez appeals 90-day suspension order
articles.summary: Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez has asked the Sandiganbayan to reconsider its order imposing a 90-day suspension against him as he faces a P7.4-billion plunder case in connection with alleged kickbacks…

blocks.text: November 26, 2026 | 12:00am
Martin Romualdez on October 24, 2025
The STAR / Ryan Baldemor

MANILA, Philippines — Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez has asked the Sandiganbayan to reconsider its order imposing a 90-day suspension against him as he faces a P7.4-billion plunder case in connection with alleged kickbacks from government infrastructure projects.
In his motion for reconsideration, the former speaker argued that some issues have yet to be resolved, including the validity of the charge filed against him.

Romualdez said the court erred in finding the charge against him valid, considering that the prosecution did not identify a main plunderer, even if a 2016 Supreme Court ruling on the Arroyo v. People case requires that such should be identified when a case is filed against several individuals.

The Leyte lawmaker pointed out that the charges accused him and former Ako Bicol party-list representative Zaldy Co of receiving money and taking undue advantage of their official positions to unjustly enrich themselves.

“It does not state which of the two is the main plunderer. Neither does it state how much of the aggregate P7.4 billion each of them supposedly amassed. This should be resolved before the Information may serve as the basis for preventive suspension,” he said.

He also questioned the court’s finding that the acts attributable to him, his degree of participation where he supposedly gained kickbacks or commissions, are matters to be threshed out during the trial, saying whether those acts have been sufficiently alleged is a question concerning the charge itself.

Romualdez’s co-accused in the P7.4-billion plunder case include former House appropriations chairpman Co, Romualdez’s personal assistant Joselyn Sereño and Felicito Cristobal Guevarra, president of Samchan Foreign Exchange Corp.

articles.title: Marcos wants multisector nutrition project sustained
articles.summary: President Marcos wants a multisectoral nutrition project to continue even after the end of its implementation this year, citing the need to sustain health measures and ensure the delivery of key…

blocks.text: November 26, 2026 | 12:00am

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has urged government agencies and local government units to sustain nutrition and health services for mothers and children beyond the Philippine Multisectoral Nutrition Project (PMNP).
Presidential Communications Office

MANILA, Philippines — President Marcos wants a multisectoral nutrition project to continue even after the end of its implementation this year, citing the need to sustain health measures and ensure the delivery of key services in the midst of a growing population.

Launched in March 2023, the Philippine Multisectoral Nutrition Project aims to bring together health, nutrition, water and sanitation and early childhood services from different sectors and bring resources closer to communities.

The World Bank-supported program, covering prenatal care and micronutrient supplementation for pregnant women, breastfeeding, complementary feeding, improved diets for children and sanitation access, is set to end on Dec. 31.
Speaking at a gathering in Pampanga marking the culmination of the project, Marcos said the government has to continue taking care of children despite leadership changes.

“That’s why Ms. (UNICEF Country Representative Kyungsun) Kim, what you said to us, that each program has an ending, I was just discussing with (Health Secretary) Doc Edwin (Mercado) that we have to find a way so that this program has no ending,” the President said.

“We keep making babies. So, we have to keep taking care of them. It doesn’t matter if we are still here, the LGU (local government unit) changes leadership, we still have to continue, those children still need help,” he added.

Marcos noted that malnutrition remains a serious concern for many families, particularly in vulnerable and underserved communities. In 2025, about one in four Filipino children under five years was stunted, he added.
“We know improving nutrition involves more than providing adequate food. Families need access to health care, clean water, sanitation, other essential services,” the Chief Executive said.
“And the challenge now is ensuring that these services are responsive and consistently delivered, especially in communities where they are needed the most.”

Marcos said the nutrition project has reached 6.17 million beneficiaries in 235 participating municipalities. He reported that 549,000 children under five have been tracked and eventually served while 134 participating municipalities have recorded significant reductions in stunting after two years.

articles.title: AFP confirms China plane in West Philippine Sea
articles.summary: The Armed Forces of the Philippines yesterday confirmed it has monitored a Chinese H-6 strategic bomber plane over the West Philippine Sea this week.

blocks.text: November 26, 2026 | 12:00am
This file photo shows a Chinese Xian H-6 bomber flying over the sea near Japan in late 2025.
MANILA, Philippines — The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) yesterday confirmed it has monitored a Chinese H-6 strategic bomber plane over the West Philippine Sea (WPS) this week.
The Chinese plane was observed between Bajo de Masinloc and Luzon, 170 nautical miles away from Metro Manila.

At the Kapihan sa Manila Prince Hotel forum, AFP spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea retired Rear Admiral Roy Vincent Trinidad said the improved surveillance and monitoring capabilities helped in monitoring the aircraft.
He said the aircraft’s presence was not a reason for concern as there is no indication that the aircraft was rehearsing for a missile strike.
“It only shows that the entire PLA (People’s Liberation Army) is now flexing its muscles. Their patrols before were closer to the mainland of China. Today, they almost reach us,” he said.

Meanwhile, the Philippine Coast Guard managed to avoid a dangerous maneuver made by China while authorities repelled two illegally anchored ships off Panata Island, Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela, PCG spokesman for the West Philippine Sea, said on Tuesday.

According to Tarriela, the PCG deployed BRP Cabra and its rigid-hull inflatable boat to drive away Chinese maritime militia vessels, which were anchored about five nautical miles from the Philippine-occupied feature. A China Coast Guard ship was also present in the area during the incident.
Meanwhile, PCG Commandant Admiral Rommel Supangan led the commissioning of three additional vessels into Coast Guard service to further strengthen the organization’s operational capabilities.

PCG spokesperson Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said the BRP Patag, BRP Pag-asa and BRP Kalikasan were put into service yesterday at the National Headquarters in Port Area, Manila, in line with the celebration of Coast Guard Fleet’s 62nd anniversary. — Andrew Ronquillo, Bella Cariaso

articles.title: Senate cuts P19.8 billion budget for 2 ayuda programs
articles.summary: The Senate has slashed P19.8 billion from two major cash aid programs to raise the subsidy for Philippine Health Insurance Corp. to P94.2 billion under the proposed national budget for next year,…

blocks.text: November 26, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The Senate has slashed P19.8 billion from two major cash aid programs to raise the subsidy for Philippine Health Insurance Corp. (PhilHealth) to P94.2 billion under the proposed national budget for next year, Senate finance committee chairman JV Ejercito said yesterday.

In a chance interview with reporters before the start of plenary deliberations on the budget, Ejercito said the panel cut P9.9 billion each from the Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations and the Medical Assistance Program, reallocating the funds to boost PhilHealth’s subsidy from the P73 billion approved in the House of Representatives’ General Appropriations Bill.

“The ayuda partly we will slash and place much of it in PhilHealth. Therefore, PhilHealth’s subsidy will increase by almost P20 billion,” he said. “We were targeting P100 billion, but the fiscal space is tight.”

Alongside a higher PhilHealth subsidy, Ejercito said the Senate increased funding for zero-balance billing, as well as for preventive care such as immunization and health promotion and for the Health Facilities Enhancement Program to upgrade provincial and locally funded hospitals.

He also said the Senate is pushing for a wrap-up of plenary debates by tomorrow so as to avoid a Saturday session, out of consideration for exhausted staff who had to work overtime from 1 p.m. Tuesday to 2 a.m. yesterday. The bicameral conference is tentatively set for Dec. 9 or 10.

Also yesterday, the Senate swiftly approved the budgets of the Office of the Ombudsman at P8.262 billion and the Commission on Elections at P29.163 billion. Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla and Comelec Chairman George witnessed the chamber’s approval of their budgets.
Ping: P600 million wasted

Sen. Panfilo Lacson, meanwhile, revealed that roughly P600 million in public funds has been wasted on commitment fees and penalties for unimplemented foreign-assisted projects (FAPs), with the realigned allocations likely ending up in anomalous flood control projects.
In posts on X, Lacson blamed congressional realignments for stalling the projects, leaving taxpayers shouldering the penalties incurred.

“During our budget plenary debates last Monday, it was revealed that we already paid $1.5 million and $8 million in commitment fees and penalties because foreign-assisted projects were not implemented. This may be because Congress moved the funds elsewhere using its ‘power of the purse.’ Together, that’s about P600 million of public money wasted,” Lacson said.
“And worse, we have good reason to suspect, most probably, the realigned FAP funds went to some ghost and substandard flood control projects,” he added.
Ejercito disclosed during Monday’s budget deliberations that the government paid $1.5 million in commitment fees in 2024 and $8 million in 2025.

“Wasted. Is that good economic sense? Definitely not. And these are long-term, high-impact projects. Not implemented because Congress realigned the budget,” Lacson said, noting that there is still time for lawmakers to restore FAP allocations to their original National Expenditure Program (NEP) levels in the 2027 budget bill.

While the Senate restored the overall 2027 FAP allocation to P459.16 billion from the House’s P328.45 billion, Lacson noted that the chamber altered the funding mix – increasing unprogrammed support to P102.34 billion from the NEP’s P42.55 billion, while reducing loan proceeds to P223.41 billion (from P271.22 billion) as well as counterpart funds to P133.4 billion from P145.37 billion.
He cited the Laguna Lakeshore Road Network, whose P35.209-billion NEP allocation was cut by the House to P8.209 billion and only partially restored by the Senate to P22.209 billion.
Earlier, Lacson proposed an overhaul of the 2027 budget by scrapping P54 billion for multipurpose buildings (MPBs) and P85 billion in fragmented cash aid outside the 4Ps program.
His team has detected multiple appropriations for 30 MPBs and double funding for a Zamboanga flood control project.

“This is the time when Congress has to make some sacrifice. The ball is in our court. We must do our part,” he said. “Can we at least do our part for nation building, (for) economic growth instead of the usual more of the same misplaced priorities?”
Unfinished classrooms
During budget deliberations last Tuesday, it was revealed that only about 500 of the 18,950 classrooms targeted for 2026 have been completed and put to use.

Pressed by Sen. Imee Marcos on the status of the classroom-building program, DepEd budget sponsor Sen. Bam Aquino confirmed that while the rest are still undergoing construction or bidding, only a fraction has been turned over and opened to students.
Marcos expressed frustration over the sluggish pace despite last year’s record education allocation.

“What was allocated last year was so big, it was really a blockbuster last year, first time in history. Then there was finger-pointing, there was blame game. Huge money, and then nothing. Still, no classroom, why? That’s the question,” she said.

Aquino explained that of the P21.45 billion assigned to the Department of Public Works and Highways for 6,000 classrooms, only P7 billion has been transferred so far and only one of three lots has been subjected to bidding, with DPWH conducting its own validation on top of DepEd’s.
Education Secretary Sonny Angara thanked the Senate for approving the department’s P915.49- billion budget.

“We are deeply grateful to Sen. Bam Aquino and the entire Senate for keeping our learners front and center during these budget talks. Every peso we invest in basic education goes straight to where it matters most: safer classrooms, well-nourished kids and better equipment and resources for our teachers,” Angara said. — Bella Cariaso

articles.title: After 12 years, man receives P12.3 million lotto jackpot
articles.summary: A man who spent more than a decade fighting for his P12.39-million lotto jackpot received his prize yesterday, despite his winning ticket having been partially burned by a flat iron.

blocks.text: November 26, 2026 | 12:00am

Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office (PCSO) general manager Mel Robles turned over the P12,391,600 check to Antonio Mendoza, whose ticket won the Lotto 6/42 draw on Oct. 2, 2014, at the agency’s headquarters in Mandaluyong.
Contributed photo

MANILA, Philippines — A man who spent more than a decade fighting for his P12.39-million lotto jackpot received his prize yesterday, despite his winning ticket having been partially burned by a flat iron.
The release of the prize followed a final Supreme Court ruling and an authorization from the Commission on Audit.

Mendoza’s ordeal began after his granddaughter crumpled the winning ticket. His daughter tried to straighten it by ironing it with a piece of cloth, but the ticket became blackened, leaving only portions of its details visible.
The damaged ticket retained the first digits of three number combinations, the lotto outlet, draw and purchase dates and part of the purchase time.

Mendoza presented the ticket to the PCSO on Oct. 5, 2014 and submitted an affidavit explaining what happened. The agency, however, informed him that it could not award the prize because the ticket could no longer be validated.
He sued the PCSO after the agency failed to pay him despite a recommendation from the House of Representatives committee on games and amusements that the prize be awarded to him.
In a decision issued in September 2023, the Supreme Court’s Second Division denied the PCSO’s petition challenging lower court rulings in Mendoza’s favor.
The court ruled that Mendoza had sufficiently established that he selected the winning six-number combination, saying the lotto ticket served as proof of the bettor’s chosen numbers.

It also held that the PCSO’s rules were ambiguous on whether possession of a complete physical ticket was an absolute requirement for payment and that secondary evidence could be considered because the original ticket was damaged.

articles.title: Education curriculum includes CPR, first aid
articles.summary: Life-saving cardiopulmonary resuscitation, first aid and basic life support training have been integrated across the basic education curriculum to equip students with the confidence and skills needed…

blocks.text: November 26, 2026 | 12:00am
In a statement, DepEd Secretary Sonny Angara emphasized that teaching life-saving skills is fundamentally about protecting loved ones and caring for one another in critical moments.
Pixabay / FatCamera

MANILA, Philippines — Life-saving cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), first aid and basic life support training have been integrated across the basic education curriculum to equip students with the confidence and skills needed to assist in emergencies, the Department of Education said yesterday.

DepEd said Republic Act 10871, commonly known as the Samboy Lim Law, is embedded across basic education through the Revised K-10 Physical Education and Health curriculum and the strengthened senior high school (SHS) program.
The curriculum establishes a progressive, age-appropriate learning continuum from elementary through SHS.

Elementary learners in Grades 4 to 6 start with foundational safety awareness and basic injury prevention. In junior high school, learners build on these basics by mastering first aid principles and immediate care for common injuries, environmental emergencies and road and water safety. By Grade 10, learners gain practical training in basic life support and emergency care procedures.

In SHS, subject to school offerings and partner programs, learners undergo training in responder-level skills, such as compression-only CPR, automated external defibrillator operation, rescue breathing, foreign body airway obstruction maneuvers and mass casualty response protocols, with an opportunity to earn official certification from recognized and accredited health organizations.

“We are working to provide hands-on training for our teachers and ensure that schools are adequately equipped, ultimately aiming for a point where helping others and sustaining life becomes second nature to every student,” Angara said.

DepEd encouraged Schools Division offices to maximize available local funds and build public-private and community partnerships, such as with the Department of Health, local government units and accredited health organizations, to standardize training, expand access to life-support equipment and help schools and communities respond promptly during emergencies.

articles.title: Flood control back; House vows no ghost, substandard projects
articles.summary: Despite the massive flak lawmakers have received, House leaders yesterday confirmed that flood control projects have been restored in the 2027 national budget and gave assurance there will be no…

blocks.text: November 26, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Despite the massive flak lawmakers have received, House leaders yesterday confirmed that flood control projects have been restored in the 2027 national budget and gave assurance there will be no irregularities.

Speaking on behalf of the House leadership, Deputy Speaker Janette Garin said flood control projects must continue to protect lives, livelihoods and the economy without compromising transparency and accountability.
“We believe that the House and the Senate will be united in our call for effective budget implementation – no substandard, no ghost and no overpriced projects,” Garin said yesterday.

The assurance came a day after the House approved on third and final reading House Bill 11602, or the proposed Metro Manila Flood Control and Drainage System Management Act, which would establish a unified flood control and drainage master plan for the metropolis.
Principally authored by Rep. Sandro Marcos, HB 11602 secured 212 affirmative votes, with no negative votes or abstentions.

Its passage came amid the restoration of P107.4 billion in proposed flood control funding under the Department of Public Works and Highways’ budget for fiscal year 2027, subject to final congressional approval.
More bills OKd

On Tuesday, the House approved several measures on third and final reading, including bills strengthening the Safe Spaces Act (or Bawal Bastos law) and lowering to 56 from 60 the retirement age of government personnel.

HB 10995’s proposed early optional retirement age aligns with the retirement age in the military, which is now 57 years, and in the Philippine National Police, which is 56 years for uniformed personnel.
HB 11264, meanwhile, imposes tougher penalties for gender-based sexual harassment and criminalizes grooming to better protect children from sexual abuse and exploitation.
Grooming is punishable by imprisonment or fines of up to P600,000, or both, regardless of whether the act leads to actual sexual abuse or exploitation, according to the bill.
Imprisonment shall be mandatory if the perpetrator is an adult and the victim is a child.
The measure imposes imprisonment or fines of up to P500,000, or both, for gender-based sexual harassment in workplaces and educational and training institutions.
Public officials and state workers who promote or encourage sexual harassment and misogynistic, transphobic, homophobic and sexist slurs will face stiff penalties.
First-time offenders face fines of up to P200,000 and mandatory suspension without pay for at least six months.
Repeat offenders face fines of up to P300,000, mandatory dismissal from office and disqualification from holding any public position for at least five years.

To combat online sexual harassment, the measure requires internet intermediaries to remove or block access to offending digital content within 24 hours of receiving a notice or lawful order from a competent authority.
Lower sodium

Health advocates and families of children with kidney disease have renewed calls for the passage of the Iwas Alat, Iwas Sakit bill requiring food manufacturers to gradually reduce sodium content in prepackaged products, citing the need to prevent chronic illnesses among Filipinos at an early age.

“Kidney health begins in childhood. By promoting healthy eating habits, reducing excessive sodium intake and encouraging healthier lifestyles early in life, we lay the foundation for preventing kidney disease and other chronic illnesses in adulthood,” said Johnny Tamon of the Philippine Society of Nephrology.

Kim Louise Areño, a registered nurse and representative of ImagineLaw, said educating children and their families about healthy lifestyles should be complemented by policies that improve access to healthier food products. — Christine Boton

articles.title: 9.8 million families poor, 5.8 million experienced hunger – OCTA
articles.summary: Self-rated poverty hardly moved in the third quarter of the year, with an estimated 9.8 million Filipino families rating themselves poor, a survey by the OCTA Research group showed.

blocks.text: November 26, 2026 | 12:00am
From 39 percent in July, self-rated poverty was at 37 percent in the latest survey conducted from Sept. 28 to Oct. 4.
STAR / Ryan Baldemor

MANILA, Philippines — Self-rated poverty hardly moved in the third quarter of the year, with an estimated 9.8 million Filipino families rating themselves poor, a survey by the OCTA Research group showed.
OCTA said this translates to an estimated 9.8 million poor families, from approximately 10.3 million in the previous survey.
Those who said their families were not poor increased from 18 percent to 21 percent, while those who can’t say if their families are poor or not remained at 42 percent.

Like in previous polls, self-rated poverty was highest among those in Mindanao at 56 percent (from 58 percent), followed by those in the Visayas at 49 percent (from 46 percent), balance Luzon at 26 percent (from 33 percent) and Metro Manila at 20 percent (from 18 percent).
“The Q3 results show national self-rated poverty holding at the elevated level reached in Q2; the two-point difference is within the margin of error and should not be read as a decline,” OCTA said.

“The persistently high incidence in Mindanao and among Class E households underscores the continued vulnerability of lower-income families and the need for targeted measures that strengthen household incomes, employment stability and protection against rising living costs,” it added.
Hunger rate
The latest poll also showed almost similar hunger incidence rate from the previous quarter, from 21 percent to 22 percent.
OCTA said this translates to an estimated 5.8 million families, from 5.6 million in July.
Meanwhile, 78 percent said they did not experience hunger in the past three months, from 79 percent.

Across areas, hunger incidence was highest among those in the Visayas and Metro Manila at 29 percent (from 17 percent and 19 percent, respectively), followed by those in rest of Luzon at 21 percent (from 27 percent) and Mindanao at 16 percent (from 14 percent).
“These results show that the steady national figure conceals different patterns across the country. The increases in NCR and the Visayas contrast with the decline in balance Luzon,” OCTA said.
The survey had 1,200 respondents and a margin of error of plus/minus three percent.

articles.title: VP: The majority won’t support me if I’m wrong
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte has maintained her innocence, saying she still enjoys the support of the majority of the people despite all the accusations hurled against her before the Senate…

blocks.text: November 26, 2026 | 12:00am
Vice President Sara Duterte led the commemoration of the 128th Araw ng Kalayaan at Rizal Park in Davao City on June 12, 2026.
Facebook / Inday Sara Duterte

MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte has maintained her innocence, saying she still enjoys the support of the majority of the people despite all the accusations hurled against her before the Senate impeachment court.
In an interview with Politiko, Duterte said she continues to draw strength from her followers amid speculative reports that the senator-judges have made up their minds ahead of the final verdict.
“I think that God would not have put me here if He didn’t have a purpose, right? God is not that unreasonable. I trust His purpose. I have faith. He is there somewhere watching,” Duterte said.
Reports said senators have secured the numbers to convict the Vice President, currently facing serious allegations of unexplained wealth.
“Even with so many attacks, so much mudslinging, the people are still there, especially in 2016, 2019, 2022. Last year, they helped. They didn’t leave, they didn’t give up,” Duterte added.

Certain legal quarters have said Duterte could resign before a guilty verdict is reached to spare her from the penalty of disqualification from public office. Resignation will then allow her to pursue her presidential bid in 2028. “It gives me confidence that I am right because how can the majority be there for me if I am wrong? That means the majority is wrong. So that gives me confidence that I am right, because the people are there,” Duterte noted.
Other legal experts, however, said disqualification from public office automatically goes hand-in-hand with conviction.
The impeachment court will resume trial sessions on Dec. 1, as the tribunal targets a final judgment before Congress adjourns on Dec. 18.
Defense spokesman Michael Poa said the legal team of Duterte is expected to present at least five to six witnesses in the coming weeks.
Thanksgiving
The Vice President and her allies, including former president and Pampanga Rep. Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo, gathered over the weekend for a thanksgiving party.

During the Kapihan sa Manila Bay forum, Bagong Henerasyon (BH) party-list Rep. Robert Nazal and his wife, former representative Bernadette Herrera, confirmed that the occasion was held in their house.

“Basically, she probably just wanted to thank her supporters, especially those (congressmen) who voted no to the impeachment. She conducts thanksgiving every year, when Christmas is approaching. It was like an early celebration of the Christmas season for those who helped her,” Nazal said.
For her part, Herrera said some of the allies of Duterte were not able to attend the get-together as they were abroad.

“Because it was a last-minute thing, many were out of the country because every year, she organizes a get-together so she just wanted to gather politicians first because every year, she really invites different sectors,” Herrera noted.
According to Herrera, the ongoing impeachment trial was not discussed.
“She told us, she just wanted to get together, no politics. She didn’t want to talk about politics. She just wanted to say thank you,” Herrera said.
She added that Duterte also held a thanksgiving party for bloggers who support her.
“The bloggers were invited to the Vice President’s office,” she said.
Herrera said Duterte does not want to discuss politics until the impeachment trial is over.

articles.title: U.S. army blows up bomb chemicals in Iowa despite fears toxic plume could endanger residents
articles.summary: The U.S. army intentionally blew up the nation's entire stockpile of lead azide at an ammunition plant in southeastern Iowa on Wednesday, after officials said the degraded materials were at risk of…

image.caption: The U.S. army detonates a degraded stockpile of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, on Nov. 25, 2026. (Jim Urquhart/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

The U.S. army intentionally blew up the nation's entire stockpile of lead azide at an ammunition plant in southeastern Iowa on Wednesday, after officials said the degraded materials were at risk of exploding uncontrollably as temperatures cooled.
Environmentalists voiced concern about possible health, ecological effects of controlled detonation

The U.S. army intentionally blew up the nation's entire stockpile of lead azide at an ammunition plant in southeastern Iowa on Wednesday after officials said the five tons of degraded bomb-making materials were at risk of exploding uncontrollably as temperatures cooled.
The controlled detonation set off concerns about potential health and environmental impacts from lead dust, and frustration over a lack of information.

Video footage from several miles away showed two white plumes rolling over the detonation site before the clouds quickly dissipated. Journalists reported hearing a loud boom at the same time, around 9 a.m.
Despite warnings to stay inside, some residents pulled to the side of a road to watch the blast upwind from the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown.

Schools that weren't already closed for the Thanksgiving holiday cancelled classes, and a gas station near the detonation site posted a note on the front door saying they'd be back open once it's safe. Some residents sealed their windows and doors as a precaution.

The blast was originally planned for last Friday. The army changed the detonation date three times amid public backlash and to allow more time for safety measures and favourable wind, according to court documents.
Why the U.S. army is about to blow up 5 tons of lead explosives in Iowa | About That

The weather forecast around the time of the blast called for a gentle breeze to the southwest and temperatures around the freezing mark. One of the concerns has been that the stockpile would become volatile as temperatures dropped.
"Inaction is no longer an option," said Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, the army's leader of the operation.

Government officials encouraged residents within five miles (eight kilometres) of the site to evacuate to avoid lead dust in the air, while also assuring them that barriers around the blast zone should limit much of the plume from the detonation.

Officials overseeing the detonation said the wind on Wednesday was expected to carry the plume southwest toward Missouri and away from nearby Burlington, a city of just under 25,000 people that sits along the Mississippi River.
But hundreds of homes and farms could still be in the path of a toxic dust cloud laced with lead — a metal that's not safe at any level and is especially dangerous to children and pregnant women.
Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said the public should not panic.
The army set up additional "blast barriers" around the bunkers where the 68 barrels of lead azide were detonated. The materials were surrounded by concrete and sand barriers two stories high.
Ballistic gels and foams were intended to absorb the lead dust, and the army planed to douse the materials with more than 100,000 gallons (379,000 litres) of water to tamp down the plume.
A video of the site released by the army showed the bunker encased by an earth berm and sand-filled blocks.
Spontaneous detonation a concern

The country's stockpile of lead azide was brought to the Iowa location from bases around the country in 2009, according to Robert Cekada, director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. The chemicals, used in munitions production, were stored in barrels in case the military needed to use them again.

During an inspection in March, staff at the ammunition plant found the lead azide had partially crystallized, making it sensitive to friction and cold temperatures and creating the risk of spontaneous detonation.
The army assembled experts to formulate a plan, and they found that alternative solutions like thermal treatment and neutralizing the drums' contents were not as safe as a controlled detonation.

items: U.S. army says it will detonate Iowa bomb-making material Wednesday, after court's approval

blocks.text: Environmental groups filed a lawsuit to halt the plan, but a court ruling on Monday put the detonation back on track. A federal appeals court found the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency adequately incorporated safeguards to minimize the dispersal of lead dust.

Residents expressed a mix of concern and resignation. Some said the timing could be better, given that it is happening the day before Thanksgiving, but acknowledged it needed to be dealt with now. Others worried about the impact on water, farms, animals and their own homes.

"I don't think lead danger goes away any time soon," said Lucy Giehl, who lives nearby in West Burlington. "It seems someone might have thought about all of this a little sooner before it came to this."

articles.title: Canadian astronaut welcomes baby girl from space station
articles.summary: Joshua Kutryk, currently on his first space mission, is just the fourth astronaut in history to miss the birth of a child while aboard the International Space Station.

blocks.text: A Canadian astronaut aboard the International Space Station is celebrating the birth of his third child from hundreds of miles above Earth.
Joshua Kutryk and his wife, Heather Kutryk, welcomed their daughter as the astronaut takes part in a six-month space mission that began in October, the Canadian Space Agency announced on Tuesday.
"Even with the distance between us, we feel incredibly connected as we welcome our new little star into our lives," said the couple in a statement shared by the agency.
Joshua Kutryk, currently on his first space mission, is just the fourth astronaut in history to miss the birth of a child while aboard the International Space Station.
The couple have two older children, aged five and seven.
"We are very proud of our growing family and are looking forward to getting our little crew of five all reunited."
In a statement, the couple said that Joshua's spaceflight was a "childhood dream" come true.

"We hope to show our children that big dreams are worth pursuing, that hard work and determination matter, and that with the support of family and a strong community, extraordinary things are possible," they said.
Prior to becoming an astronaut, Kutryk, from Fort Saskatchewan, Alberta, was a fighter pilot and a colonel in the Royal Canadian Air Force. He was recruited by the Canadian Space Agency in 2017.
Kutryk was the only Canadian selected to be part of NASA's SpaceX Crew-13 mission, where four astronauts are conducting scientific experiments and testing new technologies in space.
The crew also includes two US astronauts, Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins, and one Russian astronaut, Sergey Teteryatnikov.
Before their take off on 1 October, Heather Kutryk told Canada's public broadcaster CBC News that her family had been preparing for years before the mission, saying it was "a long time coming".
Heather added that her pregnancy was "not exactly planned" but that it was "a great thing".
"I'm not that stressed out. I feel like we have a really good community. I feel well supported by both CSA and Nasa," she said.
"It's six months, I feel like we'll be fine."

In a separate interview with BBC's US news partner CBS News, Joshua Kutryk said he hopes his new child will look at her dad's mission as "making some sacrifice, taking some risk, but doing so in the name of public service and the name, in my case, for Canada."

articles.title: Brussels on split-screen: where it flexes – and where it bends
articles.summary: From a choreographed summit that dominated Westminster but barely registered in Brussels to a climate showdown in Turkey, last week revealed the EU’s priorities – and the limits of its collective…

blocks.text: Two very different European diplomatic dramas played out almost simultaneously last week. On Friday, a tightly choreographed EU-UK summit transfixed London, while barely registering on the continent. On Sunday, Cop31 collapsed after a united EU forcefully vetoed a watered-down climate pact, even as it relaxed its own green rules at home.
What do these two events reveal about the EU: how it works, what takes up its bandwidth, how it exercises its clout – and where it’s vulnerable?
Part 1: The 95% British summit
If you were a consumer of most British media last Friday morning, you could have been forgiven for thinking Britain was going to rejoin the EU before lunchtime.

Live blogs tracked Andy Burnham’s every step in the Europa building, as he arrived for a summit that Downing Street billed as a landmark “reset” but that was actually aimed at sealing a package of relatively narrow post-Brexit fixes. A Cabinet Office “mythbuster” assured voters the forthcoming deal wouldn’t ban smoky-flavoured crisps. Westminster was plunged into passionate debate over whether a technical three-part trade package was a Brexit betrayal by instalments, or a national reckoning.

Across the Channel, the UK’s domestic psychodrama was, well, no big deal. For Le Monde, the only question that mattered about the EU-UK summit – and the one that remains unanswered – was “what does Britain actually want?” For Germany’s FAZ, a “swift UK return” to the EU was in any case “an illusion”.

It was a fair reflection of where things stand. For Britain, the EU remains its single largest trading partner, and the deals to ease border checks on food, link carbon markets and launch a capped youth experience scheme marked domestic progress – politically and, hopefully, economically.

By Monday, indeed, Burnham was touring a supermarket, touting a victory in the battle against the cost of living. For the EU, however, the UK remains a third country like many others. It has bigger fish to fry than the paperwork mountains involved in the UK exporting cheddar (or importing chorizo).

That doesn’t mean the EU is indifferent to London, just that its priorities lie elsewhere. Westminster obsesses over food checks; Brussels is more interested in the hard-power domains where the UK is a valuable, even indispensable partner.

Both sides have moved to integrate the UK into EU military mobility networks and deepen support for Kyiv. They are looking into closer electricity market integration, and operational intelligence sharing on issues such as smuggling gangs.

Beyond those strategic interests, the EU largely saw Friday’s summit as theatre for Britons: a not-too-demanding EU contribution to the delicate Downing Street balancing act that aims to boost struggling businesses and placate pro-EU voters, without handing too much ammunition to the Conservatives or Nigel Farage.

The European Commission and Council presidents played their parts with aplomb. But the harsh underlying reality was that while London was quick to hail a “done deal”, EU member states let it gently be known that actually, no, a dispute over university tuition fees would have to be resolved first.

And beneath it all lay a barely concealed European frustration: Britain keeps submitting shopping lists of bespoke, sector-by-sector fixes, without ever deciding what long-term relationship it really wants. Thinktanks in Paris (Ifri) and London (Institute for Government) made the point: the UK is trapped in what might be called an “incrementalism loop”.

Europe values the UK as a nuclear-armed neighbour, a North Sea energy partner and a security ally. Beyond that, it is not the main character in Europe’s story. So while London decides whether it wants long-term third-country status, Swiss-style dynamic alignment, or a return to the single market, customs union – or even the EU – Brussels won’t lose much sleep waiting for the answer.
Part 2: Heroes or hypocrites?
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Activists unsatisfied with the second draft text at Cop31 hold a silent protest outside the plenary hall. Photograph: Kaan Soyturk/Reuters

blocks.text: If the UK summit showed the EU more or less on autopilot, the concluding hours of Cop31 in Antalya, Turkey, showed it exercising some raw institutional muscle – and, simultaneously, exposing its sharpest internal contradictions.

When Cop31 ended almost 48 hours over deadline – making it the longest UN climate summit in history – the headlines were all about what wasn’t there: no overarching pact, because no mention of fossil fuels.

At the centre of the collapse stood the 27 EU member states. Facing intense pressure to sign a watered-down “Antalya pact”, Brussels held firm alongside the UK and vulnerable island nations, formally objecting and pulling the plug on the centrepiece agreement.

The bloc stayed together thanks to three mechanisms. First, EU climate negotiators had – unlike on foreign policy – a binding mandate agreed by environment ministers in October, locking in red lines to defend the bloc’s 2023 pledge to transition away from fossil fuels.

Second, the EU’s climate commissioner, Wopke Hoekstra, and Ireland’s Darragh O’Brien, representing the bloc’s rotating council presidency, worked in tandem, leaving little room for wedges between the Brussels bureaucrats and national capitals.

Finally, member states shared the same economic self-interest. Having already priced carbon at home and rolled out a Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, even conservative EU governments had no wish to let international competitors off the hook.

Look closer, though, and it all gets a bit more conflicted. EU finance ministers had strictly boxed in new funding, leaving the bloc demanding maximum ambition on emissions while offering minimum movement on money. To developing nations, European unity looked less like principled leadership and more like a coordinated refusal to pay its share.

Even more striking was the timing back home. As Brussels was lecturing the world on fossil fuel ambition in Turkey, EU lawmakers were finalising a two-year delay to the bloc’s own flagship methane rules for oil and gas importers – giving in to fierce lobbying from fossil fuel companies and the Trump administration.

For Brussels, speaking with one voice in Antalya proved it absolutely can draw global red lines. But it might have a harder time ensuring the green standards it defends with such principle abroad are not quietly dismantled at home.

articles.title: EU must set out a new timeline for cage-free farming, court rules
articles.summary: European General Court ruled that the European Commission has failed to set out a timeline after pledging to end caged farming by the end of 2023.

image.caption: The European Commission pledged to pass a legislation in 2021 after 1,4 million people signed a petition to end caged farmingImage: Felix Kästle/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A European Union (EU) court told the bloc on Wednesday to draw a new timeline for plans to ban cages for farm animals.
Judges at the European General Court ruled that the EU has failed to follow through on a pledge to ban the practice.

In 2021, the European Commission set out the goal to pass a legislation by the end of 2023 to stop farmers from cooping hens, rabbits, sows and other animals in cages. The move came after 1,4 million people signed a petition.
But it failed to follow up on the pledge. This resulted in the campaigners requesting a new timeline and eventually led to a court case when that was also not happening.
The Luxembourg-based General Court, the European Union's second-highest, on Wednesday ruled in favor of the animal rights campaigners.
Cage-free: India's movement for eco-friendly egg farming
"The Commission is under an obligation — which is not limited in time — to set out a timeline for all the measures which it intends to take in response to such an initiative," the court said.

According to the "European citizens' initiative" system, the Commission has to receive the petitions that gather over one million signatures across at least seven bloc countries. However, it is not obligated to meet the demands.
The court noted that if the Commission decides to take action, it has to keep the public and the European Parliament posted on a timeline in accordance with the principle of "good administration."
About 143 million chickens are kept in cages in EU
The Commission said it was analyzing the ruling before making a decision. It can still appeal the ruling.

It has previously stated an intention to put forward a proposal for the phased elimination of cage systems for chickens by the end of this year, as well as a separate proposal to transition from farrowing crates to pen-based systems for pigs by 2027.
According to the Albert Schweitzer Foundation, no timetable has been set for calves, rabbits, ducks, geese and quail.
In the EU, about 143 million egg-laying chickens are kept in cages while the majority of female pigs spend at least part of their lives caged.
The use of cage systems in agricultural production accredited as "organic" is already prohibited in the EU.
Butchers against factory farming

articles.title: Nigeria's upcoming election marred by rising AI disinformation
articles.summary: As Nigeria inches closer to the 2027 polls, the use of artificial intelligence in the electoral process has prompted questions about integrity and institutional readiness. Can Nigerians trust their…

image.caption: Nigeria's 2027 general election will take place against the backdrop of AI-driven disinformationImage: Adekunle Ajayi/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Nigeria has just over two months to go until its general election, with incumbent Bola Tinubu running on a ticket focused on combating raging insecurity and resolving the nation's economic crisis. He faces off against former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and senior opposition figure Peter Obi.

The country's electoral body, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), recently released its preliminary voter's register, which reportedly is riddled with images believed to have been generated using artificial intelligence (AI).

Among the telltale signs of AI usage were exaggerated facial features in images and inconsistencies on the electoral registers, such as duplicates of names and even identities of people who since the previous election had died.

The development raises concerns about the body's overall preparedness ahead of the country's upcoming 2027 general election. Instead of making the upcoming vote more transparent by allowing access to its procedures, INEC has come under fire amid broader controversies about the expanding influence of AI in elections across the continent.
Is Nigeria becoming a one-party state?
Fake news: Nothing new in Nigeria
Joash Amupitan, the chairman of the electoral commission, said the body is now investigating the development, focusing on discrepancies potentially created by AI use.

To this end, he announced the establishment of a dedicated unit to monitor AI-related threats, detect deepfakes and strengthen the integrity of the electoral process, warning that the credibility of the upcoming election could otherwise be under attack.

blocks.caption: Supporters of a particular candidate in the election can be easily manipulated to believe AI-driven fake newsImage: Sani Maikatanga/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: However, even prior to the proliferation of AI across Africa and the globe, this would not be the first time that Nigeria has found itself in the unfortunate position of having to deal with the circulation of fabricated images, doctored audio and fake videos online. In the run-up to the 2023 election, deepfakes falsely linking candidates to terror-related activities filled social media platforms.

These are often designed to promote certain candidates or to discredit opponents in a bid to influence public perception, which now with the use of AI could create disinformation campaigns of new proportions.
Artificial intelligence has various effects on voter behavior
Lois Ugbede, the assistant editor at the factchecking platform DUBAWA, told DW that "based on our monitoring so far, AI-driven disinformation is serious and is becoming commonplace."

"This could influence political discourse and voter behavior ahead of 2027 because we are already seeing parties using inflated crowds to show that they have a large followership or support," she added.
Have some elections become an empty ritual?

At the same time, rather than influencing the vote in favor of any particular candidate, "the deeper danger is that people may begin to doubt authentic information simply because they know convincing AI-generated fakes are possible," said Akintunde Babatunde, executive director of the Abuja-based Centre for Journalism, Innovation and Development.

"We often focus on the risk of people believing an AI-generated falsehood, but there is another problem where genuine evidence can be dismissed as AI-generated," he noted, citing instances of a lawmaker who recently made inflammatory remarks during a campaign rally — but then claimed the clips were manipulated.
Further pitfalls behind a lack of safeguards against AI

Chibuike Mgbeahuruike, an election consultant at the Centre for Democracy and Development, told DW that apart from the spread of synthetic content online, AI intrusion into the electoral commission's portal could also "undermine its institutional credibility, especially with the low level of confidence that we are already witnessing."

He added, however, that AI itself is not inherently a threat to electoral integrity. The real threat lies in "the absence of effective accountability for its deployment," as innovations in tech increasingly appear to infiltrate governments and their democratic processes.
"Voters must have confidence … that the technology is also transparent, accountable and independently scrutinized, and ultimately subject to human and institutional oversight," said Mgbeahuruike.

blocks.caption: Journalists can be just as susceptible to disinformation created by AI and other technologiesImage: Emmanuel Osodi/AA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Mallam Jibrin Baba Ndace, the director-general of state-owned broadcaster Voice of Nigeria, agrees, urging journalists at a recent conference also to not fall into the trap of believing reports, which later could turn out to be false due to AI manipulation.

He stressed the importance of protection measures and due diligence in news media, with the growing inability of public institutions like INEC to provide impartial information due to the use and influence of AI and other election-related tech.
Nigeria's marred relationship with new tech
Beyond AI, Nigeria's electoral processes have undergone various technological shifts over the years in hopes of improving transparency while increasing efficiency.

Electoral authorities first deployed electronic assistance in 2011, when Direct Data Capture Machines were introduced; the devices collect voters' biometrics by scanning fingerprints or capturing facial recognition data with webcams to stop voters from submitting multiple ballots.

Ten years later, a system called the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) was introduced as the new standard, designed to combine fingerprints with facial recognition. However, during the 2023 general election, this voting process was marred by system failures, as poor cell signals delayed these voter accreditation procedures.

blocks.caption: Nigeria's voting procedures have increasingly been digitalized since 2011Image: Pius Utomi Ekpei/AFP

blocks.text: However, with INEC tallying more than 103 million Nigerians registered to participate in the coming poll, disinformation, fake news and technological challenges amount to only a few of several concerns pertaining to Nigeria's democracy.

Voter apathy has become a particular concern, especially among the country's youth. The 2023 election recorded the lowest voter turnout since the country's return to democratic rule in 1999, with merely 27% of registered voters going to the polls.

articles.title: US Army detonates unstable lead-based explosives in Iowa
articles.summary: The Army says a controlled blast is the safest way to deal with explosive chemicals that began crystallizing in storage, but residents say changing guidance has left them confused about where the…

image.caption: The detonation was planned as the decades-old lead azide was crystallizing, posing the risk of spontaneous combustionImage: Austin Johnson/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The United States Army detonated nearly 5 tons of aging lead azide at an Iowa ammunition plant on Wednesday, saying the explosive chemical has become too unstable to store.

The controlled blast occurred a little after 9 a.m. local time (1500 GMT) at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, and will destroy the country's entire stockpile of the chemical. Plumes of smoke were seen on camera in video footage after the controlled blast in Middletown.
The US Army has said residents of a small town and other nearby areas should leave "out of an abundance of caution."

"We don’t believe that the public should be in a panic," said acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle. "Our goal is to keep as much of it as we can here on our Iowa Army Ammunition plant to prevent it from traveling."
What do we know?
The material was moved to Iowa for storage from bases around the country in 2009.
But a March inspection found that it had partly crystallized, which makes it sensitive to friction and cold and could set off a spontaneous explosion.
"Inaction is no longer an option," said Major General Eric Shirley, who leads the operation.
Rob Cekada, director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, told reporters: "It's not a matter of if, it's a matter of when, and that would not be a great place for us to be in."
Is it safe to detonate the chemical?
To limit toxic lead dust, the Army has built barriers around the bunkers holding the material and will use foam and water to trap particles.
Reuters reported that Army projections show dust could settle up to 40 miles (64 km) southwest, reaching northern Missouri.
Officials expect the wind to carry the plume away from Burlington, a city of nearly 25,000 people.

blocks.caption: The date of the planned explosion has been changed three times over public backlashImage: Austin Johnson/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: While residents within 5 miles (8 kilometers) were encouraged to evacuate, the Federal Emergency Management Agency has also advised people 5 to 20 miles away to stay indoors with windows closed.
How have people reacted?

The date of the detonation changed three times after public backlash over its impact on the environment and public health. A federal appeals court cleared the plan on Monday after environmental groups sued.
Farmer Jill Holler, who organized a protest, told Reuters: "I'm not opposed if this is the only safe option."
"What I'm saying is that it's been so mishandled that people are confused and don't trust anything they're saying," she added.

articles.title: House passes bill penalizing piracy sites, counterfeit sellers up to P1 million
articles.summary: A bill increasing penalties on piracy sites and other counterfeit art sellers to P1 million has been approved on third and final reading in the House of Representatives.

blocks.text: Published November 25, 2026 11:01pm
A bill increasing penalties on piracy sites and other counterfeit art sellers to P1 million has been approved on third and final reading in the House of Representatives.
This developed after House Bill 11616 got 234 yes votes during the House’s plenary session on Wednesday.

The bill allows copyright owners and rights holders such as Filipino writers, musicians, filmmakers and business owners to ask the Intellectual Property Office of the Philippines (IPOPHL) to block access to websites or other online locations whose primary purpose or effect is to infringe copyright or facilitate infringement.

Blocking would require due notice and hearing, while notification of a complaint to the site operator could be dispensed with only under specified conditions involving unsuccessful reasonable efforts to identify, locate or notify that operator.

Once a petition for blocking is found meritorious, internet service providers would then have to comply with a disabling order within 48 hours of its issuance by applying effective technical measures to prevent access to the identified location.

An existing disabling order would also cover additional online locations associated with the infringing operation through their name, branding or operator, addressing attempts to evade blocking by moving to another address.
As for the fees, the bill pegged the administrative fines to P100,000 to P1 million or way above the existing P5,000 to P150,000.
The measure also includes infringing electronic and digital content in its definition of pirated goods, recognizing that unauthorized reproduction and distribution also occur online.
Trademark protection could extend beyond visible signs, provided a sign is capable of distinguishing one enterprise’s goods or services from another’s.
A single complaint could cover multiple infringing online locations, allowing rights holders to pursue related sites together when the required information is supplied.

The bill also grants IPOPHL authority to gather intelligence, investigate suspected violations, visit establishments during reasonable hours and recommend that the appropriate authorities cancel business permits or licenses.
— BM, GMA News
Follow facebook.com/gmanewsonline for real-time news and developments in the Philippines and around the world.

articles.summary: Poland urged NATO allies to be vigilant at their borders after repeated Russian airspace incursions. Allies have also offered different opinions on Kyiv attacking Russian ships in Libya. Follow DW…

image.caption: The proposed no-fly zone will cover several dozen kilometers of Polish territory along the border with UkraineImage: Lukasz Glowala/File Photo/REUTERS

blocks.text: November 25, 2026
Russian sources say Europeans must take up Putin's offer for Moscow talks

Numerous sources inside Russian foreign policy circles on Wednesday underscored the Kremlin's desire for European diplomats to travel to Moscow and explain their intentions before they be allowed to participate in any Russia-Ukraine peace negotiations.

Russian President Vladimir Putin originally extended the invitation last month. On Wednesday, Foreign Policy Advisor Yury Ushakov said the invitation stands but that no Europeans have so far agreed to embark on the diplomatic sojourn.
Russia's Ambassador to Germany Sergei Nechayev on Wednesday told France's AFP news agency that reaction to Putin's invitation has been "restrained."
Nechayev claimed that Moscow remains, "ready to continue the dialogue and carry on with negotiations."

He also repeated the Kremlin claim that it is Europe that is the impediment to stopping the war, and that Russia — which launched and continues to execute its unprovoked years-long war of aggression in Ukraine — is the only party truly interested in peace.

Nechayev said the Kremlin doesn't see the same "honesty" from the Europeans that it does from US President Donald Trump's team — made up of his son-in-law Jared Kushner and his friend Steve Witkoff — and wants to "know precisely what their intentions are."

Russia has been accused of foot dragging as a way to prolong attacks on Ukraine. On Wednesday, Nechayev continued in that vein, saying: "Our request to Europe is this: Decide what it is you want, determine whom you will appoint as negotiators, and, most importantly, clarify what you aim to achieve."
