articles.title: Five Russian military jets hit in airfield strike, says Ukraine
articles.summary: The Savasleyka airfield hosts aircraft used by Russia to launch hypersonic missiles and glide bombs at Ukraine.

blocks.text: Ukraine has said it damaged five Russian military aircraft in an attack on Russia's Savasleyka airfield, 300km (185 miles) east of Moscow.

Three MiG-31 and two Su-34s aircraft were hit, Kyiv's General Staff said, adding that the extent of the damage was still being assessed but that "there may be even better news to come". It did not elaborate on what weapons it had used to hit the airfield.
Russia has not commented on the strikes.
The airfield at Savasleyka, in Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region, has been a target for Ukraine for several years. It hosts aircraft used by Russia to launch hypersonic missiles and glide bombs.

The take-off of MiG-31s in particular frequently triggers nationwide alerts across Ukraine, as the Kinzhal missiles they carry have been known to hit large infrastructure and military targets and are difficult to shoot down.

Overnight, Kyiv also said it hit two oil refineries in Russia's Samara region some 800km (500 miles) from the front line – the latest in a series of long-range strikes which have dented Moscow's oil processing capacity.
"Did you repair them? We'll hit them again," the defence ministry in Kyiv said.

Samara region governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said the night-time attacks had been "a true ordeal", with more than 145 drones shot down. One person was killed and several towns experienced power outages, Fedorishchev said.
Kyiv also said it had hit a radar system as well as fuel and logistics depots across Ukrainian territories currently occupied by Russia.
"Without fuel, military vehicles cannot move; without ammunition, artillery falls silent," the defence ministry said, adding that every successful hit meant Moscow could carry out fewer strikes.
Kyiv has developed a thriving weapons industry and Ukrainian strikes on Russian targets well beyond the front line have become commonplace in the years since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion.
On Tuesday, President Vladimir Putin called for a tightening of security measures across the country's energy facilities.
But he also argued that Russia had managed to stabilise its domestic fuel market without suffering "critical damage" and added that Moscow would "inevitably" retaliate against Kyiv.

Ukraine continues to come under daily attack. Ten people were killed across several regions between 24 and 25 November, while thousands are without power after Russian strikes on energy infrastructure.

articles.title: German firms eye Africa as global trade shocks hit traditional markets
articles.summary: German businesses are optimistic about Africa, but Berlin's cautious approach to risk is holding them back from cashing in on the opportunities that their competitors from countries like the UAE and…

image.caption: Business leaders complain that German firms lack adequate financing and risk protection for projects in Africa [FILE: May 8, 2020]Image: Issouf Sanogo/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: "Africa is a land of opportunity." "The German-African relationship is a win-win." "The continent is the market of the future."

That's what many business leaders and politicians have to say about Africa at the sixth edition of the German-African Business Summit in Accra, Ghana. While these descriptions aren't new, there's a palpable sense of urgency and seriousness this time.

German firms are increasingly viewing Africa as an attractive destination as they scramble to find new markets amid wars in Ukraine and Iran, high energy prices, punishing US tariffs and slowing growth in traditional markets like China.

"For a long time, many German companies had a secure source of revenue from the major export markets in North America and China, but the geopolitical ruptures of our time have undermined this certainty," German President Frank-Walter Steimeier said during the event.
"One could also say that it is time for new horizons, time to take a closer look at economic opportunities still waiting for us."
Why Africa matters?

Africa is home to some of the fastest growing economies in the world like Ethiopia and Rwanda. Even as European and other advanced economies contend with declining working-age populations, Africa is expected to add hundreds of millions of workers in the next decades, emerging as a key source of future labor.
Germany has already signed a migration pact with Kenya and is working on one with Ghana as it seeks to attract skilled workers to help ease acute labor shortages in certain sectors at home.

Even as Africa remains one of the poorest regions in the world, economic growth in parts of the continent has created a larger and more affluent consumer class over the past three decades. This group is aspirational and a growing source of demand for many of the goods that German firms want to sell, from cars to cosmetics.

The continent, with its mineral wealth and renewable energy potential, is central to European Union efforts to diversify its sources of critical raw materials and reduce reliance on China-dominated supply chains.
It is also playing an increasingly important role in strengthening the EU's energy security after the bloc phased out most energy imports from Russia.
German firms have committed to invest billions of euros in green hydrogen projects in countries such as Mauritania and Namibia.

"We don't have the capital to develop them [natural resources]. So foreign investors are coming to help us develop those resources. Whilst we are getting jobs and industrialization is taking place, they are also making profits," said Amin Amidu Sulemani, energy and infrastructure commissioner at the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS).
"It's not a relationship where we send raw materials outside of Africa every time, when we can actually process them here," he told DW.
What is wrong with Germany's Africa strategy?
Despite Africa's growing economic appeal, many obstacles to investment remain, including corruption and governance concerns, unreliable energy supplies, foreign exchange risk and poor infrastructure.
African leaders say they are working to address these challenges and improve the ease of doing business.
Yet while German companies have largely remained on the sidelines, competitors from countries such as the UAE, Turkey and India have made significant inroads across the continent.

German firms enjoy a strong reputation in Africa because of their engineering expertise, vocational training programs and long-term industrial investments, which are more likely to create stable jobs than investments in extractive industries.

However, they have struggled to translate that goodwill into a larger commercial presence. Africa, for instance, accounts for less than 2% of the total foreign investment made by German firms over the past several decades.

blocks.caption: 'Be curious, take risks and invest in our common future,' Steinmeier said as he urged German firms to seize opportunities in AfricaImage: Bernd von Jutrczenka/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Business leaders complain that German firms lack adequate financing and risk protection for projects in Africa. They also criticize excessive bureaucracy and the absence of a coherent German strategy, with engagement fragmented across ministries and agencies.
Industry bodies say German institutions and firms often perceive risks too broadly, treating diverse African markets as if they pose the same level of risk.

"German companies can be a bit more bold and maybe also innovative in the way they approach the continent," Khadi Camara, deputy CEO of the German-African Business Association, told DW. "We see that in the companies that are successful, they don't do business as usual. Every country has its nuances that companies keep in mind and say, okay, this model works here, that model works there."

The 2026 World Investment Report by UN trade body UNCTAD showed that investors from the Gulf and Asia are becoming important sources of investment in Africa, especially in energy, logistics, real estate and infrastructure.

The UAE has been a major investor in greenfield megaprojects in recent years, including the $34 billion (€31 billion) Infinity Power renewable energy project in Mauritania, the $24 billion Ras El Hikma real estate development project in Egypt and the $6 billion H2 Global Energy hydrogen project in Tunisia.
China, US and EU all want to do business in Africa
How can German firms seize the African opportunity?
Business leaders are calling for better financing and guarantees and more risk-sharing and easing of bureaucratic hurdles.
Meanwhile, others, including the German president, are urging German businesses to take on more risk and seize opportunities in Africa. Otherwise, they risk being edged out by foreign rivals.
"Be curious, take risks and invest in our common future," Steinmeier said.

articles.title: Winning lotto bettor gets P12 million prize after 12 years
articles.summary: A man who won the lottery 12 years ago was finally able to get his P12 million prize.

blocks.text: Published November 25, 2026 10:37pm
A man who won the lottery 12 years ago was finally able to get his P12 million prize.

According to a report from Vonne Aquino on What We Know So Far, a bettor was able to get the winning combination for the Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office's (PCSO) 6/42 Lotto draw on October 2, 2014
However, the PCSO denied his claim to the prize after his child accidentally ironed the winning ticket, causing part of it to become blackened.
The PCSO argued that the ticket should be readable.
The bettor questioned the decision before the court, and the case reached all the way to the Supreme Court (SC). The SC eventually ruled in favor of the bettor.
The SC ordered the PCSO to give the bettor the prize back in 2023, but due to several processes, the office was only able to give him the money on Wednesday, November 25, 2026.
PCSO General Manager Melquides Robles personally handed over the check to the winning bettor.
In addition to the P12,391,600 prize, the amount accrued 6% annual legal interest, bringing the total to P14,157,281.
The bettor said that the money is a big help to his family, as they have a lot of debts. He also plans to start his own business with the cash. —Jean Mangaluz/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: China sends first foreign astronaut to ISS rival as it globalises space operations
articles.summary:
Muhammad Zeeshan Ali – the first Pakistani to reach orbit – greeted with Chinese ‘space handshake’ at Tiangong station

China has flown the first foreign astronaut to its Tiangong space…

blocks.text: China has flown the first foreign astronaut to its Tiangong space station, starting what it says will be the globalisation of its space operations as the US-led International Space Station (ISS) enters its final years of operation.

Floating through a hatch to enter Tiangong, Pakistan’s Muhammad Zeeshan Ali grinned broadly as he was embraced by the onboard crew in what China’s space agency called the country’s first foreign “space handshake”.

Tiangong, completed in 2022, is the jewel in the crown of China’s space programme. The government has invested billions into its celestial ambitions in recent years to catch up with the US and Russia, two of the five partners involved in the ISS, along with Europe, Japan and Canada. After 25 years of continuous occupation, the ISS is set to cease operations from 2030, according to Nasa.
On Wednesday China’s president, Xi Jinping, told his Pakistani counterpart Beijing was “willing to work with all countries … to uphold the banner of the peaceful use of outer space”.
Ali was part of the crew of Shenzhou 24, the most recent iteration of the series of missions that rotate astronauts in the space station every six months. He is the first Pakistani to reach orbit.

blocks.caption: People watching a broadcast of China’s Shenzhou 24 mission in Islamabad, Pakistan. Photograph: Sohail Shahzad/EPA

blocks.text: “Sending another country’s astronaut to space is a major undertaking,” Blaine Curcio, the managing director at Orbital Gateway Consulting, told the Guardian. “Pakistan is putting a lot of trust into Beijing by having him fly into space on a Chinese-built rocket. There are also considerations related to security: Ali is getting detailed insights into China’s crewed space programme … It makes China better prepared to do it again, and also makes it clear to other countries that China is open to this type of collaboration.”

Space cooperation between China and Pakistan dates back to the early 1990s. China has launched Pakistani satellites and a Pakistani-built rover ‌is also due to fly on a Chinese lunar mission around 2028.

Shenzhou 24 blasted off from the Jiuquan launch centre in north-west China against a pink-tinged dawn sky on Wednesday, footage showed, and first docked with the space station three and a half hours later.

Ali, a 40-year-old Pakistan air force pilot and payload specialist, will conduct experiments including one cultivating microalgae as a potential food and another testing the effects of spaceflight on quinoa seeds. To prepare for the mission, he ​trained for seven months in Beijing, including intensive Chinese-language classes.

At a press conference the day before the launch, Ali recited a line from a classical Chinese poem. Commander Tang Hongbo told reporters that differences in language and culture had made learning to work together more challenging, but that the effort had paid off.

Ali will not stay for the six-month term usually demanded of Tiangong astronauts. Instead, he will return to earth with two of the Shenzhou 23 crew while its commander, Zhu Yangzhu, will remain to complete another milestone – the first full-year stay in space by a Chinese astronout.

Beijing’s accelerated achievements in the skies have spooked its rivals. China is the third country to put humans in orbit and has landed robotic rovers on Mars and the moon, where it hopes to send crewed missions within the next decade. In racing to the moon before 2030, Beijing is competing with the US’s Artemis programme. The US has excluded China from the ISS since 2011, banning Nasa from collaborating with Beijing. In 2025 Nasa went further by blocking Chinese citizens from its facilities altogether.

“We know that China is quite keen to develop Tiangong as an international hub,” said Curcio, pointing to China Manned Space Agency documents published in coordination with the UN outlining “resources for international cooperation” onboard the station.

In the future, he said, he would expect countries such as Brazil and Egypt to seek out the opportunity to send astronauts on Chinese missions. He added: “I think when the ISS is retired, if there is no western replacement (government or commercial), then yes, we may eventually see European or other ISS-involved countries – like Russia – send astronauts to Tiangong.”

articles.title: Israeli strike kills senior Hamas security official and family in Gaza City
articles.summary: Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, head of Hamas's internal security service in northern Gaza, was killed with his wife and two teenage daughters, doctors say.

blocks.text: Wednesday's strike in Shati caused extensive damage to the Abu al-Ouf family's apartment.
Photos showed the exterior wall and several interior walls were destroyed, with rubble and broken furniture left scattered across the floor.
An interior ministry statement said that Abu al-Ouf was killed along with his wife Noura, 41, and their daughters Yusra, 15, and Jana, 13.
It condemned the attack as a "heinous crime" and accused Israel of targeting security personnel in Gaza "in an effort to spread chaos within Palestinian society".
Hamas's internal security service is responsible for enforcing discipline, protecting the group's infrastructure and rooting out informants.
Israel's military said in a statement that Abu al-Ouf was a "significant figure" who had served as "a key source of expertise" in efforts to restrict Israeli counter-terrorism operations in Gaza.
"His elimination is a blow to the apparatus's leadership capabilities and follows yesterday's elimination of his commander," it added.
On Tuesday, an Israeli drone strike in western Gaza City killed Naeem Abu Nahel, the head of Hamas's internal security service.
He had only been in the position since September, when his predecessor was captured in a raid in Gaza City by Israeli special forces.
Near daily Israeli strikes continue in Gaza despite a ceasefire agreed in October last year.
At least 1,679 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza during the same period.
The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,740 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

articles.title: Swiss tourist killed and British and Americans injured by elephants in Cameroon
articles.summary:
Alain Throo, insurance executive based in London, reportedly gored and later died on hike near Mount Cameroon national park

A Swiss tourist has been killed and British and American tourists…

blocks.text: A Swiss tourist has been killed and British and American tourists have been injured when a group of hikers encountered a herd of elephants in Cameroon.

The group of six tourists, four British, one Swiss and one American, accompanied by local guides, were hiking near the village of Bakingili in the south of the Mount Cameroon national park on 19 November, on a path used by elephants to access a nearby lake, when they encountered the herd of about 15 animals, according to media reports.

The elephants attacked the group and Alain Throo, a Swiss insurance executive based in London, was reportedly gored and one of the guides tossed into a ditch on top of Throo, while the others hid in trees.

Throo had a black eye and was initially responsive and complaining about an injury to his arm, one of the British female hikers told Cameroonian media, which said they had feared he was bleeding internally.
“He said that the elephant attacked him,” an unidentified Cameroonian man added, according to a video posted by CBS Radio Buea FM. “It smashed him.”

blocks.caption: An African forest elephant. Photograph: Danita Delimont/Alamy

blocks.text: Throo later died of his injuries and his body was carried out of the park by a combined team of park staff and the military to a mortuary in the town of Limbeon 21 November. The American hiker was treated at the same hospital and later discharged, according to local media.

One of the British tourists, who said he had hid in a tree stump for two hours, recalled the moment the elephants attacked their group. “I saw these elephants almost next to me. And I thought, if I go down this path as well, I’m going to get hit. So I just moved to the opposite direction. They ran down the path, I ran and hid in a bush. And I heard some screaming.”

Sean McGovern, the UK chief executive of the insurer Axa XL, where Throo had worked for 13 years, confirmed the death, saying Throo was a “valued member of our team, respected colleague and friend whose contribution, professionalism and warmth touched many people”.
Cameroonian media reported that clashes between elephants and local people had been happening for the past 10 years.
after newsletter promotion

Mount Cameroon is the highest mountain in west and central Africa, at more than 4,000 metres. The African forest elephant was declared critically endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature in 2021. There are about 195,000 left in the wild, less than 15% of its population 50 years ago, according to the World Wildlife Fund.

Just 5% of forest elephants, which are smaller than their savannah-based counterparts, are found outside central Africa. In Cameroon, there are about 6,000 forest elephants, according to the NGO Global Conservation, which said the species was at risk from poaching syndicates.
A spokesperson for Britain’s Foreign Office said: “We offered assistance after a number of British nationals were injured in Cameroon.”

articles.title: US plans new tariffs on EU, China and 12 others
articles.summary: The Trump administration is planning new import duties of up to 20% to counter excessive manufacturing abroad. The measures could put further pressure on US consumers already struggling with high…

image.caption: US President Donald Trump speaks at a press conference in February after the Supreme Court struck down his global tariffs [FILE: February 20, 2026]Image: Kevin Lamarque/REUTERS

blocks.text: The Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) unveiled new tariffs on imports from 14 economies, including the European Union and China.
A senior US official said the proposed duties follow a months-long investigation into allegations that excessive manufacturing abroad puts American producers at a disadvantage.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC that the proposed tariffs largely stick to rates set under existing trade agreements, although some could be "topped up" by a few percentage points.

China would face an additional tariff of 20%, bringing the combined rate for some Chinese goods to 45%. The proposed duties would respect the 15% tariff cap agreed with the European Union, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, according to a senior US administration official.
Other affected economies include India, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Thailand and Vietnam.
The tariffs could take effect in January at the earliest, following a public comment period.
Why is Trump planning new tariffs?
The measures are also intended to replace revenues lost after the US Supreme Court struck down US president Donald Trump's sweeping global tariffs in February.

The proposed duties could further fuel US inflation, which reached 3.7% in September. High living costs were a key issue in November's midterm elections, in which Trump's Republican Party lost control of both chambers of Congress.
The tariff plans come just weeks before Trump is due to host G20 leaders in Miami in December.
The US official played down concerns about renewed trade tensions and said Washington could sign further trade agreements at the summit.

articles.title: Aidan is one of thousands of students forced to verbally defend his honours thesis as universities take on AI
articles.summary:
Honours students are increasingly being asked to sit oral assessments – but at the University of Sydney it’s become a requirement for all

  • Get our

blocks.text: When Aidan Elwig Pollock signed up for an honours program at the University of Sydney, he did not expect his 20,000-word thesis to be accompanied by a spoken component.

But, as AI increasingly makes written research an unreliable form of assessment, the university has demanded all students taking the one-year program defend their arguments in conversation with professors.
Top Australian universities are increasingly asking honours students to sit oral assessments, with Sydney the first known to require it across honours programs.

Exams have moved from computers back to paper or interviews in the four years since the release of ChatGPT made AI plagiarism a concern. Some educators have adopted the debate-focused tutorials traditional at Oxbridge colleges or the viva voce assessments typical of PhDs.

But honours programs – a year of intensive research for dedicated students after their bachelor’s degree – have been slower to adapt as they’re typically focused on a single project, which accounts for most of their grade.

Elwig Pollock, a history student, said he had not used AI at all on his work on how the commemoration of Captain Cook has evolved over time, and that the new demand was “insulting” to students and the professors who supervise them.

“If you’ve used AI to do your honours thesis and your supervisor has not figured it out throughout your regular meetings, then what’s stopping you from communicating that material successfully in a 15-minute conversation,” Elwig Pollock said.

blocks.caption: Elwig Pollock sat for a short pass or fail conversation, but it is worth 0% of his grade as most marks come from his thesis. Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The Guardian

blocks.text: Since 2024, Sydney bachelor’s degrees have included a mix of assessments that are vulnerable or secure to AI tools. This year, the university has formally extended that to honours programs, though the format is different for every faculty.

On Wednesday, Elwig Pollock had a short conversation which was a pass or fail hurdle task but was worth nothing towards his final grade. In his case most of his marks are coming from his thesis but his degree will not be awarded if he fails the conversation.
Engineering student Isabelle* had an entirely different experience.

Last week, the University of Sydney student had an hour of interviews with professors in a single room with five classmates, as the school rushed through assessing 250 students in two days. It accounted for 50% of her grade.
Her 20,000-word thesis was worth just 20%.
“There were people coming in and out of the room while we were being assessed so it was distracting,” said Isabelle, who asked for a pseudonym to avoid being penalised.
“[We had to] move to the other side of the room so my marker could hear me.”

The change has stressed students who aren’t used to speaking up in class, don’t speak English as a first language or need their honours to become qualified in their field – including engineers like Isabelle.
“I think it’s particularly bad in engineering because writing skills are poor, but I think it’s a Band-Aid solution,” she said of the verbal component.
Adam Bridgeman, the university’s acting deputy vice-chancellor for education, said honours degrees needed to change.
“We necessarily treat honours theses as open assessments as we can’t reliably restrict AI use,” Bridgeman said.
after newsletter promotion
Staff and students were offered guidance and practice to manage the transformation and ensure English fluency and speaking ability were not “inadvertently rewarded”, he said.
“We appreciate some students might be nervous about the experience, especially if it’s their first time,” Bridgeman said. “We’ll take feedback on board as we plan for 2027 assessments.”

While Sydney is the only major institution to mandate interviews for honours programs, schools at the University of Melbourne, Monash University and Australian Catholic University are bringing them in.

Adelaide University, which was previously among the first in Australia to reintroduce viva voce tasks, is using “interactive oral assessments” in which students and teachers role-play real-world professional situations.

There are no public reports of Australian honours students cheating with AI. Kurt Iveson, an honours coordinator for Sydney’s School of Geosciences, said the change was still needed to respond to AI’s growing role in education.
“They’re not the kind of people that I would personally be worried about getting Claude to write their honours thesis for them,” Iveson said.
“But … [management] want to be able to demonstrate to the world, as part of their social licence and external accreditation, that things are being assessed securely.”

The interviews are a heavy addition to professors’ workloads – and no casuals have been brought on to help. Staff and students contacted by Guardian Australia said the new rules had left supervisors feeling rushed and overworked.
But, Iveson said, interviews are a valuable way of helping students learn and understand the significance of their research.
“Assuming that you have actually written it, you know your shit, you’ll be fine, and you’ll have a good conversation.”
*Name has been changed

articles.title: EU plans €50 billion sovereign tech equity fund to boost quantum technology
articles.summary: The European Commission proposed a tech fund with a target size of €50 billion to boost quantum computing efforts. The bloc aims to keep up with the US and China in the global race.

image.caption: Quantum computing technology is still in the early stages of developmentImage: Ross D. Franklin/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The European Commission proposed a €50 billion ($54.73 billion) equity financing fund on Wednesday to boost artificial intelligence and quantum computing in Europe.
The draft "Quantum Act" aims to help Europe compete in a race against the United States and China.

"Quantum technologies will shape the future ‌of industry, security and innovation, and they will have a ‌profound ​impact on our societies. Europe needs to accelerate now," EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen said in a statement.
"We want to build a fund and our target scale is now €50 billion," she said, calling it a "sufficient starting point."
Virkkunen introduced the officially named "Sovereign Tech Equity Fund" while presenting new rules to support Europe's quantum technology sector.
Will quantum computers destroy the internet?
The new rules will push public authorities to favor European companies when giving public contracts and funding.
The European Union (EU) also wants to reduce its dependence on third countries amid concerns that US companies could use so-called "kill switches” to disable their products in Europe.
Why is quantum computing important?
Quantum computing technology is still at the early stages of development, with both the US and China competing to achieve dominance in the field.
While classical computers process data using bits — which are either 0 or 1 — quantum computers use qubits (quantum bits), which can exist in a blend of both states at once.
By using qubits, these machines could eventually solve complex problems much faster than today's supercomputers.
Are quantum computers creating a new future?
The EU expects the quantum computing to lead to breakthroughs in several areas, including drug development, earlier medical diagnoses or super-efficient batteries and even AI development.

Although quantum technology offers significant potential, it also poses cybersecurity risks, as it could undermine encryption and other safeguards for digital data at a time when governments are battling AI-driven cyberattacks.
Europe is home to one-third of the world's quantum companies

Around one-third of the world's quantum companies ⁠are ​based in the European Union, according to ​the Commission. Last year, public funding for quantum technologies reached €8.6 billion in the bloc, compared with €5.3 billion in the United States and €13.6 billion in China.
However, European quantum start-ups have attracted €1.1 billion in private funding so far, compared with €7 billion in the United States.
The EU launched its "quantum Europe" strategy in July 2025, aiming to be a global leader in quantum technologies by 2030.
The bloc is already a global leader in quantum research but it falls short when it comes to transforming this into viable commercial opportunities.
The draft legislation must be negotiated with EU member states and the European Parliament in the upcoming months before it can be law.

articles.title: Number of women killed by men in Ireland almost doubles in a year
articles.summary:
Figures from past 30 years show more than half of victims killed by current or ex-partner

The number of women in Ireland killed by men…

blocks.text: The number of women in Ireland killed by men has surged in the past five years and risen especially sharply in the past 12 months, according to a study.
After falling for two decades, the number of violent deaths began going up in 2021 and has risen sharply this year, with 13 deaths so far, the report by Irish charity Women’s Aid said on Wednesday.
“That should alarm every one of us,” said Sarah Benson, the organisation’s chief executive. “After years of decline, the number of women killed is rising again.”

The vast majority of victims over the past three decades were killed by a man they knew and over half were killed by a current or former partner. The findings match UN and EU data showing the most dangerous place for a woman is her own home, and the most likely killer is a man she knows, said Benson.

“Ireland is one of the wealthiest countries in the world, and we have good laws. Yet women are still being killed by the men closest to them. Most men choose never to behave this way, and that is exactly why we need everyone to recognise this violence and call it out.”
Since 1996, when the Dublin-based charity began collating femicide statistics, 291 women have been killed by men.

Measured in five-year blocks, the levels of violent deaths peaked at 67 between 1996 and 2000 and fell to a low of 31 between 2016 and 2020. During the 2021–2025 period, 40 deaths were recorded, a 29% increase on the previous period.
The 13 women who died in violent circumstances this year is almost double the figure of seven for all of last year.
However, Ireland’s overall murder rate of 0.66 per 100,000 people remains well below global and European averages. The country has a population of 5.5 million.

Of the 235 cases of violent deaths resolved since 1996, 89% of the women were killed by a man known to them, 57% were killed by a current or former partner, 32% by a male relative or acquaintance and 11% by a male stranger. More than two-thirds – 68% – died in their own homes. Just over a quarter were women aged 26 to 35.

“Intimate partner femicide rarely comes out of nowhere,” said Benson. “Separation, coercive control, non-fatal strangulation, threats to kill and stalking are all known warning signs. When a woman tells Women’s Aid that she is afraid for her life, we believe her.”

Leaving an abusive partner did not always end abuse, said Benson. “Risk rises sharply around separation and stays high for about a year. For every woman whose life is taken, thousands more are living on a knife’s edge of fear.”
The Femicide Watch report, which coincided with International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women, recorded that 25 children were killed alongside a woman, usually their mother.

articles.title: Ice hockey prospect Max Calce follows Leon Draisaitl's path, leaving Mannheim for Canada
articles.summary: The player widely seen as Germany's biggest ice hockey talent to come along in years is leaving the country's top professional league for Canada – changing tracks in his bid to make it to the NHL.

image.caption: As he is still under 18, Max Calce had to wear a full cage during DEL gamesImage: Udo Herrmann/Herrmann Agenturfotografie/IMAGO

blocks.text: Max Calce made the surprise announcement that he would be moving to the Brantford Bulldogs of the Ontario Hockey League (OHL) in a statement issued on the website of his German Ice Hockey League (DEL) team, Adler Mannheim late on Tuesday.
"I have long had three goals," he said. "To play for the Adler, in the Canadian Hockey League (CHL), and in the NHL. Today is a difficult and emotional day for me, as I say goodbye to my home."
Having started the season in Mannheim, many thought the 17-year-old would finish the season in the DEL.
The announcement came after Calce, who had been a regular in Mannheim's lineup this season, had been left off the team sheet for Tuesday night's game in Straubing.

This comes less than a month after he became the youngest-ever player to score a goal for the German men's national team – against Slovakia in Germany's final game of the annual Deutschland Cup invitational.
Mature decision-making on the ice
"It was only a matter of time; he's an incredible player," said former NHL player Tobias Rieder, who frequently played on a line with Calce during the tournament.
"The most impressive thing is that, at 17, he plays a very mature style of hockey—he almost always makes the right decision."
Calce is also the youngest goal scorer in DEL history, having found the net for Mannheim in September 2025 at just 16 years and 100 days old.

blocks.caption: Max Calce was named player of the game after scoring his first goal for GermanyImage: ActionPictures/IMAGO

blocks.text: In his statement, the centerman thanked Mannheim, which has produced a number of NHL players over the years, including Leon Draisaitl, Moritz Seider and Tim Stützle.
"The trust, support, and experiences I gained through my coaches, teammates, and everyone within the organization have played a major role in my development—both as a player and as a person."
This season, his second in the DEL, Calce has six goals and two assists in Mannheim's first 19 games.
"We believe in preparing young players to take opportunities at the highest level of the sport," Dallas Eakins, Mannheim's head coach and sporting director said.
"As much as we would have loved to continue to have him play for us, we respect and welcome his ambition."
Increased visibility ahead of NHL draft

On the surface, the notion of moving from a men's professional league to a junior league may seem like a step backwards, but Calce's move to the OHL will give Calce increased exposure to NHL scouts. The OHL is one of the top three junior leagues in Canada and according to figures released by the CHL last season, they produce more NHL players than any other developmental system.

In doing so, Calce is now following the path of Edmonton Oilers superstar Draisaitl, who left Mannheim's youth program at the age of 16 to pursue his NHL dream, joining the Western Hockey League's Prince Albert Raiders.

This, of course is not the only path to the NHL; Moritz Seider of the Detroit Red Wings and the Ottawa Senators' Tim Stützle were both first-round draft choices plucked directly from Mannheim. Calce is hoping to be taken in the first round of next summer's NHL Entry Draft.
Born to Russian parents in Mannheim, Calce changed his birth surname, Penkin, to that of his mother and stepfather last summer.

articles.title: Why Indian nationals are still ending up in Russia's war on Ukraine
articles.summary: Whether through deception or desperation, Indians continue to be drawn into Russia's war in Ukraine. What can New Delhi do to protect its citizens from ending up fighting in Ukraine?

image.caption: Modi raised Russian recruitment of Indians when they met in Moscow in July 2024 [FILE]Image: Alexander Zemlianichenko/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Gurpreet Singh Randhawa, a 40-year-old from Jalandhar in India's northern Punjab state, said he traveled to Russia for work after responding to a Facebook advertisement for a driving job at a garment factory.
But instead of finding work as a driver, he was sent to fight in Ukraine for the Russian armed forces.
After escaping from his unit, he surrendered to Ukrainian forces in November. He is now being held as a prisoner of war.

In an interview with Ukrainian YouTuber Volodymyr Zolkin, Randhawa described how, after arriving in Russia, he was taken to a military facility, made to sign a contract and sent for training. He said they confiscated his passport and phone. His account has not been independently verified.
Randhawa's story is a familiar one in India.

He is the second Indian national known to have escaped the Russian military. Sahil Majothi, a 23-year-old from Gujarat, surrendered to Ukrainian forces in October 2025. He had joined the Russian military while serving a prison sentence in Russia, reportedly believing that military service would help him secure his release.
Ukraine war: Plight of Indians trapped in Russian army
India's efforts to bring recruits home
The cases underline how little has changed since Prime Minister Narendra Modi raised the issue with Russian President Vladimir Putin during his visit to Moscow in July 2024.
At the time, Putin assured him that Indians who were misled into joining the Russian army would be discharged. But the recruitment of Indians has continued.

In an October filing before the Supreme Court, India's Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said approximately 267 Indians have joined the Russian armed forces since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Of these, 139 were discharged and 51 were killed. The whereabouts of the 77 others were unknown. Russian authorities have confirmed that seven of them are missing.
The problem extends beyond Indians who travel to Russia seeking civilian employment, only to find themselves exposed to recruitment networks and the dangers of a war zone.

The MEA has also highlighted cases of Indians knowingly enlisting in the Russian military for the supposed financial benefits on offer, believing they could later secure release through government intervention.
Some had also approached Indian authorities to renounce their citizenship and obtain Russian passports. "This is a dangerous path and is strongly discouraged by the government," the ministry said.
Lured into war: Russia's foreign fighters in Ukraine
Duped or desperate?
Former diplomat Anil Trigunayat said the growing movement of Indian workers to Russia presents both economic opportunities and new challenges for their protection.
"Inadequate oversight of recruitment networks could leave vulnerable workers exposed to exploitation," Trigunayat told DW.
He said Indian workers were often burdened by substantial recruitment fees and continued deductions from their salaries by intermediaries.

"Some of them had paid between 300,000 to 500,000 Indian rupees [$5,400 /€4,900] to Indian recruitment agents, and even while working in Russia, more than 30% of their agreed monthly salary was taken away by local and foreign agents," Trigunayat said.

The former diplomat added that some Indians who had overstayed their visas in Russia were particularly vulnerable. Military service was allegedly offered to earn substantial wages and regularize their immigration status.
Mohammad Sufiyan, from Hyderabad in the southern state of Telangana, said he was lured to Russia under false pretences and forced into active combat in Ukraine.
He had traveled abroad in search of employment and a better livelihood, but ended up in a war zone. He has since returned home to India.
"Many people are duped. Some decide it is better to seek citizenship than come back to India. It's a tough life, and people will go to any lengths to get some sort of employment," Sufiyan told DW.
Sufiyan's experience points to the economic desperation that makes such offers attractive, even when they carry the risk of being caught up in a war.

Rajan Kumar, a professor at the Center for Russian and Central Asian Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University's School of International Studies, said some Indians who traveled to Russia for work could find themselves caught up in the fighting without having joined the military.
"Some of them, they don't join the army, but they end up in the army region. They're caught in the crossfire," Kumar told DW.
He said India was negotiating with Moscow to secure the return of its citizens caught up in such situations. "Russia is very cooperative so far," he said.
India's special relationship with Russia explained
Moscow prioritizes military aims over strategic diplomacy
India has been pressing Russia to take action, but the issue persists.

The recruitment efforts reflect Russia's need for more manpower for its nearly five-year war in Ukraine , and the limited influence New Delhi can exert over Moscow, despite the close political relationship between the two countries.
Mohsin Raza Khan, a professor at the Jindal School of International Affairs, told DW that Putin's need to sustain the war effort was taking precedence over the concerns of a strategic partner.
He points out that the Russian president was reluctant to impose another mobilization on his own population for fear of domestic unrest.
"In these circumstances, sustaining the war effort appears to take precedence over concerns raised by India. Neither Modi nor New Delhi has sufficient leverage to change that," said Khan.
Khan also said the willingness of some Indians to enlist, and even consider giving up their citizenship, is down to the lack of decent employment opportunities at home.
"For young, educated men without contacts or connections, the chances of respectable employment are so low that the risks of a high casualty war are preferable," he said.

articles.title: Justice Leonen concurs with dismissal but says SC should have ruled on Duterte arrest
articles.summary: Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen concurred with the Supreme Court's decision to dismiss the consolidated habeas corpus petitions challenging the arrest in March 2025 on a warrant from the…

blocks.text: Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen concurred with the Supreme Court's decision to dismiss the consolidated habeas corpus petitions challenging the arrest in March 2025 on a warrant from the International Criminal Court but stressed that the court should have also ruled its legality

In his 58-page concurring and dissenting opinion, Leonen agreed to dismiss the petitions for mootness, yet dissented from the majority's failure to “address unresolved, grave, and serious constitutional questions that can recur yet may evade judicial review.”

“I concur in the finding that the Petition for Habeas Corpus should be dismissed. The International Criminal Court (ICC) has competence to determine its own jurisdiction, which includes the disposition of any person physically surrendered to it,” Leonen said.

“However, I dissent from the Court's failure to provide clear guidance for future cases. The situation involves clear, serious, and grave constitutional issues that are capable of repetition and would otherwise evade review. Our silence can be interpreted as complicity in a violation of the Constitution, our concurrence with a treaty, and the relevant law,” he added.
Leonen said that by leaving these questions unanswered, the high court failed to provide much-needed guidelines for future cases.

“The constitutional issues raised in the present Petitions are grave and serious and capable of repetition, yet evading review. This case cannot simply be dismissed on the ground of mootness, even if doing so may be the politically expedient resolution,” Leonen said.

“As the Court of last resort, we must not shirk our duty of providing the clearest guidelines, for the bench and the bar and, by implication, our law enforcement agencies. That is the resolution that would best safeguard and operationalize the human rights provisions under the Rome Statute, which are read through our Constitution,” he added.

Pointing to the risk of similar incidents happening again, Leonen said that Duterte’s purported co-perpetrators remain at large in Philippine territory and “may, at any time, be seized by Philippine authorities and surrendered in the same manner” as the former president.
“In the present case, the manner in which petitioner was seized and surrendered, if repeated in a future case, would evade judicial review,” Leonen said.
The former President was arrested on March 25, 2025 and taken to the Scheveningen prison in The Hague on a warrant of arrest from the ICC.

Duterte is facing charges of crimes against humanity of murder and attempted murder in connection with the deaths under his war on drugs when he was president of the Philippines and mayor of Davao City.

In separate petitions filed in March 2025, Duterte's youngest daughter Kitty and her half-brothers Davao City Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte and Davao City 1st District Rep. Paolo “Pulong” Duterte asked the SC to order the government to present the former President before the High Court.
The Duterte camp said that the ICC arrest warrant cannot be used as the basis for the arrest and detention of the former president, claiming that it has no jurisdiction in the Philippines.
It said that the ICC may only exercise its jurisdiction if the country’s legal system is not functioning, stressing that the Philippine judicial system is working.
The Philippines withdrew from the Rome Statute, the treaty that established the ICC, in 2019 after the Hague-based tribunal began a probe into the Duterte administration's drug war.
Kitty will appeal the decision of the SC.
Duterte's trial before the ICC will start on Nov. 30, 2026.
'Violated rights, equal protection'
Leonen criticized the failure to subject the ICC arrest warrant to Philippine judicial review.

He noted that Duterte should have been promptly brought before a national court—where his identity, the regularity of the arrest, and the observance of his constitutional rights could be confirmed—before any surrender abroad.
Leonen added that the same court should have ensured the arrested person understood their rights and had a genuine opportunity to exercise them, especially when applying for interim release.

“The principal constitutional defect lay not in the absence of a fresh determination of probable cause–that question belonged to the issuing international court or tribunal—but in the total absence of any judicial review: former President Duterte was taken and flown to The Hague within hours, without any judicial imprimatur sought by his captors," Leonen said.
"That omission was a real violation of his right to be free from seizure except through judicial process,” he added.

Leonen acknowledged that surrendering Duterte and his former lieutenants has its advantages, but stressed that doing so does not represent complete accountability and should not stop the court from scrutinizing the process.

“Insisting on respect for human rights is not advancing a political cause or placing anyone beyond the reach of prosecution. It is insisting that justice be pursued through means worthy of its name-humane in application and legitimate in exercise,” Leonen said.

“A proper legal and just procedure for everyone matters. The procedure that protects a former president is the same procedure that protects the farmer taken at night and the young father picked up in an operation in a crowded barangay. Whatever we refuse to the powerful, we will soon be unable to guarantee to the powerless,” he added.
Dissenting opinions

The justices who voted against dismissing the petitions were Associate Justice Ramon Paul L. Hernando, retired Associate Justice Amy Lazaro-Javier, Associate Justice Henri Jean Paul Inting and Associate Justice Antonio Kho Jr., according to the SC.

Hernando argued that Duterte’s surrender to the ICC violated constitutional rights including due process, protection against unreasonable searches and seizures, freedom of travel, and the rights of persons under custodial investigation.
He added that the former president’s surrender through Republic Act No. 9851 is unconstitutional.

Meanwhile, Lazaro-Javier rejected the majority’s view that the petitions had become moot, pointing out that the cases question the conduct of Philippine authorities rather than the ICC’s current custody of Duterte.
She explained that the legality of the respondent law enforcement officers’ acts—the arrest, detention, and rendition of Duterte to the ICC—is separate from the ICC’s custody.

She further stressed that a writ of habeas corpus examines not just physical detention, but also its legality and the constitutional principles involved, adding that the Executive branch’s decision not to seek Duterte’s repatriation remains open to judicial review.

For his part, Inting noted that determining whether the arrest and surrender followed the Philippine Constitution and domestic laws is a legal issue for the courts to resolve, not a political question left solely to the executive or legislative branches.

“The case continues to present a controversy on whether FPRRD was validly arrested and detained by the Philippine authorities on March 11, 2025, when he was surrendered to the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court (ICC). The issue is not a purely political question and should be resolved by the Court,” Inting said.

He also mentioned that an SC ruling could have practical value for ICC proceedings and case law, particularly under the abuse of process doctrine, where the ICC may suspend or terminate proceedings if improper or unlawful procedures were used to carry out an otherwise lawful process, such as an ICC arrest warrant.
'Sans domestic law, court authority'

Finally, Kho argued that the government cannot surrender a Filipino citizen to a foreign tribunal, or carry out an “extraordinary rendition,” without a valid domestic law and prior authority from the courts.
“Absent any such domestic law and prior judicial authorization, the extraordinary rendition of FPRRD to the ICC by the Philippine government is unconstitutional per se,” Kho said.

He also pointed out that if the SC were to dismiss the petitions as moot simply because Duterte had already been surrendered, similar actions in the future could evade judicial review just by being carried out quickly.

In March 2025, Duterte was transferred to the custody of the ICC in The Hague, Netherlands. He is set to stand trial for crimes against humanity before the ICC starting November 30, 2026. —NB, GMA News

articles.title: Senate realigns P19.8B from MAP, AICS to boost PhilHealth
articles.summary: Senator JV Ejercito says the realigned funds would go directly to hospitals to support the implementation of the Zero Balance Billing program

blocks.text: GAB. Senator JV Ejercito, chairperson of the committee on finance, sponsors the proposed 2027 General Appropriations Act on November 23, 2026, at the Senate of the Philippines, Pasay City.
Senate Facebook
Senator JV Ejercito says the realigned funds would go directly to hospitals to support the implementation of the Zero Balance Billing program

items: The Philippine Senate has realigned nearly P20 billion from various government assistance programs to increase funding for PhilHealth in the proposed 2027 national budget.
Senator JV Ejercito stated that the realignment would raise PhilHealth's allocation from P73 billion to P94.2 billion, with a target to eventually reach P100 billion despite fiscal constraints.
Concerns about potential duplicate funding for infrastructure projects were acknowledged, with Ejercito urging budget watchdogs to help identify any irregularities in the budget.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Senate has realigned nearly P20 billion from government assistance programs, including the Medical Assistance Program (MAP) and the Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations (AICS), to augment funding for the Philippine Health Insurance Corporation (PhilHealth) under the proposed 2027 national budget.

Senator JV Ejercito, chairperson of the Senate finance committee, said on Wednesday, November 25, that the P19.8-billion realignment would help increase PhilHealth’s allocation from P73 billion in the House version of the General Appropriations Bill (GAB) to P94.2 billion in the Senate version of the budget measure.
PhilHealth subsidies in the national budget cover the premium contributions of vulnerable sectors that cannot afford to pay their own health insurance premiums.

“Our target is to increase PhilHealth subsidy to P100 billion but we have a tight fiscal space. Hopefully, we can reach our target so PhilHealth can have better subsidies,” Ejercito told reporters in a mix of English and Filipino.
Of the P19.8 billion, P9.9 billion was realigned from MAP funds and another P9.9 billion from AICS.

Ejercito said the funds would go directly to hospitals to support the implementation of the Zero Balance Billing (ZBB) program. This includes P7.6 billion for Department of Health (DOH) hospitals, P2 billion for legacy hospitals, and P1 billion for local government unit (LGU) hospitals.

The Senate also provided an additional P5.49 billion for the Hospital Facilities Enhancement Program (HFEP), P1.099 billion for health promotion, P1.599 billion for immunization programs, and P736 million for the Sulu Transition Program.

Ejercito also addressed concerns raised by Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson over possible duplicate funding for infrastructure projects, including multi-purpose buildings (MPBs), under the proposed 2027 national budget.

“If we saw red flags, including double entries in the GAB, definitely, we’ll remove that. But of course, it is not humanly possible to check everything at once. That’s thousands of entries, so we need to check it slowly,” Ejercito said.

He acknowledged that some questionable entries might have escaped the committee’s scrutiny, but said this was not intentional. He also called on budget watchdogs to help identify possible irregularities.

“If some entries have been let out of our sight, that’s not intentional. So we’re seeking everyone’s help, including budget watchdogs, to tell us if they observe some red flags. If we found that it has basis, we’ll definitely remove the items,” Ejercito added.

The Senate began plenary deliberations on the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for fiscal year 2027 on Monday, November 23. Lacson, ahead of the deliberations, flagged alleged double and triple appropriations for some flood control projects in the GAB, saying some of them had already received funding in previous years. – Rappler.com

articles.title: In Afghanistan, no female doctor often means no treatment for women
articles.summary: Millions of women in Afghanistan, particularly pregnant women, are suffering under Taliban restrictions and are increasingly losing access to life-saving medical care.

image.caption: The UN has been training women as midwives to work in local communities [FILE 2023]Image: Ali Khara/REUTERS

blocks.text: In many parts of Taliban-ruled Afghanistan, male doctors are no longer allowed to treat women. The consequences have been highlighted in a recent United Nations report, which offers disturbing insight into the harsh reality many women face.
In one case, a woman from Kunar province described how she suffered several miscarriages without being able to access medical care.
Her case highlights the increasing number of pregnant women who urgently need medical assistance and are unable to receive it because of restrictions imposed by the Taliban.
And overall, women in Afghanistan are increasingly losing access to essential healthcare. This is due both to the Taliban's restrictions and to cuts in international aid funding.
Taliban remove women from public life in Afghanistan
"If a pregnant woman dies because male doctors are not allowed to treat her, her husband can marry another, younger woman. That is how the Taliban think," said 28-year-old Tamana Zaryab Paryani.
Paryani is an Afghan women's rights activist and one of the best-known voices of resistance against the Taliban.
'Don't send us back': Afghan women in India fear deportation

A trained lawyer, she worked as a newspaper journalist before the Taliban returned to power. Following their takeover in August 2021, she took part in protests against restrictions on the rights of women and girls. In January 2022, she was detained by the Taliban in Kabul alongside her sisters. After her release, she managed to reach Europe.

Since then, she has continued to advocate internationally for the rights of Afghan women. At the end of October, she addressed the UN Security Council, describing the repression of women in Afghanistan and urging the international community not to normalise their systematic disenfranchisement.
"This is gender apartheid. We expect the international community to recognise it and stand with the women of Afghanistan," Paryani told DW.

Since returning to power in 2021, the Taliban have issued more than 100 decrees severely restricting the lives of women and girls. Girls are barred from secondary education, while women are denied access to universities. Women's opportunities to work outside the home are also severely restricted.
In Afghanistan, girls study in secret to skirt Taliban ban

The UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA), which monitors and regularly documents the human rights situation in the country, reported in September 2025 that inspectors from the Taliban's Ministry for the Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice were further restricting women's access to healthcare through the enforcement of regulations and decrees.

According to the UN, around 2.6 million girls are excluded from secondary education. This is likely to lead to more girls being married off at an early age and to an increase in maternal mortality, UN Women warns.
Afghanistan has a population of around 45 million. With a median age of approximately 17, it has one of the youngest populations in the world. Around 42% of its population is under the age of 15.
The world's 'worst women's rights crisis'

"What is happening in Afghanistan goes beyond gender-based persecution, as already defined under the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court," Haroon Mutasem, professor of International Criminal Law at the American University of Afghanistan and research fellow at Berlin's Humboldt University, told DW.
The Afghan legal scholar examines how the systematic oppression of women in Afghanistan can be classified and prosecuted under international law.

"This is not just about individual acts of persecution, but about an institutionalised system of oppression and domination of one gender group by another. They have established a system that considers women as secondary and defines a life for them as raising kids, working at home, and also actually satisfying the sexual desires of their men."

Mutasem argues that a failure to respond to the systematic oppression of Afghan women could undermine the universal validity of human and women's rights. He warns that other authoritarian regimes and extremist movements could adopt similar practices.
According to UN estimates, in 2027 more than 4 million children under the age of five, as well as around 1.27 million pregnant and breastfeeding women, will require treatment for acute malnutrition.

Susan Ferguson, the UN's Special Representative in Afghanistan, described the situation in her latest report as "the world's worst women's rights crisis." Afghan women, she said, are now "fighting for their very survival."
Cuts in aid funding have forced humanitarian organisations to make "impossible decisions about which women and girls can receive support and which have to be turned away," Ferguson said.
Exiled Afghanistan envoy still advocating for women's rights
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Veteran Nigerian Nollywood actor Pete Edochie dies aged 79
articles.summary: Odochie rose to prominence in 1987 after starring in a television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart.

blocks.text: Veteran Nigerian actor Pete Edochie, one of Africa's most celebrated film stars, has died at the age of 79, his family has announced.

Known for his deep voice, commanding screen presence and memorable use of African proverbs, Edochie became a household name across Africa, often portraying powerful traditional rulers, wealthy businessmen and family patriarchs.
In a statement, his family said Edochie died in the early hours of Wednesday in the south-eastern Nigerian city of Enugu following a prolonged battle with prostate cancer.
Tributes are pouring in from fans and fellow actors, remembering him as a Nollywood legend who helped shape Nigeria's film industry.

Edochie began his career as a broadcaster in 1967 before turning to acting. He rose to prominence in 1987 after starring in a television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart.

His portrayal of Okonkwo, the proud but troubled Igbo warrior in Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart, earned him international recognition helping establish him as one of Nigeria's most respected actors.
The television series depicted the struggles of an African community as British colonial rule and Christianity began to transform its traditional way of life.
He went on to become one of the most recognisable faces of Nollywood, Nigeria's film industry, which has since grown into one of the world's largest film industries.
Over a career spanning several decades, he appeared in numerous films, including Igodo, Rituals, Billionaire's Club and the 2018 romantic comedy Lionheart.
His contribution to the arts was recognised in 2003 when he received one of Nigeria's national honours, the Member of the Order of the Niger (MON).
He also received several other accolades during his career, including the Industry Merit Award at the Africa Magic Viewers' Choice Awards.
In recent years, his distinctive facial expressions, witty remarks and memorable scenes from his films found a new generation of admirers through viral social media memes.

"As we mourn this painful loss, we pray that Almighty God grants his gentle soul eternal rest and gives the entire family the fortitude to bear this irreparable loss," a statement shared on Instagram by his son Leo said.
Enugu State Governor Peter Mbah said Edochie's death was a huge loss to Nigeria, praising the actor for introducing international audiences to Igbo traditions and inspiring younger performers.
"Pete Edochie was more than an accomplished actor, he was an institution," Mbah said.
The Actors Guild of Nigeria (AGN) president, Abubakar Yakubu, described Edochie as a "father figure" in the entertainment industry, saying his influence would be felt for generations to come.
Edochie had spoken publicly about his deteriorating health during a visit to Ghana in October, saying he was struggling to walk and experiencing swelling in parts of his body.
He is survived by his wife, Josephine, and their six children, including fellow Nollywood actors Yul and Linc Edochie.

articles.title: DAR assures P600-M quick response fund amid El Niño threat
articles.summary: The Department of Agrarian Reform (DAR) said it has a P600-million quick response fund (QRF) ready to cushion agrarian reform beneficiaries against the looming effects of Super El Niño.

blocks.text: Published November 25, 2026 8:20pm
The Department of Agrarian Reform (DAR) said it has a P600-million quick response fund (QRF) ready to cushion agrarian reform beneficiaries against the looming effects of Super El Niño.
Budget sponsor Senator Francis “Kiko” Pangilinan said this during the Senate plenary deliberations into the proposed P16.121 billion budget of the DAR for fiscal year 2027.

“Dati walang quick response fund ang DAR. Naglaan tayo this year ng P600 million in anticipation of the impact of El Niño. Kaya meron silang quick response fund para matutukan ‘yung magiging impact ng El Niño lalo na sa ating mga magsasaka that form part of the agrarian reform beneficiaries and the communities,” he said.

(Previously, the DAR did not have a quick response fund. This year, we allocated P600 million in anticipation of the impact of El Niño. This provides them with a quick response fund to address the effects of El Niño, particularly for our farmers, that form part of the agrarian reform beneficiaries and the communities.)
Pangilinan gave the update after Senator Bong Go asked about the preparations of DAR to mitigate the expected effects of El Niño on agrarian reform beneficiaries (ARBs).

“With the threat of El Niño, we are concerned about its potential adverse effects on our agricultural sector, particularly on our agrarian reform beneficiaries whose livelihood heavily depends on farming,” Go said.

“Hindi po sapat na mabigyan lang ng sariling lupa ang ating mga magsasaka. Kailangan ding tiyakin natin na mayroon silang sapat na suporta lalo na sa panahon ng kalamidad at matinding tagtuyot,” he added.
(It’s not enough to simply provide our farmers with their own land. We must also ensure that they have sufficient support, especially during times of calamity and severe drought.)

According to Pangilinan, the DAR is implementing solar-powered irrigation projects in partnership with the National Irrigation Administration (NIA) to ensure a more reliable water supply amid the El Niño.
He said the agency is also endorsing the use of El Niño-resilient crops and is offering climate-resilient farm productivity support to help increase yields and improve household incomes of the ARBs.
The senator said these projects are expected to benefit 579 communities, 734 agrarian reform beneficiary organizations (ARBOs), and 26,900 ARBs.

Of the P949 million allocated for the two programs, Pangilinan said P219 million is proposed for the Sustainable Livelihood Support for Disaster Areas, while P730 million would go to the Major Crop Farm Productivity Enhancement.

articles.title: Mandarin Oriental is reborn, 12 years and a pandemic later
articles.summary: The 275-room luxury hotel reopens its doors just across the street from its old home, this time as part of the Ayala Triangle development

blocks.text: Composite by Guia Abogado/Rappler; Ayala Land photos
The 275-room luxury hotel reopens its doors just across the street from its old home, this time as part of the Ayala Triangle development

items: The new Mandarin Oriental hotel in Ayala Triangle, Makati, officially opened on November 26, 2020, after delays due to the pandemic, fulfilling a promise made in 2014.
The new hotel, designed by Skidmore, Owings & Merrill in collaboration with Leandro V. Locsin Partners, features 275 rooms, significantly fewer than the original hotel's 413 rooms.
Ayala Land aims to position the Philippines as a luxury tourism destination by emphasizing Filipino culture and craftsmanship in the hotel's design, rather than imitating other Asian luxury markets.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – When the last guests checked out of the Mandarin Oriental in September 2014, the hotel promised to be back in six years.
Makati would have to wait twice as long – with a pandemic in between that set back its original 2020 opening date – but the day has finally arrived.
On Thursday, November 26, Ayala Land opens the new Mandarin Oriental at Ayala Triangle, making good on a promise made more than a decade ago.

The original Mandarin opened on Makati Avenue in 1976, just in time for the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. Designed by National Artist for Architecture Leandro Locsin, it was among the first Mandarin Oriental hotels outside Hong Kong, arriving at a time when Makati was not yet the skyscraper-lined business district it is today.

That iconic structure has since been demolished, and in its place rises Park Central Towers, another Ayala Land development, billed as an ultra-luxury residential twin tower. (READ: Luxury condo resilience: Half of Ayala’s Laurean buyers staying despite pause)

Still, its successor, built just across the street, keeps a connection to the old Mandarin. American architectural firm Skidmore, Owings & Merrill designed the new hotel in collaboration with Leandro V. Locsin Partners, the practice founded by the late architect.

blocks.caption: REINVENTION. The 275-room Mandarin Hotel in Ayala Triangle, Makati City is owned by Ayala Land Hospitality and managed by Mandarin Oriental Hotel Group. Ayala Land handout

blocks.text: The new Mandarin is considerably smaller, at 275 rooms compared with its predecessor’s 413. That was part of the plan from the beginning, when Ayala Land first announced the project in June 2014.

The return of the Mandarin is also part of Ayala Land’s continuing reinvention of Ayala Triangle. Once part of Nielson Airport, the property went on to first house the Makati Stock Exchange and has today evolved into a hub anchored by Ayala Triangle Gardens Towers, with upscale restaurants and landscaped gardens – and finally, a luxury hotel to round it all out.

With the Mandarin, Ayala Land is also making a wager on the Philippines’ place in Asia’s luxury tourism market. The company believes Filipino culture and creativity can be a selling point in their own right, rather than looking to Singapore, Hong Kong, or Bangkok for a blueprint.

Filipino art, craftsmanship, and design feature prominently throughout the property. Ayala Land said it was designed around the idea that “the Philippines need not imitate other luxury destinations to compete with them.”

In the first nine months of 2026, Ayala Land’s leasing and hospitality revenues grew 8% year-on-year to P37.8 billion. Recurring-income businesses also now account for a greater part of the company’s earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA), standing at 55% and up from 44% in the same period last year. – Rappler.com

articles.title: UK embassy in Japan warns of rise in drink spiking and credit card fraud at Tokyo bars
articles.summary:
Social media campaign fronted by British rapper Shao Dow advises tourists not to let their guard down

The British embassy in Tokyo has launched a social media campaign warning visitors to…

blocks.text: The British embassy in Tokyo has launched a social media campaign warning visitors to exercise caution after a rise in cases of drink-spiking and credit card fraud against tourists in the Japanese capital.

In a recent clip made in conjunction with the embassy, the British rapper and manga artist Shao Dow, a frequent visitor to Japan, notes that although the country “is incredibly safe, that doesn’t mean you can let your guard down”.

He warns that young male tourists are particularly susceptible to being lured into bars on the promise of being able to chat to attractive, English-speaking women. They are then served drug-laced drinks and enormous sums are charged to their credit cards.
Drink-spiking cases involving British and other international tourists have been on the rise in the past two years in popular nightlife districts such as Roppongi, Shibuya and Kabukicho.

Some victims have lost up to £30,000 (US$39,000) in a single night, Dow says, and wake up with no memory of what happened. “Look, do me a favour,” he adds, “Stay alert, trust your gut, keep an eye on your stuff and don’t follow strangers into bars.”

Police in Tokyo have come under pressure to tackle the rise in incidents targeting tourists. Earlier this month, 160 riot police conducted predawn raids on two establishments in Kabukicho after reports they had ripped off customers. Five people were arrested.

Between January and October, police recorded 340 cases – up 195 from last year – in the Shinjuku area after customers, some of whom were lured into bars by street touts, were charged extortionate sums. In one case, ¥9.6m ($60,000) was allegedly charged to a customer’s credit card.

According to the newspaper Asahi Shimbun, victims have paid ¥390m in total and foreign nationals had been the targets in 70% of cases. The newspaper quoted a senior investigator as saying the reported crimes were the “tip of the iceberg” since many visitors returned home before they realised they had been swindled, while others had left Japan without reporting the incidents to police.
Reports say the rise in cases was being fuelled by Japan’s tourism boom. A record 42.7 million people visited Japan last year, including 530,000 from the UK.
