articles.title: Protesters call on Israel to free Palestinian student held without charge
articles.summary: Mahdi Tunsi, 26, was taken from his university dormitory earlier this month and has since been held without charge.

blocks.text: Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images
Mahdi Tunsi appears by videolink in front of his attorney Nasser Odeh during his hearing at the Jerusalem District Court on Tuesday
ByKaty Watson
Reporting fromEast Jerusalem

Israeli students, activists and academics are calling for the release of a Palestinian undergraduate who was taken from his university dormitory by Israeli police earlier this month and has since been held without charge.
Mahdi Tunsi, a 26-year-old sociology and criminology student at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, appeared in an Israeli court in the city on Tuesday - a hearing that was held behind closed doors.
Israeli police say he was arrested "concerning ties to an act of terrorism".

Authorities have requested what is known as "administrative detention", which allows the Israeli state to detain people indefinitely without charge on the basis of secret evidence that they cannot see.
"We definitely think this is a political arrest," said Dr Yael Berda, one of Tunsi's university professors.

Tunsi, a Palestinian resident of occupied East Jerusalem who works with well-known Jewish-Palestinian campaign groups, was arrested a month after Israel held an election that saw Arab-led parties win a record 19 seats in parliament, the Knesset, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing coalition lose its majority.
Since then, Berda said she had seen an intensifying campaign against Palestinian rights.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Knesset Member Dr Ofer Cassif was one of the those gathered outside the court

blocks.text: Knesset Member Dr Ofer Cassif was one of the those gathered outside the court
Outside the Jerusalem District Court on Tuesday, demonstrators waved placards with a black-and-white image of Tunsi, while crying out "shame" in unison.

"There's no due process - [administrative detention is] a sugar-coated term for being kidnapped and held as a hostage," said Dr Ofer Cassif, a Member of the Knesset representing the Arab-led Joint List alliance.
"We must all stand firm against such crimes. It's unacceptable."
Since the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, which triggered the Gaza war, the number of people in administrative detention has more than doubled.

In October, there were more than 3,100 in administrative detention, according to Israel Prison Service figures published by Israeli rights group HaMoked. Most of them are Palestinians from the occupied West Bank.
Israel says that its use of the policy is compliant with international law and a necessary preventative measure to combat terrorism.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Protesters held signs calling for Tunsi to be freed in Arabic and Hebrew

blocks.text: Protesters held signs calling for Tunsi to be freed in Arabic and Hebrew
In a statement, Israeli police said they would "not elaborate further regarding the investigation" into Tunsi.

He appeared via video link from prison - his hair and beard shaved off. His friends also said that he was without medication as well as his glasses, despite a judge requesting them to be brought to him in detention.
The Israel Prison Service said it acted in accordance with the court's rulings.

"When the process was complete and all the necessary approvals had been received, the detainee's lawyer was told he could pass the eyeglasses to the detainee immediately, subject to security procedures," it added.
Berda asked to enter the courtroom on Tuesday but was denied entry. According to Berda, not even Tunsi has been told of the evidence against him.
The judge has said more time is needed to consider the state's request for administrative detention. A decision is expected in the coming days.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The judge has said more time is needed to consider the state's request for administrative detention

blocks.text: The judge has said more time is needed to consider the state's request for administrative detention
"If they have evidence, have them bring it or release him," said Berda.
"That's why we're demanding his immediate release or moving it to a criminal track where he could defend himself."
Berda said that while Tunsi could not vote in Israel's general election because he is not an Israeli citizen, he was "engaged" and very supportive of Arab parties' involvement.
"Mahdi is one of the best human beings I know," said Noga Kaplan, who studies with him at the Hebrew University.
"He has a really pure heart and is very passionate about his studies."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Protesters demand the release of Mahdi Tunsi outside the Jerusalem Central Court during his hearing.

blocks.text: Protesters demand the release of Mahdi Tunsi outside the Jerusalem Central Court during his hearing.
After Tunsi's arrest, the Hebrew University issued a statement saying it was notified a few minutes before it took place.

"The university is not a party to the legal proceedings involving the student, and we do not have information that would allow us to comment on the circumstances leading to the arrest or on the ongoing legal proceedings," it said.
It added that it was concerned for Tunsi's well-being and hoped "that the matter will be resolved promptly and that his rights will be fully respected throughout the process".

Tunsi is a resident of Silwan, a neighbourhood in East Jerusalem where, in recent years, Palestinians have been evicted by Israeli authorities, who say their properties were built illegally. Israeli settlers have since moved into some of those properties.
"Political organisation stopped after October 7 because people were getting super scared about the consequences," explained Kaplan.
"Mahdi saw studying as one of the ways to speak about it in class."
"He didn't do a lot of public stuff because what's happening now is his biggest fear."

articles.title: She grew up in group homes. Now she’s piecing together her past
articles.summary: Marisa Wright, 37, is trying to piece together her broken childhood through school, police and government records. Some agencies initially supplied only a limited amount of information in a few…

image.caption: Marisa Wright, 37, accessed her personal records earlier this year. She was in provincial care from the age of 12 to 15. (Dave Irish/CBC)

blocks.text: WARNING: Details in this story discuss thoughts of suicide.
When Marisa Wright opened a thick paper file earlier this year detailing her childhood in government care, she thought she was ready.
Then she found a suicide note she'd written at the age of 15.

Typed in bold italic letters, Wright addressed the goodbye message to her friends and family saying she wanted to be “out of this world.” She recalls writing it on a school computer in Truro, isolated from her classmates.
“Honestly, I just wanted to die,” said Wright. “I felt so unloved.”
More than two decades later, she was shocked to see the note had been stored in her personal records for all of that time.
“I see a girl that was broken that really needed help. And nobody gave her help. Literally crying out on a page,” she said.
Why this woman fought to learn about a childhood spent in group homes

Wright, 37, is trying to decipher the holes of her childhood through school, police and government records. As an adult, she has faced a series of traumatic events that left her questioning how she became so fragile.

“I'm piecing everything together and seeing all the areas and all the times that I really needed help, and nobody gave it to me. So now I'm giving myself that help that I needed back then, and I'm building myself up,” said Wright.

Some agencies initially supplied only limited information in a few summary pages and others denied access completely — a common response, according to one expert who says former youth in care have a right to full, unredacted files and mental health support.

“It can be very traumatic to see how you were talked about in your case files from the various social workers that were in your life,” said Melanie Doucet, adjunct professor at the McGill University School of Social Work and project lead of the National Council of Youth in Care Advocates.
Melanie Doucet, a McGill University adjunct professor and former youth in care, says people deserve access to their full records with mental health support. (Submitted by Melanie Doucet)

As a former child in care in New Brunswick, Doucet understands how triggering it can be for people with a history of complex trauma to receive information about their childhood. She says that’s why she has been pushing for better access to therapy for youth currently and formerly in government care.
“This is a lifelong healing process for a lot of young people who've been through the system and it needs to be offered as soon as they enter into the system, not after they're adults,” said Doucet.

Robert Wright, president of the Nova Scotia College of Social Workers and founder of the Peoples' Counselling Clinic in Halifax, believes at the very least anyone receiving their personal file should have a clinician present when they open it for the first time.
“We recognize that reviewing a history, even though you were there, reviewing the history is traumatic,” he said.
“People need to — when they’re unpacking their history, whether that’s their history of sexual violence, their history of abuse, or their history of being in care — they need very real support.”
Marisa Wright's file was released through the province's disclosure program in February after a one-year wait. (CBC)

For Marisa Wright, seeing her own file validated memories from her childhood that were often brushed away. But then, feelings of despair and anger bubbled to the surface and quickly became overwhelming.

While she has sought counselling support in recent years, funding for sessions has been limited through non-profit programs. She says she does not have the means to access private therapy and wishes more free services were available.

In a written statement, the Department of Opportunities and Social Development said when people access their files through its disclosure program, a social worker is assigned to “assist people through the process of requesting, receiving and learning about their history.”
Wright said that support wasn’t made clear to her.

“I don’t think that the unit that provides information to people about their history of child welfare is sufficiently staffed to provide the necessary clinical support to the people who are inquiring,” said Robert Wright.
According to documents obtained through a freedom of information request, the disclosure program has eight provincial staff members including six social workers.

Marisa Wright received her personal file through the disclosure program in February. There were details she wasn't expecting in the stack of documents, while other details were not included at all. (Dave Irish/CBC)

In the weeks after she received her file last February, Marisa Wright wrestled again with thoughts of giving up. Then she started writing poems and posting videos on social media, which she says eased the burden inside her head.
“The more that I write, the more that I put this out, the more that I read … it's all coming back to me, and I feel like I deserve a place in this world,” said Wright.
“I deserve answers.”
Broken childhood

From the age of 12, Wright bounced between group homes and schools throughout Nova Scotia until she was discharged from provincial care at the age of 15 — the same year she typed the suicide note in school.

She says her life completely unravelled following a sexual assault in 2004 that happened while she was "gone without permission" from a group home in rural Pictou County. A provincial document in her personal file outlines how police questioned the credibility of Wright’s allegations and did not proceed with charges. Staff members at the home noticed she became anxious and angry, according to the documents.

Then, following a weekend visit with her family soon after the incident, Wright refused to return because she didn’t feel safe. Her bed was held for one month as she struggled with whether to come back, according to an unsigned release letter included in her file.
“Historically, Marisa was noted to be a runner and although for the most part she physically stopped this behaviour she proceeded to emotionally run from her issues,” the letter stated.
Marisa Wright spent her early teen years bouncing between schools and group homes in Nova Scotia. (Marisa Wright/Submitted)

Her file consistently paints her as a child who tended to bully her peers and lash out — points Wright doesn’t deny. However, she maintains no one ever asked why she was acting out, or what happened before she ended up in government care.
To this day, Wright doesn’t understand how provincial staff members allowed her to return to an unstable home environment.
“I just remember my house being a crack house. It was the party spot where people would come to get messed up, and a lot of bad things happened,” she said.
“The province had a duty to protect me, and they didn't.”
In a written statement, the department told CBC it was unable to comment on individual cases but “a care and custody order would be a determination made by the courts.”
Expert says Wright’s experience is widespread
Doucet said this is, sadly, a common story across the country. But she believes Wright’s account should be a wake-up call for officials in charge of youth in care.
“Dismissing cries for help like that is what results in deaths in the system,” said Doucet.
“We have to be going to the root causes of things if we want to truly make a difference in the lives of young people and have things resolved so that they have a chance to have a successful future.”
Wright also believes change within the system is possible. She continues to recite poems and share her lived experience on social media, which she says has resulted in a surprising response.
“The amount of people that commented and encouraged me and said, you know, this is amazing. And we see you, we hear you and we believe you,” Wright said.
“I've always wanted to help people, and I feel like if I put my stuff out there, my story, that I can resonate with other people.”

They are among society's most vulnerable: children who experience traumatic instability and end up in government care. In this series called “Left Behind,” the CBC Atlantic investigative team explores the challenges and outcomes through the eyes of people who lived through this and those trying to help them.

articles.title: Colombian police storm supermarket to free 20 held hostage for 17 hours
articles.summary: One gunman was killed in the operation to free around 20 shoppers and employees after a 17-hour hostage ordeal.

blocks.text: Residents living near the supermarket reported hearing explosions as the security forces moved into the building.
Police later confirmed that officers had used stun grenades to overpower the hostage takers.
De la Espriella described it as "an extraordinary joint operation", which he said had been carried out "flawlessly".
He flew into the northern city to oversee the operation.
In footage released since then, he can be seen speaking into a walkie-talkie and carrying a handgun strapped to his side.
Speaking after the successful rescue of the hostages, he said that the gunmen had been given the chance to hand themselves in, which they had refused.
Earlier in the day, the men had freed 10 of their hostages, among them elderly women.
But they continued to hold around 20, even as a police helicopter hovered above and special forces erected a perimeter around the building.
Local media said that as well as demanding safe passage out of the supermarket, the gunmen also demanded nearly $2m (£1.5m) and armoured vehicles.
According to President De la Espriella, they had no political affiliations but had taken the hostages once their plan to rob an armoured car carrying money had been foiled.
"It's not that a terrorist group carried out a kidnapping - no, these are criminals who were caught off guard, had no way out, and then kidnapped a group of people," he said.
Photos taken during the rescue operation show armed soldiers inside the building while people are kneeling with their hands behind their heads.

articles.title: Climate loss and damage fund exists, but the money doesn't
articles.summary: Climate-vulnerable countries fought for years to create a loss and damage fund. Four years on, demand far outstrips funding, pledges are scarce, and disaster-hit nations are still waiting for support.

image.caption: Nepal in the aftermath of August flash floods that killed more than 1,500 people, with thousands more missingImage: Arun Sankar/AFP

blocks.text: On the sandbars and river islands of Bangladesh's Brahmaputra and its branches, families have little to fall back on when the water rises.
"The floodwater swallows everything," said 16-year-old Rasel Babu who had traveled to Antalya, Turkey to speak to delegates at the UN climate conference.

Created after years of pressure from vulnerable nations, the loss and damage fund was designed to help countries recover from climate disasters and irreversible climate impacts. This includes extreme weather events such as floods, heat waves and wildfires as well as slow onset impacts such as sea level rise, desertification and damage to infrastructure and crops.
But the fund is already struggling to meet demand. It received $2.8 billion (€2.56 billion) in urgent requests in a first call for funding, with only $342 million available at the time.
Even the money promised has not fully arrived. Only about half of the money currently pledged had been received by this summer.

While the European Commission signed a €25 million ($27 million) contribution agreement to the fund on the margins of COP31, formalizing an earlier pledge made at COP28, and Spain pledged an additional €15 million, other contributions to loss and damage remained scarce.
First payout will go to Nepal after glacier collapse

The fund's first emergency response is going to be paid out to Nepal. The board of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage had provisionally set aside $21.6 million following the catastrophic glacier collapse that triggered flash floods in August, killing more than 1,500 people with 5,600 more missing.
But the money has not moved yet. Nepal must first submit a funding request setting out how it will be spent.

"It's asking for a country that is dealing with the climate emergency to work on a proposal," Nepali climate finance expert Bibek Raj Kandel said, adding a layer of bureaucracy inefficient to address the urgency.
UN warns climate change could force millions to move

Nepal is already waiting on another request, filed after floods in Kathmandu and landslides in the eastern hills. "There's already one pending proposal sitting on the table," Kandel said. Unless the fund speeds up, he warned, it's "going to disappoint many, many countries."
Pakistan which led the push for the fund in 2022 after floods affected 33 million people and killed more than 1,730, also hasn't seen any of the money yet.

"Pakistan was one of the countries which really spoke up and managed to get the loss and damage fund on the climate agenda. But it takes a long time," Pakistan's Minister of State for Climate Change, Shezra Mansab Ali Khan Kharal, told DW.

blocks.caption: In 2022, monsoon and floods killed more than 1,730 people in Pakistan, with 33 million people affectedImage: Akhtar Soomro/REUTERS

blocks.text: "We have still not really got anything. We haven't seen anything on the ground at all as yet," Kharal said. Pakistan has submitted two projects and was told the cap is $200 million.
Other forms of aid often come in the form of loans.

"These promises, they are hollow promises," said Abid Qaiyum Suleri, Executive Director of the Sustainable Development Policy Institute (SDPI) in Islamabad, adding that for a heavily indebted country, the form of the money matters as much as the amount.
"We do not want that a climate disaster in Pakistan should translate into further debt for Pakistan," Kharal said, calling for grants rather than loans.

articles.title: More connected but lonelier than ever: How do we navigate an AI-reliant world?
articles.summary: Mental health advocates say that tools like AI chatbots normalize isolation and provide a false sense of connection. Where do we draw the line, especially for the youth?

blocks.text: Mental health advocates say that tools like AI chatbots normalize isolation and provide a false sense of connection. Where do we draw the line, especially for the youth?

items: The rise of artificial intelligence and social media has transformed childhood experiences, leading to increased reliance on screens and AI chatbots for companionship and support.
Mental health advocates express concern that AI chatbots may normalize isolation and prevent meaningful human connections, particularly among children and vulnerable individuals.
Experts emphasize the need for a systemic approach to address the impact of technology on mental health, advocating for stronger community support and human-centered policies.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Childhood looks different for many kids nowadays in the age of artificial intelligence and social media.

Toys are no longer the only things keeping them busy. Screens dominate their free time. And when they want to play with their friends, they don’t always just head outside anymore; they log onto gaming platforms instead.

And when they become lonely and need someone to open up to, it’s no longer a human hearing them out — but an AI chatbot. For mental health advocates like actress and She Talks Asia co-founder Iza Calzado, the rise of these tools is alarming. Under the guise of connection and offering safe spaces, AI chatbots often just work to normalize isolation, and it’s a reality that many humans who have fallen for the trap have to face.

“It’s safer to chat with a bot in this landscape. It agrees with you all the time. It does not judge you. It’s never disappointed when you say something. So imagine a child, who perhaps does not feel as confident or as safe in their own home, is lonely, starts talking to a bot, and then eventually becomes friends with a bot,” Calzado illustrated during a panel discussion at Rappler’s 2026 Social Good Summit last Saturday, November 21.
“Because you know what? This friend will not unfriend me, will not spread rumors about me in school, and will not bully me. That’s how it begins, and that to me is very concerning.”

Even among adults, AI chatbots have become pseudo-therapists who help rationalize their thoughts, make sense of whatever they’re going through, and validate their feelings — even when they may be in the wrong. The chatbot pulls you in by making you feel seen, and before you know it, you’ve been completely hooked.
But why does it do this?
For Empath CEO and founder Steph Naval, it’s simple: AI chatbots are there to make money.

blocks.caption: Steph Naval at We the Humans, Social Good Summit at BGC, Taguig City, on November 20, 2026.

blocks.text: “Chatbots, when you go there for a replacement of therapy or well-being, what happens is that you don’t get the benefit of having difficult conversations and corrective behavior. Because that’s something that you do in therapy,” Naval said, adding that it was in her painful therapy sessions that she was actually able to heal and grow most.

blocks.caption: Unpacking mental health chats with AI: Finding comfort, but not treatment

blocks.text: It’s the same with social media, which has become a fierce breeding ground for insecurity. Naval said these apps can detect that through your images and videos, and “responds by pushing certain products or content that can exacerbate these negative thoughts.

“For example, it takes a lot of photos of your body or the gym and then they can detect if you feel insecure. Then they’ll push products to you. So I find that’s something to definitely take note of because that has really caused and affected a generation,” said Naval.

Social media and chatbots, however, don’t just offer you a false sense of companionship and feed on your biggest vulnerabilities. They have also doubled a platform for groups to promote violence among young children — and this is something that has become apparent in the alarming rise of school shooting incidents in the Philippines.

blocks.caption: [Be The Good] Not another school shooting please

blocks.text: Still, Akbayan Representative Perci Cendaña believes that the growing reliance on these chatbots isn’t something you can blame on those who turn to it, especially in countries like the Philippines where mental health services are scarce. From then on, it only leads to a bigger set of issues that the country is not yet equipped to properly address.

“We lack mental health assistance, that’s why our countrymen go online instead. They rely on chatbots. They rely on the warmth and affirmation they get from these platforms, and this phenomenon, combined with other social realities, are fueling these isolated incidents,” Cendaña said in a mix of Filipino and English.
“Nauuna ang teknolohiya sa polisiya. Nauuna ang teknolohiya sa government framework (Technology is prioritized over policy. Technology is ahead of the government framework),” he added.

blocks.caption: Perci Cendaña at We the Humans, Social Good Summit at BGC, Taguig City, on November 20, 2026.

blocks.text: This is what Cendaña hopes to address through the National AI Governance Act — which is anchored on human-centeredness. It contains the AI Bill of Rights, which holds that humans should have the authority to override platform systems.

Cendaña then believes that tech executives and government officials shouldn’t be the only ones making decisions about AI governance. Because it’s human well-being at the very core of it all, civil society should have a seat at the table, too.

The solutions to the impact of AI and technology on community mental health requires an intensive systemic approach. But these policies are not what we should only rely on, because these safeguards should start at home.
“Home should be the safest space. That’s the first line of defense — families, friends… So let’s make sure that we are that for our children,” Calzado said.

blocks.caption: Iza Calzado at We the Humans, Social Good Summit at BGC, Taguig City, on November 20, 2026.

blocks.text: Parents need their own community, too, however. It takes more than a village to raise a child in this era, and parents also need their own kind of support and human connection so they can come home strong to their kids.

For Naval, one of the best ways to do that is to dedicate time to activities that will allow you to interact with other human beings. Take a wellness class. Join clubs for your hobbies. Make the effort to see your friends in person.
Technology and AI are here to stay. Decentering it, then, requires us to go back to our roots as humans and hone in on that. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Germany's women's football team take stand against domestic violence
articles.summary: Germany's women's football team are to wear UN Women badges in games against Argentina and Peru, as domestic violence hits a record high in Germany.

image.caption: Germany's women have been strong supporters of the campaign, as the orange logo of 'stop violence agianst women' reveals on Lea Schüller's sleeveImage: imago images/Beautiful Sports

blocks.text: Domestic violence has reached a record high in Germany, with 16 women subjected to physical abuse behind closed doors each hour.

UN Women Germany is one of 13 UN Women national committees worldwide, each an independent, non-profit, non-governmental organization committed to gender equality and the empowerment of women and girls.

Their current campaign "Orange The World" runs from the start of International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women on November 25 to December 10, International Human Rights Day. It is designed to raise awareness around violence against women in the country and worldwide. The 2026 campaign's focus is particularly on men's responsibility in ending gender-based violence.

"In these 16 days of activism, we can deliver a lot of information. Survivors of gender-based violence can find out where to get support and be reminded that they are not at fault," UN Women Germany chair, politician and long-standing campaigner for women's rights Elke Ferner told DW. "The debate helps and it's a chance to change consciousness about the topic."

Germany captain Giulia Gwinn said in a statement via the German Football Association (DFB): "Violence against women and girls affects us all and must have no place in our society. As the women's national team, we therefore want to once again use our reach to create awareness for this important issue and jointly set a visible sign against violence."
The campaign with the women's team is not new. Two years ago, the team joined the campaign, delivering a moving video that saw players reveal the truth of statements by crossing out words.

During Germany's upcoming South America tour — part of their preparations for the 2027 World Cup in Brazil — they are to wear special UN Women Germany badges on their sleeves in their games against Argentina and Peru.
Role models pivotal for the campaign

Ferner believes the work with role models is pivotal and that the campaign is powerful, especially in a football context. A 2022 study from Warwick Business School in the UK revealed alcohol-related domestic abuse rises by nearly 50% after England's men's football team win a World Cup game, never mind lose.

Currently, there is no data on domestic abuse during Germany games, however during the 2026 World Cup last summer, Berlin police recorded a 31% increase in domestic violence compared to the week before.

Ferner is encouraged that sport has understood the importance of the issue, and that the German Olympic Committee (DOSB) and other sports clubs and organizations are helping move the conversation forward.

In sport, this is particularly important given the problematic nature of dependency relationships that so often exist in high-performance environments. But violence against women is really a societal issue that is not specific to class, origin, religion or societal space, such as sport.

"Violence against women has structural origins and to change that you need to change the structures," Ferner said. "You just need to do it. I always say, this isn't about a lack of knowledge but rather a lack of action."
Performance is an integral part of sport, but a multi-dimensional understanding of it might help shift perspective in a country that remains driven by a performance culture.

"What is performance? Higher, faster, further? Or is it managing to look after a family of three?" Ferner asked. "Why do people who repair washing machines earn more than those looking after your kids in nursery? This is about changing business culture, but also awareness around the role men play at home and in the family.

"The picture boys and young men get of girls and women in school is a problem that needs addressing. We can't wait for generational change. This is about saving lives. We need to change societal structures."
Male power structures a problem

Sports structures are also in need of reform. Non-profit organization Safe Sport provides independent support for people affected by sexual, physical and psychological violence in both amateur and professional sport in Germany.

They are the only organization with a specific focus on violence in grassroots sports in Germany, and one of only two in professional sport in the country. They also have to contend with structures, in a sporting context, that make spaces less safe for women.

"Gender roles have become more fluid in the last few years, but in associations and clubs management positions are still occupied by men, regardless of the sport," Safe Sport manager Ina Lambert told DW.
"In professional sport, there are a lot fewer women involved in training and so the space remains male dominated, and, as a result, so do the power structures.

"We have people in search of advice, men included, who see the problems and want to enforce change, and we offer them support so they are not alone," Lambert said. "But whether in a big association or a small club, perpetrators are frequently protected, incidents are ignored and so the people who want to enforce change are often prevented from doing so."

Safe Sport, which provides free psychological and legal support, has only been in action since July 2023, but in that time the number of support requests they have received continues to grow. Psychological violence in sport in Germany is the most common case they are faced with, but sexual violence is also a major problem.
"There is finally recognition of the problem and there is a seriousness about tackling it," Lambert said.

"There is a lot of good work being done in the right direction, with many good concepts for prevention, intervention and processing violence, as well as more education, holistic training and focus on women's menstrual cycles."

blocks.caption: Germany is backing UN efforts to highlight that more must be done to tackle violence against womenImage: imago images/Lucca Fundel

blocks.text: Comprehensive support on the way

Germany's Interior Ministry is leading the process with participants from the country's states, organized sport, affected parties and academia to create a central hub. The center for safe sport was founded in July 2026, but investigative and sanctioning work is expected to begin in the spring of 2027.
Support from leading figures clearly makes a huge difference, but it's also clear that more data is needed. Addressing the underlying issues, such as social norms and gender stereotyping, is a must.

After all, as UN Women Executive Director Sima Bahous said: "No country has yet eliminated violence against women. Ending it requires transformative action — greater investment, innovation, and unwavering political will."

articles.title: All hostages rescued after Colombian security forces storm supermarket, says president
articles.summary:
Operation in which one hostage-taker was killed ends daylong siege in Cartegena shopping centre, where 30 people were initially held

Colombian security forces have stormed a supermarket in…

blocks.text: Colombian security forces have stormed a supermarket in the Caribbean city of Cartagena, ending a daylong hostage siege, with the president saying all those held had been rescued and one hostage-taker killed.
Several explosions were heard before security forces entered the building, where about 20 people were believed to be being held by armed men.
President Abelardo de la Espriella, said: “In an extraordinary joint operation between the national police and the armed forces, all the hostages were rescued.”

Shortly after midnight on Wednesday, a police helicopter was hovering low over the shopping centre as security forces massed outside the supermarket. Explosions then echoed around the complex as tactical teams moved in.
Ten of an estimated 30 people that were initially held had already been released during the 17-hour standoff, including several elderly women.
Moments later, soldiers could be seen inside the Éxito supermarket as security forces secured the building.

De la Espriella, who appeared at the scene wearing fatigues and carrying a sidearm and a walkie-talkie, described the operation as a success. He said: “We gave them the opportunity to surrender and free the hostages. They rejected that opportunity and we acted decisively.”
Cartagena’s mayor said all the hostages were “safe and sound” and would be reunited with their families before undergoing medical checks.
The siege gripped Cartagena, a Caribbean port famed for its colonial walled old town, beach resorts and cruise-ship tourism. Supermarket employees had been among those feared trapped inside.

blocks.caption: Hostages inside the supermarket. Photograph: Sergio Jimenez Ciro/EPA

blocks.text: “My son is there,” Jacob Pérez, the father of one of the workers, said earlier in the standoff. “He didn’t leave work and he’s not answering his phone. I think they took it from him.”
Images broadcast by Colombian media and shared online appeared to show masked gunmen in tactical gear alongside zip-tied hostages inside the store.

De la Espriella was quick to rule out the involvement of guerrilla or paramilitary groups. “It’s not that a terrorist group carried out a kidnapping – no, these are criminals who were caught off guard, had no way out, and then kidnapped a group of people,” he said.
Authorities said the siege began after an attempted robbery on an armoured vehicle at the shopping centre.

According to local media, the hostage-takers were demanding nearly US$2m (£1.5m), two armoured vehicles and safe passage to the city of Barranquilla, about 80 miles (130km) north-east of Cartagena. AFP could not independently verify those reports.

The siege began on the 10th anniversary of Colombia’s landmark peace accord with Farc guerrillas amid a series of attacks across the country. Despite the deal to end the region’s largest insurgency, dissident guerrilla groups and criminal organisations still fight for control of parts of the country.
On Monday, authorities blamed a dissident Farc faction for a car bomb attack in the city of Villavicencio that wounded 25 people and caused extensive damage.

Separately, the presidency said a “terrorist attack” on electrical infrastructure had disrupted power supplies in several south-western departments and prompted additional measures to protect energy facilities.

articles.title: ‘Russia wants more than Ukraine,’ Germany’s Merz warns – Europe live
articles.summary:
German chancellor, in wide-ranging speech, says Moscow is ‘escalating on a massive scale’

Merz also touches on this week’s EU summit, starting tomorrow, and the likely…

blocks.text: 'Russia wants more than Ukraine,' Germany's Merz warns, as he says Moscow is 'escalating on a massive scale'

In his wide-ranging budget speech, Merz talks about Germany “neglecting fundamental issues for far too long” on defence, infrastructure, demographic change, and the economy – and the need to address these issues urgently.
But the starkest part of his speech comes as he talks about the external situation – and particularly the threat from Russia - to explain why some decisions, particularly on defence, are needed.
“Russia knows exactly what it wants and Russia wants more than Ukraine,” he warns.

“Anyone who fails to grasp this either does not understand the world as it is, or is pursuing an entirely different agenda – one that stands in opposition to the freedom, openness, and liberal values ​​of our own country.”
Merz warns that “Russia is escalating tensions in the Baltic region, in Poland, in the Black Sea, and even in the outer space.”

“It is escalating on a massive scale – including here within our own borders, even at the cost of human lives. That is the situation, ladies and gentlemen. And that is why we, as Europeans, must—and will – set clear boundaries for Russia.”
Key events

items: 14m agoGermany has 'begun to change course' amid major challenges, Merz says
22m ago'By supporting Ukraine, we are supporting and protecting ourselves,' Merz tells parliament
26m ago'Russia wants more than Ukraine,' Germany's Merz warns, as he says Moscow is 'escalating on a massive scale'
37m agoMorning opening: Ukraine reporting energy outages in five regions after Russian strikes

blocks.text: Germany has 'begun to change course' amid major challenges, Merz says
Merz also touches on this week’s EU summit, starting tomorrow, and the likely contentious negotiations over the next EU budget.
He pushes back on “impressions” that he thinks Germany spends too much on EU contributions.
But he says he is “pushing for us to limit and focus our spending on what truly strengthens Europe today,” specifically on security and competitiveness.

In a pretty passionate defence of European integration, he says only such focused spending will give Europe “an assurance that we will not simply become a plaything in this world, but have a hand in shaping it.”

Summing up, he repeats his earlier point that Germany faces major challenges that have been unresolved for too long, and so one budget “is far from solving all of our problems,” but says “we have begun to change course” as economic indicators are starting to improve.
And he ends his speech there.

blocks.caption: German chancellor Friedrich Merz takes a drink of water as he sits down after his speech. Photograph: Odd Andersen/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: 'By supporting Ukraine, we are supporting and protecting ourselves,' Merz tells parliament

Merz goes back to last week’s meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Berlin, saying the US delegation was “it seemed to me, quite clearly surprised by how united … the Europeans are on this issue.”
“It is precisely this determination, ladies and gentlemen, that allows for a cautious optimism regarding the prospect of peace – a genuine peace,” he says.
He keeps coming back to his main message: “by supporting Ukraine, we are supporting and protecting ourselves.”
“This is true in a sense that may not yet be fully understood by many in our country,” he stresses.
Germany’s chancellor Friedrich Merz is speaking in the Bundestag now – mostly on the 2027 budget, but he’s also touching upon broader issues, including on Russia and Ukraine.

articles.title: South Africa's Ramaphosa wins court battle over impeachment threat
articles.summary: The break-in happened in 2020, when thieves allegedly stole bundles of US dollar bills hidden inside a sofa at the farm.

blocks.text: South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has won a legal battle to overturn a report that found he may have a case to answer over the theft of large sums of cash from his private farm.

In 2022, an independent panel said Ramaphosa may have committed serious misconduct relating to the theft of $580,000 (£443,000), hidden in a sofa, at his Phala Phala game farm in the Limpopo province. He denied any wrongdoing.
Ramaphosa challenged the findings of the report in court after the Constitutional Court ruled that parliament had violated the constitution by blocking moves to impeach him.
The Western Cape high court ruled that the panel's report was unlawful and set it aside "in its entirety".

In its judgment, the court said the panel, appointed by parliament to investigate the allegations against Ramaphosa, had "misconstrued its function, the nature of the inquiry it was to conduct and the recommendation it was required to make".

"It went beyond its lawful remit ... and made several material errors of law. [Therefore] the report of the independent panel ... is declared unlawful and is reviewed and set aside in its entirety," Judge Nolwazi Mabindla-Boqwana said.
The court also declared unlawful the steps taken by parliament in relation to the report.
The ruling effectively removes the basis for the parliamentary impeachment process against Ramaphosa, although opposition parties have indicated they intend to challenge the decision.
The scandal, dubbed "Farmgate" by local media, has has dogged Ramaphosa since it emerged in 2022, when former spy chief Arthur Fraser reported the matter to police in a dossier.
Fraser, an ally of former President Jacob Zuma, accused Ramaphosa of concealing the theft from the police and tax authorities.
The break-in took place in 2020, when thieves allegedly stole bundles of US dollar bills hidden inside a sofa at the farm.
Earlier this month, two people were found guilty of the theft.
Ramaphosa confirmed that a robbery had taken place but said the money had been from the legitimate sale of buffalo from his livestock business.
Several investigations cleared him of any wrongdoing, but parliament began an impeachment proceedings in 2022 and appointed an independent panel to investigate the allegations.
The panel made a series of damaging findings, including that there was "substantial doubt about the legitimacy of the source of the currency that was stolen".
It also concluded that Ramaphosa "has a case to answer".
Ramaphosa initially challenged the report in court but withdrew his application after parliament voted against adopting its findings.
He revived the legal challenge again in May this year after the Constitutional Court, the country's highest court, ruled that parliament had acted unconstitutionally by blocking moves to impeach him.
It ordered parliament to refer the report to an impeachment committee.
In his latest challenge, Ramaphosa argued that the panel had "misconceived its mandate, misjudged the information placed before it and misinterpreted the four charges advanced against me".
The Western Cape High Court's ruling could bring the current impeachment process to an end, unless parliament successfully challenges the decision.
If they do, and the appeal is successful, the parliamentary committee would be able to examine the charges against the president and make a recommendation.
If the committee recommends impeachment, parliament would have to vote on whether to remove him from office. This would require the support of at least two-thirds majority in parliament.
Ramaphosa's Africa National Congress (ANC) has enough parliamentary seats to block such a move.
He is the first president to face impeachment proceedings under the rules introduced in 2018.

articles.title: Large bushfire threatens homes and properties on remote island off Tasmania
articles.summary:
Blaze spreads significantly across the north of Flinders Island after being started by lightning strikes

  • Get our

blocks.text: Homes and properties on a picturesque remote island are under threat from an out-of-control bushfire that has sent smoke hundreds of kilometres south.
The blaze on Flinders Island in Bass Strait spread significantly on Wednesday after being started by lightning strikes.
Some structures had been destroyed but it was too early to tell whether they were homes, the Tasmania Fire Service incident controller Steven Richardson said.
A Bureau of Meteorology post on X featured a video showing a vast column of smoke being blown south across north-east Tasmania, as northerly winds pushed the plume across Bass Strait.

blocks.caption: Authorities said it was too early to tell whether any homes had been lost in the blaze.  Photograph: Tasmania Fire Service

blocks.text: As of Wednesday night, three emergency warnings were in place, including for the coastal settlement of Killiecrankie and nearby areas Leeka, Mount Tanner, Mount Boyes and Carnacs Flat.
Some residents were warned it was too late to leave.
Roughly 3,000 hectares had been burned by the fire on Tuesday, before it spread south on Wednesday following a wind change.
Residents on the island, which is about 130,000 hectares in size and home to 900 people, posted photos of massive plumes of smoke on social media.
Mick Grimshaw, a farmer, helped friends move cattle from their property and said they had lost some fences.
“We were under the ashes. Right there. But we’ve got them safe,” he told ABC radio.
“The fire threat for this farm looks like it has abated a bit but certainly not further down the island.
“We can see the smoke front heading right down the guts of the island.”
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: A ringtail possum near the burnt-out bush on Flinders Island. Photograph: Tasmania Fire Service

blocks.text: Nearly 40 firefighters were working to control the bushfire, plus 12 parks and wildlife staff, five helicopters and three aircraft.
“Additional resources are being deployed and Tasmania Police is also helping evacuate people, particularly in the Leeka and Mount Tanner areas,” parks minister Nick Duigan said.
“There is a lot of smoke in the area and it’s now coming down Tasmania’s coast.”
Several roads have been closed because of poor visibility due to smoke.
Flinders Island is known for high-quality exports, including beef, lamb, wool and seafood.

articles.title: Suspected North Korean computer programmers did contract work for B.C. government
articles.byline: Matthew Pierce, Scott Anderson, Mark Kelley

image.caption: A man going by the name Kevin Zhang, who worked for the B.C. government, had these two fake Chinese passports in an online account. (kzdev420 / GitHub)

blocks.text: Four computer programmers who did contract work for the British Columbia government were likely North Korean operatives, CBC's the fifth estate has learned.
Between 2023 and 2025, the four were hired to work on the province’s business registry platform.

As part of a contract worth hundreds of thousands of dollars to supply the province with software developers, an IT staffing firm based in B.C.’s Lower Mainland facilitated the hiring of a man calling himself Kevin Zhang.

"Kevin's resume was ideal for the situation that I was dealing with," said the owner of the staffing firm. He spoke with the fifth estate on the condition that he and his company not be named. He said due to the nature of remote hiring, he was completely unaware he hired likely North Koreans.
Over the last year, the fifth estate has been investigating North Korean IT workers and how they, like Zhang, have been able to infiltrate Canadian businesses and government.
"With Zhang, he's pretty known," said Michael Barnhart, a former U.S. Army intelligence officer who investigates North Korea for the private sector.

"I had tracked him before. There's a couple crypto companies that had tracked him before. A couple of other just different industries that had been tracking him. And everyone had a different piece of the puzzle."
The photo from Kevin Zhang’s website, left, does not match that of the passports saved to his GitHub account, right. (kzdev420/GitHub)
Alongside the confirmation of experts like Barnhart, the fifth estate found multiple online clues that point toward North Korean IT worker tradecraft:

In an online profile Zhang used to do work for the B.C. government, he stored two fake Chinese passports. The place of birth for the holder is the Chinese province of Liaoning, which directly borders North Korea. The U.S. Department of the Treasury has previously sanctioned companies operating IT worker cells in Liaoning.

items: Watch the full documentary, "For Hire: North Korea's IT Army" from the fifth estate on YouTube, CBC Gem or CBC-TV on Friday at 9 p.m.

blocks.text: The names on the passports appear to have been modified, with neither matching the name on the bottom stripe of the document.
A resumé-style website for Zhang contained a headshot that did not match the photo on the passports.
"This is the same guy that also goes by Kevin Chang, too," Barnhart said. "Sometimes he’ll only go by that.
"Chang, Ching or Zhang, just different variations of the beginning or ending name."

As time went on, the B.C. government hired three more remote developers via the same IT staffing firm. The owner of the firm told the fifth estate that each was recommended by Zhang, who said they were former colleagues.
The owner said the B.C. government made the ultimate decision to hire them and would have conducted a 30-minute interview focused on competency.

The fifth estate reached out to multiple people and entities within the B.C. government, but received no response or was told that because of the provincial election, which concluded Oct. 24, the government would not be able to provide a response.

In response to a freedom of information request, the fifth estate was told that the ministry where Zhang worked could not locate an employee by that name, despite having been provided the account details that logged his specific contributions to a ministry software project.
Red flags
Beyond the fake Chinese passports and differing headshots, an investigation of Zhang and his colleagues conducted by the fifth estate revealed numerous other oddities.
For instance, a resumé for Zhang found online, which listed the B.C. government as a prior employer, stated his address was "Main St. E, North Bay, ON," with the street number absent.
In email correspondence provided to the fifth estate by the B.C. staffing firm, Zhang and the other developers can be seen repeatedly changing their banking information.

"In retrospect, there's a highly unusual situation to have somebody change their bank, change their company," the B.C. staffing firm’s owner said. "I think in the years that I've been doing this, right, this happened once before, twice before."
This is a red flag, according to cybersecurity expert Barnhart.

"I’ve had the same bank account at my employer for decades. I’ve never told my company to change it, ever. If I have, it would have been once. If I’d have done it twice, that would have been like: 'What are you doing?’"

At one point last year, Zhang asked to be paid to the bank account for a company called Dev Dragon Inc. Corporate records show Dev Dragon, now defunct, was registered by a James Zhang at a derelict building in Dawson City, Yukon.
The registered address for DevDragon Inc. was a long-abandoned bank building in Dawson City, Yukon. (CBC)

One of the other remote workers, Brandon Galli, had a similarly confusing digital footprint. On the account connected to his position working on B.C. government code, Galli’s profile photo is of an Asian man. However, his closely linked personal website provides a photo of a Caucasian man.
In an email obtained by the fifth estate, Galli asked for his pay to go to the account of an Ontario company called Luk Castle Investments, registered to a home in Markham by a man named Kenny Luk.
According to his LinkedIn, Luk did computer programming jobs for a number of Canadian banks before starting a software development consultancy.

When the fifth estate contacted Luk to ask about Brendan Galli and the money paid to him, he said that "Luk Castle Investments does not participate in media inquiries or respond to unsolicited questions regarding its business activities. Neither I nor anyone associated with the company will be providing comment on this matter."
It is a common practice for North Korean IT workers to use a real person’s identity to commit their fraud. (GitHub/Brandongalli.io)
The fifth estate tracked down the real Brandon Galli in New Jersey. When told that someone using his identity had worked for the B.C. government, he said his identity might have been stolen.
But pressed further, he admitted he gave his identity to someone he was working with online. He said this person continues to use his identity without his permission, causing him a host of problems.

items: Ontario architect's seal forged by remote worker believed to be North Korean fraudster
Binance says $6.3B US hacked in what could be largest cryptocurrency theft ever

blocks.text: "It was before the pandemic. We were working together on upwork and freelancing platforms and I was receiving small payouts for a short time while I was in college just to pay for food," Galli told the fifth estate in a WhatsApp message.
Barnhart has seen this same pattern play out before.
"You'll see them targeting college students a lot that might need some money," he said.

"Where it's like: 'Hey, I don't want anything from you, I just need — can I use your LinkedIn profile? Can I use your driver's licence to try to get this job one time?’ And then once you [let them use it] one time, they have it forever."

articles.title: German auto workers on back foot as costs, competition bite
articles.summary: German auto workers profited during the industry's boom years, but are now increasingly being asked to trade past gains for future job security.

image.caption: The most sensitive issue for unions may be the demand that employees work more for the same amount of pay [FILE: May 20, 2022]Image: David Hecker/AFP

blocks.text: For decades, German auto bosses and labor representatives touted their ability to work through their disagreements in a uniquely cooperative process. Those days appear to be gone.
A series of crises across the industry and abrupt moves by management to slash costs are testing the limits of the German power-sharing agreement.
As negotiations between union representatives and Germany's largest carmaker, Volkswagen, began on Tuesday, the balance of power appeared increasingly one-sided.
Volkswagen wants to freeze wages for the next two years while cutting several allowances and bonuses.
Alongside Mercedes, it's demanding longer hours under the same pay, with both companies threatening to withhold investment from German factories.

Unions have responded with warning strikes and the threat of larger walkouts. Yet workers are aware of the grim outlook, with Germany's auto industry losing more than 123,000 jobs between 2019 and 2025, according to the Ifo Institute.

"I think that the labor representatives are in a very difficult situation," said Thomas Haipeter, a labor researcher at the University of Duisburg-Essen. "On the one hand, they have to make concessions in order to safeguard jobs. And despite these massive employment reductions to safeguard the rest of the jobs and locations, what is missing for them is a kind of more offensive strategy."
Can 'legacy' bring Volkswagen back from the brink?
A hot shower a day
Labor's outsized role in German auto companies goes back decades and includes a 1945 deal at Volkswagen promising a hot shower a day.
That year marks the start of "co-determination" at the company, in which workers are represented internally by employee-led workers' councils, as well as by outside labor unions.

Berlin then anchored labor's strong say in Volkswagen in 1960, before the firm issued public shares, ensuring government officials retained extra votes in the supervisory board. Those seats, belonging to the Lower Saxony government, tend to be sympathetic to workers.
Workers' councils, meanwhile, became a fixture across the German auto industry, with representation extending across multiple production sites within the same companies.
Pay and benefits for auto workers have risen over the years. During the last German industry boom, between 2011 and 2019, pay for auto workers clearly outpaced the average German wage.

In early 2025, auto workers were earning nearly a third more per hour than the typical German worker, when bonuses and allowances are factored in, according to Germany's Federal Statistical Office (Destatis).
That same year, Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume praised cooperation with the unions as one of the company's "great strengths” during the 80-year anniversary of the 1945 agreement.
Cracks in the relationship
Cracks were long in the making, according to case studies by Haipeter and others. Labor was increasingly forced to protect plants and jobs as companies chased cheaper workers abroad.
Workers' councils turned their attention to saving their own production lines. They focused on business strategy and even hired business consultants in an effort to sway strategy.
When combustion engines dominated, autoworkers could argue German production was the most technologically advanced, according to Haipeter. That changed with the shift to electric vehicles.

"This line of compromise is canceled now by management," he said. "They say it doesn't matter for us where we produce. We have to produce at the locations or in countries which are best-cost countries and not in countries which have higher wages."
Slow sales of electric autos and competition from Chinese manufacturers have, meanwhile, exposed the cost difference.

In 2024, Volkswagen abruptly canceled a series of labor agreements and threatened factory closures. After tough negotiations, labor agreed to significant cuts — €1.5 billion yearly in abandoned wage hikes and the elimination of 50,000 positions through attrition — in exchange for job security for current employees through 2030.

Management returned this summer with a restructuring plan that included the closures of four German plants. It delayed that decision following negotiations, but slated another 50,000 positions for attrition.
Volkswagen declined to comment for this article.
Can crisis reinvent the car again?
More hours, same pay
The most sensitive issue for unions may be the demand that employees work more for the same amount of pay, or even receive less for less work.

The union IG Metall won the concession for a 35-hour workweek in 1984 after seven weeks of strikes. It's now standard in every labor contract in the auto industry, although it's not uncommon for worksites to deviate upon employee agreement, according to Haipeter.

Mercedes has called for employees to agree to an exception across the company. The company acknowledged that the 35-hour workweek was "hard-won" and "means a great deal" to its workers. "However, the conditions under which it was agreed upon no longer exist today," it said in a statement to DW.
Volkswagen, meanwhile, is demanding greater "flexibility" as the negotiations get underway.
"They call it flexibility in both directions," Thorsten Gröger, head of negotiations for the union said last week. "In the end, Volkswagen wants its employees to perform unpaid work."
The 35-hour workweek is too sacred for unions to give in, said Ferdinand Dudenhöffer, a longtime analyst of the German car industry.

"The unions are in a difficult position," he noted. "They battled for a 35-hour workweek, and that's an incredible privilege that comes with a lot of pride. The union knows that as soon as one factory, one production hall, gives up the 35-hour workweek, then they will have a conflagration."

Düdenhöffer sees parallels in another crisis from Volkswagen's history. After a downturn in the early 1990s, the then-head of the German state of Lower Saxony, Gerhard Schröder, pushed for an agreement for workers to work less in exchange for retaining their jobs.
"We need a mediator along these lines," he said.

articles.title: VP Sara questions SC dismissal of petitions challenging Rodrigo Duterte arrest
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte on Wednesday decried the Supreme Court decision dismissing the petitions challenging the arrest of her father, former President Rodrigo Duterte, insisting that its…

blocks.text: Published November 25, 2026 4:50pm

Vice President Sara Duterte on Wednesday decried the Supreme Court decision dismissing the petitions challenging the arrest of her father, former President Rodrigo Duterte, insisting that its underlying issues concern national sovereignty.
The SC earlier dismissed consolidated habeas corpus petitions filed by the Vice President’s siblings—Sebastian, Veronica, and Paolo Duterte—challenging the March 2025 arrest of their father.

The High Court ruled that the petitions have become moot and that Philippine courts cannot enforce the writ because he is now in the custody of the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, Netherlands.
The Vice President, in response, said that no Philippine court should “lightly dismiss” a petition as moot.

“No foreign court or nation should ever stand above the sovereignty of our country. The protection of the life, liberty, and fundamental rights of every Filipino citizen must remain paramount,” Sara Duterte said.

“No Philippine court should lightly dismiss a petition as moot, when the underlying issues concern national sovereignty, constitutional accountability, and the government’s duty to protect the life and liberty of every Filipino from foreign interference,” she added.
A day after Rodrigo Duterte’s arrest in March 2025, his children separately filed petitions for habeas corpus, a legal remedy used to challenge unlawful detention and seek a person’s release.
The camp of Veronica “Kitty” Duterte said they will file a motion for reconsideration, following the SC decision. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: FACT CHECK: ICC chamber order on ‘Incident 57’ doesn’t mean Duterte will be released
articles.summary: While the ICC Trial Chamber III did order the removal of ‘Incident 57’ from the list of incidents in the charges against Duterte, this does not mean the entire case itself has been dismissed or that…

blocks.text: Claim: Former president Rodrigo Duterte is set to be released after the International Criminal Court (ICC) dropped one drug-related killing, “Incident 57,” from his crimes against humanity case.

Why we fact-checked this: The Facebook reel bearing the claim has already received 823,000 views, 12,500 reactions, 1,400 shares, and 1,200 comments as of writing. It was posted on November 17 and continues to gain traction up to this date.

The video shows a photo of Vice President Sara Duterte and her father, who is currently detained at the ICC facility in The Hague, Netherlands. The text on the photo reads, “Tuluyan nang ibinasura ng ICC ang Incident 57 drug war charges laban kay PRRD dahil sa sablay ng petsa.”(The ICC has definitively dismissed the ‘Incident 57’ drug war charges against [former president Rodrigo Roa Duterte] due to an error in the date.)
Additional text overlaid on the reel claimed that the ICC junked the case and that the Vice President has urged their supporters to pray for her father’s safety upon his supposed return.

The facts: While the ICC Trial Chamber III’s order to drop “Incident 57” from the list of incidents in the second count of charges against Duterte is genuine, it is not true that he is set to be released following this directive.
Duterte remains detained in ICC custody. There are no credible news reports or official announcements saying that Duterte can now return to the Philippines or that his case has been dismissed.

In an October 9 ruling, the ICC Trial Chamber III ordered prosecutors to remove Incident 57, a single alleged drug-related killing involving a “high-value target,” because it fell outside the confirmed timeframe of the second charge against Duterte.

The prosecution then complied with the order. In a document dated October 20, the prosecution said that all references to Incident 57 are now removed from the trial brief and replaced with redacted information.

Duterte is currently facing three counts of crimes against humanity, including murders in and around Davao City allegedly committed by the “Davao Death Squad” while he served as mayor between 2013 and 2016, targeted killings of alleged high-value targets during his presidency between 2016 and 2017, and murders and attempted murders during barangay-level anti-drug operations between 2016 and 2018.

List of incidents: Aside from Incident 57, which the ICC chamber ordered removed, there are many other active incidents included in the charges against Duterte. In October, the ICC trial chamber approved the addition of seven new incidents to the charges, raising the total number from 49 to 56.
Duterte was arrested in March 2025 for crimes against humanity. He is set to face trial on November 30.Previous fact checks: Rappler has fact-checked similar false claims about Duterte’s detention:

articles.title: Senate cuts P19.8B from AICS, MAP budget, reallocates to PhilHealth subsidy
articles.summary: The Senate has slashed nearly P20 billion from the allocated budget for the Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situation (AICS) and the Medical Assistance Program (MAP) under the proposed 2027…

blocks.text: Published November 25, 2026 4:36pm

The Senate has slashed nearly P20 billion from the allocated budget for the Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situation (AICS) and the Medical Assistance Program (MAP) under the proposed 2027 national budget.

Senate Finance panel chairman JV Ejercito announced this Wednesday, noting that the financial assistance programs each suffered a P9.9 billion reduction — which will be reallocated to Philippine Health Insurance Corporation (PhilHealth) subsidy.

With P19.8 billion reallocated, Ejercito said the budget for PhilHealth subsidy now stands at P94.2 billion, up from P73 billion initially allocated under the House-approved General Appropriations Bill (GAB).
“Ang ayuda, partly ... we will partly slash and nilagay namin ‘yung marami sa PhilHealth. Kaya Philhealth, sa subsidy will increase by almost P20 billion,” he said in an ambush interview.
(We will partially reduce the financial assistance and reallocate a significant portion to PhilHealth. The subsidy under PhilHealth will increase by nearly P20 billion.)

“P74 billion, P73 billion, magiging P94 [billion]. Ang target nga natin gawing P100 billion pero masikip ang fiscal space. So hopefully kung maabot ‘yung P100 billion para mas maganda ang subsidy ng PhilHealth,” he added.

(From P74 billion or P73 billion, it will become P94 billion. Our target was actually to reach P100 billion, but fiscal space is tight. Hopefully, we can reach that P100 billion allocation to provide a better subsidy under PhilHealth.)

The Senate Finance panel chair said that with higher subsidies for PhilHealth, there will be an increased budget for the zero balance billing, preventive care, immunization and health promotion, and for the health facilities enhancement program to improve provincial hospitals and locally funded health facilities.
“Lahat sa healthcare saka sa infrastructure, that is our priority,” Ejercito said.
(Everything related to healthcare and infrastructure, that is our priority.)
'Double funding'
Ejercito likewise committed that alleged duplicate funding for some projects will be rechecked and will be corrected if verified.
“Definitely, kapag may red flag at mga double entry, tanggal kaagad ‘yun. Syempre…humanly impossible mache-check mo, libo ‘yan. Dahan dahan, kaya nga iniisa-isa namin,” he said.

(Definitely, if there’s a red flag or a double entry, it’s removed immediately. Of course… it’s humanly impossible to check everything—there are thousands of items. We’re taking it step by step, slowly.)
“Siguro may nakakalusot. Kung may nakakalusot man, talagaang ano ‘yun, unintentional,” he added.
(It’s possible that some irregularities slipped through. If any did, it’s truly unintentional.)
Ejercito said he is seeking help from budget watchdogs and the public to help monitor any questionable items in the proposed 2027 national budget.

Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson earlier flagged duplicate appropriations for some flood control projects in the proposed 2027 national budget, raising fresh concerns over funding irregularities amid the ongoing controversy over anomalous flood control projects.
Lacson said the duplicate allocations were separate from at least 30 alleged ghost multipurpose buildings (MPBs) his team had identified in the proposed budget.

Lacson had also questioned the proposed appropriations for 3,950 MPBs, separate from the 1,584 MPBs covered by the Local Government Support Fund's (LGSF) Financial Assistance to local government units (LGUs) subprogram from 2022 to 2026. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: IVF, elective abortion, gender-affirming care and VAD to cease under Catholic ownership of private hospitals
articles.summary:
ACCC approves Calvary’s takeover of 14 hospitals around Australia, with critics concerned move will add to pressures on public health system

  • Get our

blocks.text: Advocates say access to voluntary assisted dying, IVF, elective abortions and gender-affirming care is under threat after the competition watchdog approved the takeover of 14 private hospitals by a Catholic healthcare provider.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) announced on Wednesday it had approved the takeover of the private hospitals by not-for-profit Catholic healthcare operator Calvary from collapsed provider Healthscope.
In a statement on Wednesday, Calvary welcomed the ACCC’s decision.

A spokesperson for the provider confirmed that under the proposed acquisition, reproductive services including IVF, elective abortions, voluntary assisted dying (VAD) and gender reassignment procedures would cease at any hospitals currently offering those services.
The acquisition, for which a date is not yet confirmed, is still dependent on the issuing of hospital licences by state governments.

Ahead of the ACCC’s announcement on Wednesday, the New South Wales health minister, Ryan Park, announced the state government would step in to support access to IVF at two of the hospitals, John Hunter and Newcastle private hospital, through theatre access at the publicly run John Hunter hospital.
Park said “the vast majority of [other] services will either continue or be available through alternative local providers”.
The 14 hospitals include six in NSW, four in Victoria, two in Brisbane, and one each in the Northern Territory and South Australia. They include rehabilitation clinics as well as private hospitals.
The ACCC has already approved Calvary’s acquisition of Hobart private hospital, with the provider assuming responsibility next month. It took over Holmesglen private hospital in Melbourne last month.

The regulator’s assessment was limited to examining the acquisition’s competition impacts, finding there was “no real likelihood of any operator other than Calvary buying the 14 hospitals”, which were unlikely to remain open otherwise.
But it acknowledged the concerns raised by medical practitioners and community members “that some services would no longer be provided if the acquisition went ahead”.
‘Pay more and wait longer’

As a Catholic healthcare provider, Calvary says it is guided by Catholic Health Australia’s code of ethics. The guidelines say any action or omission that “causes death with the purpose of eliminating all suffering” is not permissible.
The provider has said it will work with clinicians to provide pathways for treatments no longer offered under the acquisition.

Dr Linda Swan, the CEO of charity Go Gentle Australia, described the ACCC’s decision as “disappointing but not unexpected”, saying the organisation was “deeply concerned that Calvary’s acquisitions will reduce choice for dying people”.
after newsletter promotion
“This is not as simple as Calvary wants us to believe. Relocating seriously unwell patients at the end of life is not straightforward and can cause considerable distress and trauma.
“At the same time, the public hospital system is facing ongoing bed shortages. Redirecting more patients into that environment will inevitably increase those pressures.”

The NSW Greens health spokesperson, Amanda Cohn, said the state government had added “insult to injury” by allowing Calvary to continue to operate the troubled public-private partnership at Calvary Mater hospital in Newcastle.

Cohn, who chaired a parliamentary inquiry into the hospital, said patients receiving cancer care or end-of-life care at the hospital had already had to be transferred to Newcastle private to be able to access voluntary assisted dying.
“Where will these patients go, now that this is not an option?” she said.

Dr Nisha Khot, the president of the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (Ranzcog), said the acquisition could put “more pressure on the public healthcare system in the places where Calvary is the only private option”.
“Women who are on a public waitlist, for example, for gynecological surgery, will not get their gynecological surgery because instead somebody who’s having IVF is being prioritised.”
Endocrinologist Prof Ada Cheung, the head of the Trans Health Research Group, said state governments needed to step in to guarantee all forms of care.

“Gender-affirming surgery is mainly delivered privately at significant cost to patients, and public access is very limited across Australia. When options are this scarce, losing any of them means people travel further, pay more and wait longer.”
