articles.title: Senate prioritizes feeding program in push for higher 2027 DepEd budget
articles.summary: Senator Bam Aquino wants to increase the school-based feeding program's budget to P28.7 billion. Meanwhile, the ARAL Program has no allocation in the Senate committee report.

blocks.text: BUDGET DEBATES. Senator Bam Aquino and Education Secretary Sonny Angara during the Senate plenary deliberations on the proposed 2027 budget of the Department of Education on November 24, 2026.
Senate Social Media Unit
Senator Bam Aquino wants to increase the school-based feeding program's budget to P28.7 billion. Meanwhile, the ARAL Program has no allocation in the Senate committee report.

items: Senator Bam Aquino advocates for prioritizing the school-based feeding program in the 2027 budget, proposing an increase to P28.7 billion to expand coverage.
The Senate finance committee recommended a P915.49-billion budget for the Department of Education, but the ARAL Program remains unfunded.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – Senator Bam Aquino recommended making the school-based feeding program the top priority for an additional budget among other Department of Education (DepEd) programs in 2027.
Overall, the Senate finance committee recommended P915.49 billion for the proposed new general appropriations of the DepEd and its attached agencies.
That amount is P4.91 billion higher than the P910.5 billion approved by the House of Representatives, but P1.25 billion lower than the P916.75 billion in the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP).
Among the changes, the Senate panel added P11 billion to the school-based feeding program, pushing the proposed allocation to P22.4 billion.

But Aquino, as the DepEd’s budget sponsor, plans to seek an additional increase for the program. “At the proper time, this representation, alongside some other colleagues, will introduce an amendment to increase the budget for the school-based feeding program by P6,265,478,145,” he said during the plenary deliberations.
That would raise the program’s budget to P28.7 billion, higher than the P25.7 billion in the 2026 national budget.

The additional funding would also expand the universal feeding to cover kindergarten to Grade 2, reaching another 1.8 million students in 2027. This follows the phased implementation under the national children’s nutrition bill, which has been ratified but not yet signed into law.
The P28.7-billion budget would cover 124 feeding days, or from June to December in 2027, at P30 per meal.

blocks.caption: After Congress, expanded nutrition program bill’s next test is funding

blocks.text: Aquino remains hopeful that they can still set a higher budget for the education sector.
“I have spoken to the Senate President multiple times to share my frustration with the fiscal space provided for this important agency,” he said in the plenary.

“We have proposed a much bigger budget only to be met with an answer that we didn’t like, which was that the fiscal space is very limited — which we understand. Mr. [Senate] President, I believe that we can still increase this before the period of amendments,” he added in a mix of English and Filipino.
Aquino also supports funding for the Academic Recovery and Accessible Learning (ARAL) Program in 2027. There is no separate line item for it in the 2027 NEP.
However, in the Senate committee report, the ARAL Program remains unfunded.
“Talo pa tayo ng House. P300 million, nakalagay sila. Tayo, wala,” Senator Joel Villanueva said during his interpellation. (The House outdid us. They allocated P300 million. We did not put anything.)
Villanueva noted that 11 million students have been identified as needing remediation sessions in school year 2026-2027.
Aquino told senators that the ARAL Program still has unspent funds from this year. During the 2026 budget talks, it was the Senate that pushed P8.9 billion for the learning recovery initiative.

“More than half of the P8.9-billion budget for this year was released very late, only in July and August. Therefore, because of the late release, meron pa pong pondo, ‘yon ang gagamitin (there is still funding, which will be used) next year,” he explained.
He added that the disbursement rate, which refers to actual payments made, is only at 13%.

According to Aquino, the DepEd is already in the process of disbursing the funds in the next few weeks, with Education Secretary Sonny Angara promising a faster process. Angara was standing beside the senator during the deliberations.
“We know that it can work. We’ve been talking about our learning gaps for so many months. The main solution to the learning gap is really a remediation program,” Aquino said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Not all ferns are edible, DENR warns
articles.summary: The Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) warned that not all "pako" or Philippine endemic ferns are safe to eat.

blocks.text: Published November 25, 2026 3:55pm
The Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) warned that not all "pako" or Philippine endemic ferns are safe to eat.
There are around 12,000 fern species globally, with approximately 1,030 recorded in the Philippines, the department said.
The Lindsaea hamiguitanensis, which was first found and recorded in the Mt. Hamiguitan Range Wildlife Sanctuary in Davao Oriental, is not edible unlike the other Philippine endemic ferns.

"It is classified as Vulnerable under DENR Administrative Order No. 2026-20. Unlike edible pako varieties, there are limited studies on the edibility of this species. Thus, it is best not to forage, consume, or uproot it from the wild," the DENR Davao Region said.
The Lindsaea hamiguitanensis has relatively thin leaflets measuring approximately 1 to 1.8 centimeter long and 0.8 to 1 centimeter wide. They are also now found in other parts of Mindanao and Negros.
Moreover, the DENR said that pako plants are not only good for salads but also for the environment.

"Many ferns help prevent soil erosion, retain moisture on the forest floor, provide shelter for small organisms, and support nutrient recycling. These ecological functions play a vital role in maintaining healthy and resilient forest ecosystems," the DENR Davao Region said. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Philippine Coast Guard adds 3 vessels into service
articles.summary: The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) on Wednesday has commissioned three vessels into service as part of efforts to bolster operational capabilities in protecting the country's maritime territories.

blocks.text: Published November 25, 2026 3:28pm
The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) on Wednesday has commissioned three vessels into service as part of efforts to bolster operational capabilities in protecting the country's maritime territories.

“The newly commissioned vessels will expand our conduct of maritime safety operations and responses to emergencies at sea, including oil spills and other incidents that threaten the country's rich marine environment,” PCG spokesperson Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said in a statement.
The commissioning of the three vessels was held at the National Headquarters in Port Area, Manila led by PCG Commandant Admiral Rommel Supangan.
Two of the vessels, namely the BRP Patag (PATS-2701) and BRP Pag-asa (PATS-2702), are 27-meter marine protector-class patrol boats.
The boats came from the United States and were acquired after 24 PCG crew members completed specialized training in Baltimore, Maryland last August.
The third vessel is the BRP Kalikasan (MRSV-2001), a 20-meter marine research and survey vessel which will be used for shallow-water hydrographic surveys and ocean conservation.

The PCG said the BRP Kalikasan was built locally in Cebu as part of the PCG’s long-term capability expansion project. It was already used in a mission in Corregidor Island early this month. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Domestic violence soars to record high in Germany
articles.summary: Every three days in Germany, a man kills his wife or ex-partner. Every 10 minutes, the police record a sexual offense against a woman. "A shocking finding," according to Justice Minister Stefanie…

image.caption: Each November, the UN's Orange Day campaign highlights violence against womenImage: APA-Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: The German government has presented some grim statistics with regard to misogyny, rape, violence and murder, with reported cases of domestic violence at an all-time high.

At a press conference in Berlin on Tuesday, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, Family Affairs Minister Karin Prien and Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig released the latest figures on crimes that specifically target women: whether within families and intimate relationships, in public or online.
'Behind all these terrible numbers lie individual stories'
In contrast to the statistics pertaining to crime overall, which have remained the same or increased only slightly, reports of crimes against women have increased.
"Behind all these terrible numbers lie individual stories, people and particularly women and girls, whose lives are severely affected by these acts of violence," said Dobrindt.
Behind domestic violence: Causes, patterns and solutions

In 2025, some 280,000 people were victims of physical abuse in their own homes, a 2.8% increase compared to the previous year. Over 70% of the victims were female. Each hour, 16 women are subjected to physical abuse behind closed doors.
The male victims included boys who had been assaulted by their fathers.
The number of misogynistic hate crimes has also risen dramatically, by almost 50%, to 819 cases.

"The figures show us what it can mean to be a woman in Germany," said Hubig. "It can mean being killed by one's partner or ex-partner. Being a woman can also mean being physically abused by one's partner or ex-partner in one's own home. Being a woman can mean that one's sexual autonomy is brutally disregarded."
Perpetrators, victims getting younger

According to the latest findings, both perpetrators and victims are getting younger. In 2025, nearly half of all female victims of sexual offenses were under the age of 18. And the number of incidents of online violence against women and girls rose by 15.7%. This includes the unauthorized sharing of videos and photos, verbal abuse, manipulation of images, threats and online blackmail, as well as cyberstalking.

Because many perpetrators and victims are still in their teens, Prien, who is also minister for education, said the government wanted to focus primarily on schools, which she explained should become places of prevention.
"Ultimately, we need to bring about a change in people's mindsets, especially those of men. That will be the deciding factor in the end," she said.
Femicides to be classified as murder, not manslaughter

Over the weekend, Justice Minister Hubig had already announced that in future all femicides, the intentional killing of girls and women because of their gender, would be classified as murders. Currently, such crimes are often classified as manslaughter, for which the penalty is less severe than for murder.
Hubig told German broadcaster ZDF that it was increasingly common that femicides be described as family tragedies or as domestic dramas revolving around jealousy and then classified as manslaughter.

Martina Link, the vice president of the Federal Criminal Police Office, was also at the press conference in Berlin. She called for everybody to pay closer attention to the issue, within their own families, neighborhoods or at work.
"Violence against women is not a private matter," she said. "Not in our immediate surroundings nor in the digital world."
She also pointed out that when it came to sexual offenses and domestic violence, only about 5-10% of cases were reported.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Four years after huge asteroid crash, a spacecraft has now returned to assess the damage
articles.summary: The mission is studying an asteroid deliberately knocked off course by a colliding spacecraft.
articles.byline: Rebecca Morelle, Alison Francis, Tony Jolliffe

blocks.text: Four years after huge asteroid crash, a spacecraft has now returned to assess the damage
Image source, ESA
The Hera spacecraft will study the 150m-wide (490ft) asteroid called Dimorphos
A spacecraft has arrived at an asteroid to investigate the damage caused by an unprecedented cosmic crash.
It what may sound like the plot of a disaster movie, Nasa's Dart spacecraft deliberately smashed into the space rock in 2022 to knock it off course.

The Nasa craft was obliterated on impact. Four years on, a European Space Agency (ESA) mission, called Hera, is scouring the scene to fully assess the aftermath of the collision - with the first images set to be released later on Wednesday.
The asteroid poses no threat, instead this was the first ever test of our planetary defences to see what action we could take if a space rock was heading for our planet.
"Hera is a sort of Inspector Columbo going back to the crash scene to investigate what is the outcome of this impact," said Patrick Michel, principal investigator of ESA's Hera mission.

blocks.caption: Image caption, This was the last image from Dart before it crashed into Dimorphos in 2022

blocks.text: Image source, NASA/Johns Hopkins APL
This was the last image from Dart before it crashed into Dimorphos in 2022
The crash test focussed on a pair of asteroids: a larger one called Didymos - about 730m (2,400ft) wide - which is orbited by a smaller rock called Dimorphos, about 150m (490ft) wide.

The Dart spacecraft targeted Dimorphos, hurtling into the rock at 22,000km per hour (14,000mph). Images beamed back showed the asteroid's rocky surface coming ever closer until the feed cut out on impact.
It was such a big smash-up that the trail of debris, measuring about 10,000km long (6,200 miles), was spotted by telescopes on Earth and in space.
The crash showed it was possible to change the path of the smaller asteroid.
Before the collision it took Dimorphos 11 hours and 55 minutes to orbit around Didymos. After the Dart crash, the duration of its orbit had shrunk by about 33 minutes.
But the arrival of the second spacecraft, Hera, will help scientists to answer many more questions.
"Dart exploded in the asteroid, and therefore we don't have the information of what is its final state," explained Michel.
"The impact could have left a crater - and if it is the case, we need to understand the size and the depth. Or [the impact] may have entirely reshaped the asteroid."

blocks.caption: Image caption, A 10,000km-long (6,200 miles) debris trail was spotted by the Hubble Space Telescope

blocks.text: Image source, NASA/Hubble Space Telescope
A 10,000km-long (6,200 miles) debris trail was spotted by the Hubble Space Telescope
The Hera mission will spend the next year studying Dimorphos, and take a look at Didymos too.
The spacecraft is packed with instruments, and it also has two small shoe-boxed sized satellites onboard, which can study the impact site up close, and then later land on the asteroid.
A key task is to measure the mass of Dimorphos, to work out how effective the spacecraft's shove was.
This information would be vital if we ever spotted a space rock that was on a collision course with Earth.
"It would help us to predict what would happen if we had to hit another asteroid," said Prof Simon Green, a planetary scientist who is on Hera's science team.
"We [could] measure its properties and say: 'Well, we need this mass of spacecraft, travelling at this speed, this early, in order to deflect it enough so that it misses the Earth'."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Hera has already sent back an image of Didymos with Dimorphos in the background

blocks.text: Hera has already sent back an image of Didymos with Dimorphos in the background
Asteroids pose a significant threat to our planet.
The biggest, which measure more than a kilometre across, could cause global devastation. But medium-sized asteroids around the same dimensions as Dimorphos could wipe out a city.

"We all know what happened to the dinosaurs, right? And we don't want that to happen to us," said Carolyn Ernst, Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, who works on both the Dart and Hera missions.
"The good news for us is that there are far fewer potential threats out there in the Solar System than there were millions of years ago. But there are objects out there."
She said the biggest asteroids have been spotted, and none are heading to Earth.
"The smallest stuff isn't too much of a threat because our atmosphere protects us," she added.

"But there's a size range in the middle where we don't know where all of them are, and it could, if impacted, cause problems for humanity. And if we can find out about that and know about that, well, we sure as heck would want to try to stop that."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Hera has two small satellites onboard to study the asteroid up close

blocks.text: Hera has two small satellites onboard to study the asteroid up close
Scientists want to gather as much intelligence as they can about space rocks - to make us as well equipped as possible to deal with whatever the Universe throws at us.
A new mission is launching in 2027 to track potentially hazardous asteroids: a space telescope called the Near-Earth Object (NEO) Surveyor.
There are also more visits planned to asteroids, including to one called Apophis, which is about 450m (1,480ft) long.
Apophis was discovered in 2004 and it was initially thought it might hit the Earth as early as 13 April 2029.
But now scientists understand its orbit better, and say it won't hit us for at least the next 100 years. Instead of a crash in 2029, it will fly just 32,000km (20,000 miles) above our surface.
This will give scientists the rare chance to study a space rock up-close.

Two spacecraft will head to Apophis, including Nasa's Osiris-Apex (which previously grabbed a sample from another asteroid called Bennu) and Ramses, a joint mission between ESA and the Japanese Space Agency (JAXA).

articles.title: ‘They don’t believe in freedom’: Yemenis plan their escape as Houthis advance on Aden
articles.summary:
With Iran’s proxy fighters encircling the temporary capital, residents and NGOs prepare to evacuate

Hussein fled his home six years ago after it fell under Houthi control, moving as far…
articles.byline: A reporter in southern Yemen and William Christou in Beirut

blocks.text: Hussein fled his home six years ago after it fell under Houthi control, moving as far south as he could to the port city of Aden, where there was a measure of safety.
The Saudi-backed Yemeni government had made the city its temporary capital; the hundreds of kilometres between it and the Houthis were well fortified.

Today, Hussein is once again considering the painful decision of leaving home. In September, the Iran-aligned Houthis swept aside Yemeni government forces, and now have set their sights on Aden. Houthi fighters are amassing to the north and east of the city, and have begun encircling the government-controlled territory.

blocks.caption: People displaced by war on the Red Sea coastline receive aid near Aden, Yemen. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: “I fled my home in Sana’a and came here. I don’t think the Houthis plan to take over Aden right now, but if they get closer, I will have no choice but to flee again to Marib or Hadhramaut,” said Hussein, who was speaking under a pseudonym.

Hussein works as a schoolteacher and was formerly a member of the Islah party, an Islamist political party aligned with Saudi Arabia that is in opposition to the Houthi movement. He fears that if the Houthis take control of Aden he could face persecution for his former affiliation.
“The Houthis don’t believe in freedom, they just want to hear one voice, the one they like,” he said.

Hussein is one of many residents and organisations nervously watching the Houthi advance. The militia is still about 50 miles (80km) north of Aden, but local people fear government forces may not be able to resist another Houthi assault, having seen the dramatic collapse of government forces and allied militias in September.

blocks.caption: Houthi forces take over from Dhubab to Bab el-Mandeb, Taiz governorate, Yemen, after Saudi-backed forces withdraw from the area, 16 November 2026. Photograph: Houthi Military Media/Reuters

blocks.text: Aden has been the seat of the Saudi-backed government of Yemen since 2015. If the Houthis took the city, it would be a huge blow for the government, and a massive failure for the Saudi-led coalition which has for years fought against the Houthis.
The 12-year-long civil war would tilt dramatically in the Houthis’ favour and be a boon for Iran, which has long invested military and political support in the insurgent movement.

The Yemeni government has pulled back many of its fighters to help defend Aden and the surrounding areas, announcing last week that fighters were redeployed from areas along the south-western coast towards the port city.

Saudi Arabia has tried to halt the Houthi advance with a renewed bombing campaign, carrying out hundreds of airstrikes in Yemen since September, killing and wounding 822 civilians, including 181 children, according to statistics from the independent Yemen Data Project.
Houthi authorities have alleged that Saudi Arabia has carried out 5,500 air and missile attacks since July.

blocks.caption: A rescuer walks through the debris of a destroyed building belonging to Yemen’s Public Telecommunications Corporation following a Saudi strike in the port city of Hodeida. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The Houthis have not announced any intention to take Aden, but have instead been amassing troops north of Kirish, and in al-Bayda, areas which, if taken, would cut off the northern and eastern roads to Aden.
“The buildups in al-Bayda could threaten Aden’s eastern road links through Abyan and Saudi supply lines into the city,” said Mohammed al-Basha, the founder of the US-based risk advisory Basha Report.

“The Houthis appear to be testing how well Aden’s defences will hold. If they collapse, the Houthis could try to seize the city. If government forces hold, the Houthis could try to lay siege to it,” al-Basha added.

blocks.caption: Members of the National Security Forces at a checkpoint as security is tightened in Aden. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: Houthi forces have begun striking Aden and its surrounding areas, rupturing the relative safety the city has offered for years. Residents have watched anxiously as explosions grow nearer, and displaced people from surrounding areas have started to arrive in greater numbers.
“Since last week, we’ve started following the news every hour. When I get busy, I tell my daughter to follow it and update me,” said Rami, a resident of Aden who spoke under a pseudonym.

The 53-year-old bitterly recalled his experience during the four-month battle for Aden in 2015, when he was stuck in the crossfire between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces. He, like other people in Aden, is trying to make his own calculation of when, or if, the Houthis will arrive.
International organisations are also making contingency plans in case of a Houthi takeover of the city.

blocks.caption: A displaced woman carries an aid box at the al-Fardous displacement camp in Ras Imran, on the outskirts of Aden. Photograph: Abdulnasser Alseddik/AP

blocks.text: “We were informed by management that they are issuing termination notices to all staff this week. If the Houthis don’t reach Aden, they will continue operations and renew our contracts; otherwise this is the end of the road,” an aid worker with an international NGO said.
Already, several NGOs were forced to shut down in the city of Taiz after sweeping Houthi gains.

Not all NGOs would leave in the case of a Houthi takeover, but some are unable to work in Houthi-controlled areas either due to fears for the safety of aid workers, or because the US Treasury designated the Houthis a foreign terrorist organisation in 2025.
Yemen has for years faced a severe humanitarian crisis, with about 18.7 million people facing acute food insecurity.

blocks.caption: Displaced Yemenis from the west coast wait to receive medical care at Prince Mohammed bin Salman hospital in Aden. Photograph: Abdulnasser Alseddik/AP

blocks.text: Fighting has only exacerbated conditions, severing transport routes, pushing up the prices of goods and worsening the country’s displacement crisis – including more than 350,000 people displaced since August.

“I earn daily wages, and when there is no work, my six family members don’t get enough food,” said Ahmed, a restaurant worker in his 50s. “I don’t care about politics or wars, and I’m not involved in any of it. I’m just like millions of Yemenis struggling to provide basic necessities for their families.”
For many of Aden’s residents, the prospect of a Houthi takeover has shattered the sense of safety that they sought by coming to the government stronghold in the first place.

“I’m not stocking up on food because I won’t stay in Aden and wait for the battles to reach the city. It isn’t only me; my family is also ready to flee at any time … staying at home won’t be safe and we might get trapped,” Rami said.

articles.title: Lies, a disguise and surfboard bags: how a jealous Sydney policeman tried to cover up double murder
articles.summary: Beau Lamarre was on Wednesday found guilty of murdering his ex Jesse Baird, and Baird's new partner Luke Davies.

blocks.text: Lies, a disguise and surfboard bags: how a jealous Sydney policeman tried to cover up double murder

blocks.caption: Image caption, Thousands of hours of CCTV footage helped convict Beau Lamarre

blocks.text: Image source, NSW Supreme Court
Thousands of hours of CCTV footage helped convict Beau Lamarre
ByHelen Livingstone
Sydney
It was just after 09:00 on a warm February morning when CCTV picked up a man dressed as an UberEats rider hovering on a sidewalk in one of Sydney's wealthiest neighbourhoods.

He dawdled for around 20 minutes, "steeling himself for what he was about to do" prosecutors say, before disappearing out of sight. Minutes later another CCTV camera captured the sound of gunshots ringing out.
Former police officer Beau Lamarre, 31, was on Wednesday found guilty of murdering his former partner Jesse Baird, a TV presenter, and Luke Davies, Baird's new partner, with his work-issued gun.

In February 2024, the bloodied belongings of Baird and Davies were found in a skip in the suburb of Cronulla, sparking a frantic search for the couple. It culminated in the discovery of their bodies on a rural property, partially buried beneath sticks and debris.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Luke Davies (left) and Jesse Baird had been dating only months when they were gunned down

blocks.text: Image source, Supplied: Jesse Baird
Luke Davies (left) and Jesse Baird had been dating only months when they were gunned down
During a two-month trial filled with at-times extraordinary testimony and a wealth of CCTV evidence, the court heard Lamarre had planned his crime over months.

Jurors watched CCTV of the then police officer purchasing a surfboard bag in which to put Baird's body, after casually sizing it up against a friend in the shop, and heard from a stream of former friends and colleagues who testified that Lamarre asked them for advice about everything from mobile phone signals to where he could buy a gun.
One recounted the chilling moment Lamarre told her that if he were ever to murder someone, he would leave their belongings in a dumpster and hide the body in bushland where they would never be found.
"What would you do if I told you I killed somebody? Would you help me hide the body?" he asked, according to her testimony.
Later, Lamarre asked for help in covering up the killings; his friends - none of whom have been implicated - say they began receiving panicked calls and odd requests from him.

One told the court Lamarre persuaded her to go for a drive in the country, during which he tried to dispose of the bodies at the family farm of a man he'd met on a dating app. Over the speakers, he played Taylor Swift's No Body, No Crime.
Dark infatuation

Baird, 26, and Lamarre - a one-time celebrity blogger who also had his own swimwear line on the side of his police work - met in a nightclub in October 2022. For Lamarre, it quickly became an infatuation, but for Baird, an AFL referee and former Network Ten presenter, the relationship appeared to be casual.
After discovering in April 2023 that Lamarre had gone through messages on his phone, and unfollowed other men on his Instagram account, Baird broke it off.

But Lamarre's obsession only grew. He watched Baird having sex with another man through his bedroom window, broke into his house multiple times, deleting contacts on his phone and turning on location settings so that he could engineer meetings with the TV presenter.

On one occasion Baird woke up to find Lamarre in his bedroom; not realising who it was, he chased him down the street. Lamarre was also convicted of aggravated break and enter over that incident on Wednesday.
Prosecutor Brett Hatfield said Baird was "oblivious to the accused's scheming and manipulations", and the pair briefly rekindled the relationship before Baird ended it definitively in November.
He'd discovered Lamarre had, again, been accessing his phone and had attempted to ward off a love rival by pretending to have received flowers from Baird.
'The beginning of the plan for murder'

blocks.caption: Image caption, Beau Lamarre pictured at the annual Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras parade in Sydney in 2020

blocks.text: Image source, EPA-EFE/REX/Shutterstock
Beau Lamarre pictured at the annual Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras parade in Sydney in 2020
His pride wounded, Hatfield said Lamarre's thoughts turned to a "darker place": "revenge".
He asked an old friend if her ex-partner could get him a gun: "This was the beginning of the plan for the murder," the prosecutor said.

In the months leading up to the killings, Lamarre bought a burner phone, a motorcycle helmet, and practised shooting in the woods. On holiday with a friend in Bali in January 2024 he tried to buy a silencer.
While his murder plans percolated, he also began lashing out with petty acts of malice, prosecutors said, such as putting water in the fuel tank of Baird's car.
But at the same time as he plotted, Lamarre was still trying to win his ex back.
On one occasion he pressured a friend to send Baird a 1,600-word message he had himself composed, claiming that he had cancer, and may need to have his arm amputated.
Under questioning in court, he said a naturopath he couldn't remember the name of had diagnosed him with "a form of sporadic cancer".

By the end of 2023, Baird had met and hit it off with Davies, 29. "It was early days but they were both smitten with each other," his mother, Helen Baird, told the court. He sent her a picture of the pair at a Pink concert. "I just sent a big love heart and said 'I'm so happy for both of you'."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Jesse Baird and Luke Davies at the Pink concert shortly before they were killed

blocks.text: Jesse Baird and Luke Davies at the Pink concert shortly before they were killed

Early on the morning of 19 February, Lamarre picked up a hire car he had asked his mother to rent and drove to Baird's home. After waiting several hours for Baird's housemates to leave, while disguised as an UberEats driver, he let himself in with a key he had copied.

Lamarre told the court he had been at Baird's home to pick up some belongings, including a A$25,000 (US$16,500, £12,600) Cartier ring, and had disguised himself to avoid the embarrassment of being recognised if anyone was home.

He claimed he let himself in when no one answered the door, and the two men were killed in separate struggles. He argued that Baird had been holding a knife and the first shot was fired to disarm him, and the second by accident. Davies shot himself when he grabbed the gun, Lamarre said.
But prosecutors told the jury Baird was shot in the back and then once again through his temple as he lay gravely wounded on the kitchen floor.
The evidence, Hatfield said, pointed to one thing only: "an execution".
Davies was then shot through a bedroom door as he tried to call emergency services. The court heard the panic in his voice as the seconds-long call was replayed before it dropped out.
Covering tracks
After that, Lamarre set about trying to hide the evidence of what Hatfield called his "brazen and shocking murders".
One of his first actions was to call a friend. He testified Lamarre confessed he had "killed people" and asked him to take a day off work "to help him clean up his mess".
Later Lamarre pretended the call was a joke, saying, "Did you like my Oscar performance? Got you".

Meanwhile, Lamarre went to a DIY store to purchase mops, bleach and bin bags. After returning to Baird's house to clean up, he left the bodies wrapped in surfboard bags and tarpaulins in the courtyard.
Baird had been set to move out that week, and Lamarre used Baird's phone to reassure his housemates he had hired an Airtasker to move his belongings, adding, "I might be flying to Perth tonight".
Baird's housemates quickly spotted the surfboard bags when they returned home, snapping a photograph tendered in court which showed "red liquid" seeping out.
"I thought it was rusted water from the outdoor furniture," one of the women said.
The surfboard bags were gone the next morning.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Lamarre was captured on CCTV sizing up a surfboard bag in the days before the murders

blocks.text: Lamarre was captured on CCTV sizing up a surfboard bag in the days before the murders

Lamarre had hired a van, and over the next two days made more trips to the DIY store and a sports shop to buy gumboots, a wheelbarrow, bigger surfboard bags and 10kg weights. He squeezed in a hospital appointment for a minor procedure and paused for a sushi date with a friend, CCTV showing him laughing and eating as the bodies lay in the back of his van.
On 21 February, he picked up another friend in the van for what she thought was lunch.

There were blue tarps in the back and it smelled "lemony", she told the court. She "wasn't allowed to put the windows up or turn the aircon off" as they motored towards Goulburn, 200km southwest of Sydney, stopping only at another DIY store, where he asked her to buy an angle grinder.
His friend told the court she remembers Lamarre playing No Body, No Crime at some point: "It's a very niche song."
Arriving at a farm owned by a Hinge date's family, Lamarre used the angle grinder to cut through a padlock, making his way to a dam where he unsuccessfully tried to sink the bodies.

It was now late at night and he drove his friend, by this time upset and confused, home before returning to retrieve the bodies. He then left them in the van, parked in Sydney overnight, before driving once more to Goulburn, where he dumped the bodies near a monastery.

Later that day he visited another friend, telling her to look up the definition of schizophrenia and asking whether he could use her hose, because "there was a bit of blood he had to scrub off" the hired van, the court heard.
Lamarre faces life in prison

blocks.caption: Image caption, The deaths of Baird and Davies triggered an outpouring of horror in Sydney

blocks.text: Image source, Getty
The deaths of Baird and Davies triggered an outpouring of horror in Sydney
By this time police were closing in, and on 23 February Lamarre went to turn himself in at Bondi police station. On the way, he called a police helpline.

"I've been bullied by multiple New South Wales police force members," he told the woman on the other end of the line. "All this stress and trauma and psychological abuse and trauma - did I say trauma already? - has caused me to not sleep, get anxious, it's caused me to have some symptoms of schizophrenia."
"Actually sorry, you know what, can you just... delete that whole thing. We'll just keep it short and sweet."
He wasn't sure when he'd be back to work, he said. Shortly afterwards he was arrested and charged with murder, and the bodies of Baird and Davies were found four days later.
Lamarre's lawyer John Stratton insisted he'd acted in self-defence and had "panicked" realising how the scene would look to outsiders.
The former police officer did plenty of "foolish" and "unusual" things - "He was, it's fair to say, a poorly behaved boyfriend," Stratton said - but that did not make him a murderer.
Ultimately, however, the jury was not convinced and took just over an hour to convict him. He will be sentenced in March and faces life in prison.

articles.title: Thomas Markle indicted in US for possessing child sex abuse images
articles.summary: The FBI arrested Markle on 6 November after a search of a storage unit he had allegedly rented in Los Angeles uncovered the abuse material.

blocks.text: Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex has been indicted by a federal grand jury in Los Angeles for possessing child sex abuse images.

Markle, who remains in custody in Florida, allegedly possessed materials that include at least one image involving a prepubescent minor and a minor under 12 years old, court documents filed in California show.
The 82-year-old has denied possessing images of child sex abuse. He is expected to be arraigned in Los Angeles in the coming weeks.
Last week, a judge in Florida declared Prince Harry's father-in-law mentally competent to stand trial.
The FBI arrested Markle on 6 November at an elderly care home in Florida on a single federal charge of possessing child sexual abuse material. He now faces two counts.
US attorney Bill Essayli said Markle faces a maximum of 20 years in prison on each count if convicted.
His arrest came after a search of a storage unit he had allegedly rented in Los Angeles for almost two decades uncovered the abuse material.
Markle was initially released on conditional bail but was then ordered to stay in jail pending trial after allegedly removing a location monitoring device.

In the indictment, filed by the US Attorney's Office in the Central District of California, Markle is accused of knowingly possessing 35mm film negatives on 30 October and 4 November that contained child sexual abuse materials.
The US Attorney's Office said that during both instances Markle allegedly knew the images contained such materials.
Inside the storage units, federal agents found two images that depict an adult man - whom a witness identified as Markle - with an underage child, the US attorney's office said.

They also alleged that a third image appears to depict a child in a room believed to be part of a motel chain in the Philippines. Markle moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and he lived in Cebu until May.
"The affidavit also describes additional photographs that appear to show Markle with children in various stages of undress," prosecutors said.

articles.title: China investigates politburo star in Xi Jinping’s latest purge
articles.summary:
Chen Jining, regarded as a contender for higher office, becomes the fourth member of China’s elite politburo to be investigated since 2025

China has launched an investigation into Shanghai’s…

blocks.text: China has launched an investigation into Shanghai’s Communist party chief Chen Jining, a member of the country’s elite politburo, the state-run Xinhua news agency unexpectedly announced on Tuesday, marking the fourth member of the top leadership ⁠body to be probed since ⁠2025.
China’s anti-graft watchdog is investigating ​Chen for “suspected severe violations of discipline and laws”, Xinhua said, using a common euphemism for corruption.

For Chinese officials, especially those of Chen’s ⁠rank, the public announcement of an investigation by the central commission for discipline inspection generally signals their eventual political downfall.
The investigation marks a further escalation in President Xi Jinping’s widening anti-graft campaign, which has thinned the party’s senior leadership ranks and depleted the military’s top command.
Before the announcement of the Chen probe, three politburo members from the once 24-member body formed in 2022 – He Weidong, Zhang ⁠Youxia and Ma Xingrui – had already been purged.

Chen, 62, had an unusual rise through China’s official ranks. ​An environmental scientist by training, he earned a doctorate from Imperial ‌College London and rose through China’s elite Tsinghua ‌University to become its president.

He entered government as China’s environmental protection minister in 2015 – just as Xi was elevating pollution control and ecological protection as ‌policy priorities – before becoming mayor of Beijing. He joined the politburo in 2022 and was named party boss of Shanghai, China’s financial hub.

blocks.caption: Chen Jining waves the Paralympic flag during the Closing Ceremony for the 2018 Winter Paralympics in South Korea, in his role as mayor of Beijing.  Photograph: Adam Davy/PA

blocks.text: He has long been viewed as a political star and a plausible contender for higher national office. The investigation into him took analysts by surprise.
Joseph Torigian, an expert in Chinese politics at American University, called it a reminder of “how little we really understand about what’s going on in Chinese elite politics”.

At a gathering of leaders last month, the ruling Communist party pledged to keep waging indefinitely its high-pressure anti-corruption campaign, which has ensnared millions within ‌China’s vast bureaucracy and has seen hundreds of top officials purged, including those once thought untouchable.

Xi had called on the party to “turn the blade inward” and unleash a revolution on itself and eradicate “viruses and impurities” that corrode its health. The party views ​the drive as essential to ensuring its long-term survival.
“No matter who they are, how high their position, or how great their contributions, anyone who engages in corruption will surely receive no leniency,” Xi said in January.

Chen’s unexpected probe “sends a signal that there’s no letting up in the anti-corruption drive and the party’s ’self-revolution,’” said China expert Jean Christopher Mittelstaedt of the University of Zurich.
“If anything, it continues to intensify.”

Chen, who last appeared in public last week, was a good candidate to ​watch for elevation to the ‌politburo standing committee in the ​party’s top reshuffle next year, Mittelstaedt said. “This ​sends a signal that nobody is safe.”
The Shanghai party secretary post is one of China’s most prestigious provincial-level positions and has often served as a springboard to top leadership roles.
Xi himself briefly served as Shanghai’s party boss in 2007 before joining the politburo’s standing committee, the country’s highest decision-making body.

Shanghai’s senior party leadership pledged loyalty to Beijing and understanding of the need to “see things through ⁠to the end” ⁠after Chen ​was put under investigation, the financial hub’s official paper said on Wednesday.

articles.title: With Huang rescue, Trump riskily ties his political fortunes to Nvidia
articles.summary: The US president's intercession to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang has inextricably linked their fates.

blocks.text: After the AI chipmaker Nvidia announced it was bringing back embattled former head Jensen Huang and the company's stock shot up like a bullet, President Donald Trump took a very public victory lap.
"I made the deal," he said during a lengthy phone interview with cable business news channel CNBC.

Trump followed that with an AI-generated image posted to his social media platform that riffed on the famous photograph taken moments after the 2024 attempt on his life in Pennsylvania. But instead of Trump in the image, Huang was the one surrounded by Secret Service guards. It depicted him in front of an Nvidia banner - with a raised first clenching a red bra.
The post was classic Trump – potentially offensive, yet still a bit opaque.

Was Trump suggesting Huang survived a scandal – one that includes allegations of recklessly jeopardising US national security by consorting with a suspected Chinese spy – the way he had survived an assassin's bullet?

Was the bra a celebration Huang's reported extramarital affairs? By replacing the US flag with an Nvidia standard, was he claiming that America and one of its largest, most powerful companies are one and the same?
At the very least, the image underscores how inextricably linked Huang and Trump now are, with the fate of the former hinging on the successes and failures of the latter.
And with that comes significant risks for the American president and for Republicans, including Vice-President JD Vance, who played a key part in his efforts to rescue Huang.

While Trump has said that a "very thorough investigation" by federal officials "exonerated" Huang and his reinstatement poses no national security threat, that is far from the final word on the matter.
"Every time you have a Chinese woman that's good looking or beautiful, they say she's a spy," Trump told CNBC, adding that "with Jensen, I don't believe that's true".
Democrats and some concerned Republicans in Congress have a different view.

They are promising to launch their own oversight of Huang and Nvidia, with subpoenas and compelled witness testimony, in order to assess whether they violated laws by allowing China to access sophisticated microchip technology.
State governments could also launch their own investigations.
Any new revelations could further damage the company's standing – and, by association, Trump himself.
"I have warned the administration from the start about Communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through both smuggling and remote access," Republican Senator Tom Cotton posted on X.
"Congress has much to investigate," he said.
While Huang has a long record of success at Nvidia, there is no guarantee that he can recapture past glory now that his star his dimmed.
Even if he is free from any criminal liability, the tech mogul is about to be in a much harsher spotlight than he has ever experienced.
Trump also appears to be on the wrong side of public opinion when it comes to AI writ large.

In the recent US midterm elections, candidates on both the left and right campaigned on imposing new restrictions on data centre construction, with many calling for new legal guardrails to prevent AI-fuelled economic and social disruption.

"Rather than addressing the American people's growing concerns about AI, this administration remains asleep at the wheel or willfully ignorant as our most advanced technologies fall into the hands of our greatest competitors," congresswoman Sydney Kamlager-Dove, a California Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, told the BBC.

The president's own political base is also suspicious of the new technology, with rural conservatives often rebelling at the demands that big tech companies have placed on their local resources and civic infrastructure.

The Nvidia story has also exposed rifts in Trump's own administration, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, a China hawk, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, a vocal proponent of AI, publicly feuding over whether to impose new restrictions on AI chip exports.

Both Bessent and Lutnick travelled with Trump on his recent trip to China, although it was the commerce secretary who hitched a ride back to the White House on the Marine One helicopter when Trump returned to Washington last Thursday.
Polling also indicated that political corruption was a top issue for voters this year.
The president's willingness to intervene in the deliberations of a major private company in which he owns millions of dollars of stock could further fuel those concerns.

Trump's decision to help save Huang – noting on Monday that "we have to protect our geniuses, and he certainly is a genius" – could further inflame the public's sense that the rich and powerful, genius or not, play by a different set of rules.

"It almost feels like they've bent the rule, the regulation, to allow this to happen because it's such an important part of our economy right now," Steve Bannon, a former top Trump adviser, said on his podcast on Monday.
"Even in the crash of 2008... I never saw the government step in and take over a board of directors."
For this American president, however, these risks appear to be worth taking because of the stakes involved.
Trump has long viewed the success of the US economy as a key part of his political legacy.
He boasted of the historic growth and low unemployment during his first presidential term (while glossing over the disruptions caused by the Covid pandemic).
And since returning to office, he has celebrated as major US stock indices posted new record highs.
Recent US economic expansion has been fuelled largely by investment in AI technology, and Trump has become one of the industry's biggest boosters.

He scolded states and local governments for blocking data centre construction and predicted that the nation that wins the race for supremacy in AI – which he has tried to rebrand as "super intelligence" – will control the fate of the world.

If Trump views the economy as the key to his political success and AI as instrumental to the health of the US economy, then his dramatic, precedent-shattering actions to try to rescue Nvidia, the company at the centre of America's AI industry, make more sense.
In the weeks since concerns over Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy first surfaced, Nvidia's stock price tumbled more than 32%.
Last Friday alone, it fell 14%.
US stock indices tumbled as well, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq down 10% last week and the larger S&P 500 dropping 8.6%.

The recent financial turmoil may have given Trump a glimpse into a future where AI growth is just the latest financial bubble – like the housing market in 2008 and internet companies in 2001 – that is due for a resounding pop, with similarly dire economic consequences to follow.
Trump's intervention on behalf of Huang arrested that drop, at least for a day.

On Tuesday, Nvidia's stock price gave back much of the bounce it had enjoyed, and larger stock indices were mixed. The fate of the America economy and the AI juggernaut that has powered it is still undetermined.
Trump's intervention may not be a crisis fully averted, but only a crisis delayed.
And if an AI reckoning does come, the US president will be hard-pressed to avoid being caught in the maelstrom.

articles.title: The rising cost of putting food on the table in India
articles.summary: India's food inflation is broadening, squeezing household budgets.

blocks.text: India's inflation is rising again. And the biggest worry is what's happening to food prices.
The latest government data, external shows retail inflation climbed to 6.09% in October, up from 5.54% in September.
But look more closely at food inflation. It has surged to 8.94%.
The squeeze was sharper in rural India, where food inflation was 9.09%, compared with 8.68% in urban areas.
In other words, food prices are rising considerably faster than the overall rate of inflation.
Food inflation this year has been driven by a combination of weather disruptions, supply shortages and rising input costs, say economists.

With nearly 60% of its farmland dependent on rainfall, external, India remains acutely vulnerable to the vagaries of the monsoon. This year, the southwest monsoon was 13% below normal and unevenly distributed, while intensifying El Niño conditions have heightened risks to farm production.
Food accounts for a smaller share of Indian household spending than it once did, but remains the biggest driver of inflation, with significant economic, social and political consequences.
In India's latest consumer price index, food and beverages account for 36.75% of the basket of goods and services used to measure inflation.
That is down sharply from 45.86% under the previous series, reflecting changing consumption patterns as Indians spend more on services, transport, healthcare, education and other non-food items.
Yet a sharp increase in food prices can move the overall inflation rate significantly, while disproportionately affecting people whose incomes leave little room for adjustment.

"Adjustability for a poor country like India is significantly lower," says Rajeswari Sengupta, an associate professor of economics at Mumbai-based Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, pointing to the fact that a substantial proportion of household income is still spent on food.
The numbers bear this out.
According to calculations by Dharmakirti Joshi, chief economist at analytics firm Crisil, the bottom 20% of rural households faced inflation of 6.9% in October, against 6.5% for the richest 20%.
In urban India, the corresponding rates were 6.1% and 5.3%.
The pressure is visible even in the cost of a simple meal.

Crisil's Roti Rice Rate analysis, external found that the cost of a home-cooked vegetarian thali - a meal platter - rose 12% year-on-year in October, driven by higher prices of onions, tomatoes, vegetables, edible oil, rice and cooking gas. A non-vegetarian thali became 9% more expensive.

Rice prices were up about 10% year-on-year, pulses 8%, edible oil 13% and LPG 10%, according to Pushan Sharma, director of intelligence at Crisil. "It's no longer a few commodities that are driving this increase, it's becoming a little more broad-based," he says.
When onion prices spike, households can cut back on their consumption to some extent. But substituting rice, pulses and cooking oil is considerably harder.

And food inflation is not just about what farmers produce. It is also about how efficiently that food is stored, processed and moved to the market. Weaknesses at each stage can turn seasonal shortages into sharp price spikes - and gluts into waste.

items: Onionomics: Peeling away the layers of India's food economy

blocks.text: Onions, for instance, are particularly susceptible to seasonal price swings.

The rabi crop - winter crops, sown after the monsoon and harvested in spring - which accounts for roughly two-thirds of onion production, is harvested in March and April and stored for several months. As stocks dwindle, prices can rise sharply before the next crop arrives.
Tomatoes, meanwhile, tend to see price spikes during the summer months, when arrivals decline in some markets or heat stress affects production.
Sharma says perishables are often responsible for the sudden spikes in food inflation, while prices of staples such as rice and wheat tend to rise more gradually but can stay higher for longer.
"The perishables are what caused the volatility. The non-perishables, like rice and wheat, are the ones that structurally increase the cost," he says.
Economists say India still lacks adequate infrastructure to sort, grade, store and process much of its perishable produce.
Tomatoes, for example, can become so abundant during a glut that farmers struggle to sell them at remunerative prices, only for consumers to face sharply higher prices months later.
Better storage and processing could help turn some of that surplus into products such as puree, smoothing the extremes between abundance and scarcity, according to Sharma
There are other pressures.
Energy shocks feed into the cost of transport, irrigation and agricultural inputs. Fertiliser prices can rise. Global edible-oil markets matter because India relies heavily on imports.
To be true, India, however, has some protection against the worst effects of food inflation.

Government stocks of cereals are comfortably above prescribed minimum levels, and the free-food programme covering nearly 800 million people offers a cushion against rising prices. Rice stocks, external are particularly ample.
There is a wider economic risk, says Sengupta.

"Food inflation may begin with a supply shock, but its effects can spread. Workers who find that their wages no longer cover basic living costs may seek higher pay. Businesses facing higher labour costs may raise prices. What begins as a rise in the price of food can gradually become a more general inflationary pressure - the familiar wage-price spiral that central banks try to prevent," she says.
For India, this creates a particularly difficult balancing act.

Agriculture is a relatively low-productivity sector, and the government has long sought to protect farmers by setting minimum support prices (MSPs) for certain crops - a price floor at which it promises to buy produce, helping farmers guard against a market crash.

At the same time, food prices are politically sensitive. Sharp increases in the price of staples such as onions and tomatoes can quickly anger consumers, prompting governments to step in with measures such as restricting exports, limiting how much traders can stockpile, or otherwise trying to bring prices down.
The broader story of India's changing food consumption makes the current inflation more interesting.

Households are eating differently from a decade ago. An analysis, external of the 2011-12 and 2023-24 consumption surveys shows that the share of cereals in food spending has fallen sharply, particularly among the poorest households, reflecting the impact of subsidised food programmes.
Meanwhile, consumption of nutrient-rich foods such as dairy, fruit and meat has increased across income groups, with the biggest gains among the poorest, the study revealed.

India's food basket is becoming more diverse. But diversity is meaningful only if ordinary Indians can afford it. Ultimately, food inflation is about what makes it to the plate - and what has to be left out.

articles.title: Shot in the face at 15: The lives shattered by Cameroon's decade of conflict
articles.summary: More than half a million people have fled their homes since separatist groups demanded independence for Cameroon's English-speaking regions.

blocks.text: Shot in the face at 15: The lives shattered by Cameroon's decade of conflict
Image source, Michael Mvondo/BBC
Median Bah was shot several times in the face by unknown gunmen
ByPaul Njie
BBC AfricaReporting fromOgoja
Median Bah was just 15 when her life changed forever.
She remembers the date vividly - 7 April 2018. She was ill and confined to her bed.
Armed men stormed her family's compound in Cameroon's Southwest region, one of the country's two English-speaking areas at the centre of a separatist conflict.
Median, now 23, says she was fast asleep when her brother woke her, panicked by the approach of a group of armed men who were shooting indiscriminately.
He escaped through a window. But for Median, fleeing was not so easy.
"Since I was sick, I had no strength to jump through the window with him, so I had to pass through the door," she tells the BBC.
That decision would have devastating consequences.
She says she came face to face with two of the attackers in the backyard, who opened fire at her.
They first shot her in the thigh before firing several more rounds, which severely damaged her face.
"I kept pleading with them not to kill me, that I wasn't feeling well. However, I found myself on the floor," she recalls.
Everything went dark. She lost consciousness and could neither see nor speak.
Median initially thought she was dreaming.
"To my surprise, it was reality."
The attack left her with devastating facial injuries. Her jawbone was damaged, most of her teeth destroyed and much of her mouth severely injured.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The Anglophone crisis began in 2016, when English-speaking Cameroonians took up arms over alleged marginalisation by the French-speaking government (file photo)

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
The Anglophone crisis began in 2016, when English-speaking Cameroonians took up arms over alleged marginalisation by the French-speaking government (file photo)
Over the past eight years, she has undergone at least four reconstructive surgeries in Cameroon, Ghana and India, with more procedures expected next year.
Parts of her face have been reconstructed using tissue taken from other parts of her body.
She also lost the ability to breathe normally through her nose and mouth. She underwent a tracheostomy, a surgical procedure that creates an opening in the neck to allow air into the windpipe.
For eight years, she relied on a tube to breathe. It was only recently removed, allowing her to breathe normally again.

A teenager left with devastating facial injuries, a mother forced to flee her home and a student whose education was disrupted. Nearly a decade of fighting in Cameroon has left countless lives shattered.

The crisis began in October 2016, when lawyers and teachers in Cameroon's English-speaking regions went on strike over the alleged marginalisation of Anglophone communities by the Francophone-dominated government.
They were concerned about the appointment of French-speaking judges and teachers to courts and schools in the English-speaking Northwest and Southwest regions.
Initially, the protest was peaceful, with thousands demanding greater recognition of the English-speaking minority.
But human rights groups accused security forces of using excessive force to suppress the protests. The crackdown, critics say, helped fuel an armed separatist movement.

By 2017, a dozen armed groups had emerged, according to the International Crisis Group, seeking independence for the two English-speaking regions and the creation of a breakaway state known as Ambazonia.

blocks.caption: Map of western Cameroon and eastern Nigeria highlighting Cameroon’s two English-speaking regions. The Northwest and Southwest regions are shaded pink and labelled, along with neighbouring Cross River state in Nigeria. Major locations marked include Ogoja in Nigeria and Yaoundé, Cameroon’s capital…

blocks.text: Since then, separatist fighters have engaged in a prolonged and often brutal conflict with government forces.
Rights groups have documented serious abuses by both sides.
Separatist fighters have been accused of targeted killings, kidnappings for ransom, torture and attacks on schools and other public and private facilities.
Government forces, meanwhile, have faced allegations of arbitrary arrests and detention, torture and unlawful killings.
Both sides have denied the accusations, although in some instances they have acknowledged responsibility for abuses.
The violence has devastated communities and forced half a million people from their homes, according to data published by the UN this year.
At least 6,000 people have been killed since the conflict began, according to Human Rights Watch.
The UN refugee agency, UNHCR, says more than 70,000 Cameroonians have sought refuge in neighbouring Nigeria.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Gloria Akom is among 15,000 people who fled Cameroon for Nigeria's Cross River state

blocks.text: Gloria Akom is among 15,000 people who fled Cameroon for Nigeria's Cross River state
Glory Akom, 44, lives with a disability after surviving severe burns in an incident unrelated to the conflict.
The mother-of-two now lives in a camp in Ogoja, a town in Nigeria's south-eastern Cross River state, near the Cameroonian border.
Ogoja hosts about 15,000 refugees across three settlements, Richard Effiong, from the UNHCR, told the BBC.
The UNHCR has provided refugees with brick houses topped with tin roofs.
For many, however, uncertainty remains over when, or whether, they will ever return home.
Glory says her life in Cameroon was far better. She ran a business and was able to provide for her family.
But everything changed when fighting intensified in 2017.
She said soldiers deployed to her area in the Southwest region pursued residents into the bush, forcing them to abandon their homes and flee into Nigeria.
"We were sleeping in the bush, as we were always running," she said.
"If you slept in your house, they could kill you there."
Initially, she settled in a neighbouring village before moving to Ogoja, where she was eventually allocated a permanent home.
Like many other refugees, Glory depends on $67 (£51) monthly cash assistance from UNHCR to support her children, one of who suffers from sickle cell and requires regular medical attention.
The money is barely enough to cover food, medical bills and other necessities, she says.
Her sadness at having to leave home is shared by other Cameroonian refugees in Ogoja who spoke to the BBC.

Maurine Mangha, 21, said she and five other members of her family fled Akwaya in the Southwest region after separatist fighters opened fire during celebrations marking what they described as their independence on 1 October 2017.
"They shot a lot of people, and we had no choice but run into the bush," she tells the BBC.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Education in Cameroon's Southwest region has been severely disrupted by the conflict (file photo)

blocks.text: Education in Cameroon's Southwest region has been severely disrupted by the conflict (file photo)
Maurine had stopped attending school months earlier because of a separatist-imposed education boycott.
The 2017 boycott campaign, which sought to pressure the government, involved threats and attacks against schools and those who defied orders to stay away.
The consequences for children have been severe.

More than 200,000 children are currently out of school in the conflict regions, while nearly 2,500 learning institutions remain non-operational in the two regions, according to the UN's children's agency, Unicef, citing Cameroonian education authorities.
Despite the disruption, Maurine managed to secure a scholarship through a higher education programme for refugees managed by the UNHCR.
She is now studying microbiology at a local polytechnic.
But Maurine says she cannot help thinking about friends who remained in Cameroon.
"I feel very bad for my friends as they did not have the opportunity [to further] their education because of the crisis," she says.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Maurine Mangha has managed to get a scholarship to continue her education

blocks.text: Maurine Mangha has managed to get a scholarship to continue her education
After nearly a decade of fighting, the Cameroonian government wants the separatists to abandon their armed struggle.
In September, the authorities launched a community dialogue initiative aimed at finding grassroots solutions to the conflict.

"It is you, all of us sitting here, who have the capacity today to organise to talk to those boys [separatists], to tell them, the time has come for them to leave," Prime Minister Joseph Dion Ngute said during the launch in Buea, capital of the Southwest region.
He repeated a similar message in Bamenda, the main city in the Northwest region and one of the epicentres of the conflict.
At both events, nearly 60 people described as former separatist fighters were presented as having abandoned the armed struggle and surrendered to the state.

As of November 2026, almost 1,500 former separatist fighters were undergoing rehabilitation at Disarmament, Demobilisation and Reintegration (DDR) centres in the two English-speaking regions, a Cameroonian official from the agency overseeing the programme told the BBC.
Although a similar initiative in 2019 failed to end the fighting, the government hopes to persuade more fighters to abandon their campaign for independence.
"A lot of Amba boys [separatist fighters] have been killed, others have surrendered, and many of them have abandoned the ideology of independence," says Clovis Naseri, a former separatist commander.

blocks.caption: Image caption, President Paul Biya, who has been in power since 1982, has faced criticism over his government's military crackdown on Anglophone separatists

blocks.text: President Paul Biya, who has been in power since 1982, has faced criticism over his government's military crackdown on Anglophone separatists
Clovis spent about two years with the White Tigers of Ribbons, an armed group operating in the Southwest region, before abandoning the group in 2019.
He was subsequently admitted to a reintegration centre, where he underwent rehabilitation for several years.
He is now a vocal critic of the separatist movement and advocates peace and national unity.
Despite defections and government efforts to encourage fighters to surrender, separatist groups continue to carry out attacks across the two regions.
Some analysts argue that the conflict has persisted for so long partly because of the government's failure to address the grievances that triggered it.
Roland Fru, a researcher on the Anglophone crisis, says the authorities are yet to demonstrate a clear understanding of the issues driving the conflict.
"I've not heard even once, the government explain things in such a way that helps me understand that they even understand the problem," he says.
The BBC contacted several government officials for comment but did not receive a response.
Cameroonian authorities have frequently rejected criticism of their handling of the crisis.
Last November, President Paul Biya said the reconstruction efforts, supported by international partners, were helping restore normality in the affected regions.
"These efforts will continue steadily," he said during his swearing-in ceremony, while praising security forces for their "effective actions" and "professionalism" in improving the situation.
For survivors such as Median, Glory and Maurine, however, lasting peace may remain elusive until the fighting comes to a permanent end.
As they try to rebuild their lives and hold on to hope, Median, who still lives in Cameroon, says she remains grateful to have survived.
"I have defeated death," she says confidently. "I don't think there's anything that can stop me."
Additional reporting by the BBC's Michel Mvondo
