articles.title: Armed men take 25 hostages at supermarket in one of Colombia’s top tourist destinations
articles.summary:
Police say group seized store in city of Cartagena and local media showed footage of snipers on nearby buildings

A group of armed men with their faces covered seized a supermarket in the

blocks.text: A group of armed men with their faces covered seized a supermarket in the Colombian city of Cartagena on Tuesday and are holding 25 people hostage, the president, Abelardo de la Espriella, said on Tuesday.
De la Espriella, said the men were “common criminals” who fled into the supermarket after a failed attempt to hold up an armored truck.
Military and police forces have been deployed to the hostage site, Colombian police said.

Footage shared on social media showed dozens of people rushing out of the Exito supermarket in Cartagena’s La Castellana neighborhood, while local media have shown footage of snipers on nearby buildings in what appears to be a standoff between the armed men and police.

“Thirty people were kidnapped, five ​of whom have already been released. They are older women,” said de la Espriella from the city of ​Villavicencio, where he traveled after an overnight bombing ​there.

Cartagena is one of Colombia’s main tourist destinations. The city of a million people is famous for its well-preserved 18th-century architecture, and the thick stone walls built to defend it from pirate attacks.

The Rafael Núñez airport in Cartagena temporarily suspended its operations on Tuesday after the incident, as the armed forces used one of the runways in ​connection with ​the incident. It later said operations were slowly returning to normal and landings were reopened about 45 minutes after the suspension.
Local media reported the hostages are ​being her at the Castellana location of ​the ⁠Éxito supermarket chain.
More details soon …

articles.title: Israel attempts to jail Palestinian student at Hebrew University without trial
articles.summary:
Mahdi Tounsi appeared to have suffered maltreatment at hearing where he was not allowed to hear prosecution case against him

Palestinian student Mahdi Tounsi appeared in a closed-door court…
articles.byline: Emma Graham-Harrison and Quique Kierszenbaum in Jerusalem

blocks.text: Palestinian student Mahdi Tounsi appeared in a closed-door court hearing in Jerusalem, as academics and activists warned that Israel’s attempt to jail him without trial marked a serious escalation in attacks on Palestinian rights.
Yael Berda, a lawyer and sociology professor at Hebrew University, who has taught Tounsi for four years, came to court to call for his release.

“I have no doubt this is a case of political persecution based on identity and political activity,” she said outside the courtroom. “Mehdi’s arrest is part of a campaign that we’ve seen very much escalating since the elections.”
Her student was “almost unrecognisable” when he appeared on a video link in the courtroom, deprived of his glasses, with his hair and beard shaved and with visible bruising, she added.

blocks.caption: Mahdi Tounsi appears at the hearing via video link. Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian

blocks.text: Tounsi, a sociology and criminology student at Hebrew University in Jerusalem, was seized from his dorm on 8 November. He is held at Megiddo prison where documented abuse includes starvation rations, violent attacks on prisoners and rampant scabies and other diseases.

Thousands of Palestinians from the occupied West Bank are held under administrative detention orders but they have rarely been used against Palestinians who have Israeli citizenship or residence status in occupied East Jerusalem.
Prison authorities had not complied with a judge’s order to return Tounsi’s glasses, his brief public appearance on Tuesday showed.
Israeli prosecutors are seeking an administrative detention order, which allows for up to six months’ detention without trial or public presentation of evidence.
Security forces presented a summary of evidence in a hearing closed even to Tounsi and his lawyers, making a defence effectively impossible.

Tounsi’s arrest comes amid a racist campaign of delegitimisation against Palestinian citizens of Israel, whose votes were critical to stripping Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition of its majority in elections last month.

Noa Dagoni, executive director of Jerusalem-focused rights group Ir Amin, described Tounsi’s arrest as a dangerous escalation in political persecution of activists, particularly those “at the junction of human rights, dialogue and non-violent action”.

Many of the Ir Amin staff count Tounsi as a personal friend after years working together in his home community of Silwan, where Israeli authorities are forcing mass displacements of Palestinians, including to make way for a theme park.

Dagoni fears he may have been targeted for this work. “We’re very concerned that this [arrest] has to do with his being a non-violent peace activist, also dealing with the displacement in his community,” she said.
“The partnership of Israelis and Palestinians is very intimidating for this government because it can be effective, it can build real political power.”
Officers from the Shin Bet security force failed to appear in court to present evidence at a first hearing last week, so the judge reconvened on Tuesday.

Reflecting concern about the case, his family and lawyer were joined in the courthouse by prominent activists, Knesset member Ofer Cassif, diplomats from Ireland, the Netherlands and the EU, his tutor and the dean of students from Hebrew University.
Hundreds of Jewish and Palestinian demonstrators gathered in the street outside calling for his immediate release.

blocks.caption: Demonstrators outside the district court in Jerusalem on 24 November campaigning against the administrative detention of Mahdi Tounsi.  Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian

blocks.text: Many knew Tounsi personally from classes or activism, including Lana, a Palestinian citizen of Israel.

“Someone who I know being kidnapped was really frightening,” she said. “It makes me think of my place here also, how it might affect me and if there are more people who I know who are going to be arrested soon.”

Many protesters were angry with university authorities, including Arielle, 27, a former student at the same campus. “Israeli universities need to take accountability for this, like they can’t allow students to be kidnapped from their dorm rooms,” she said.

Hebrew University’s dean of students, Zohar Kampf, said the university asked to testify but its request was rejected. The university has not commented on Tounsi’s violent arrest, deprivation of glasses and other mistreatment.

Cassif, the Knesset member, called for a global pressure campaign. “Where is the international community, especially academia. What are they waiting for?” he said. “Speak up, do something, raise your voice.”

The police did not respond to questions about visible marks of abuse or details of the case against Tounsi. A spokesperson said: “The suspect was lawfully arrested as part of an investigation conducted by the Jerusalem District Central Investigations Unit concerning ties to an act of terrorism.”

articles.title: Ukraine's bid for NATO membership and more air defense remains controversial
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is calling for the rapid acceptance of his country into NATO. However, the necessary unanimity for this is lacking, as shown during the NATO Parliamentary…

image.caption: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy participated in the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin via video conferenceImage: Liesa Johannssen/REUTERS

blocks.text: It took a while for the video call to connect. When Volodymyr Zelenskyy finally greeted the delegates in Berlin, applause broke out. The Ukrainian president appealed to the gathered parliamentarians from 32 NATO member states to keep supporting his country, especially against the massive aerial bombardment from Russia.

"Dear friends, winter is now ahead of us. And of course, our number one priority is air defense," Zelenskyy told the delegates. His country urgently needs more Patriot and other comprehensive anti-air attack systems. "And your countries have them. Missiles that can stop Russian ballistic missiles should not be sitting in warehouses collecting dust. And we say this openly. Please help us with this."
Western allies boost Ukraine's defenses but clash over deep strikes
Ukraine seeks to join NATO

Zelenskyy renewed his call for his country to join the NATO military alliance. That issue is not for the NATO Parliamentary Assembly, which was gathered for its 72nd annual meeting in Berlin, to decide. But it was important to the Ukrainian president to reiterate his request.

After the war ends, Ukraine needs strong security guarantees and NATO could ensure those. "Wouldn't it be more effective to simply bring Ukraine into NATO?" Zelenskyy asked, arguing: "Wouldn't that be better for all of us, for everyone? Cheaper to put in place? And more reliable when it comes to actually protecting security?"

There is conflict among NATO members about the possibility of admitting Ukraine. The alliance has affirmed multiple times that the path to membership stands open to Ukraine — however, in the long term rather than the near future. This is primarily because of the ongoing war and the possible assistance obligations of other NATO countries for Ukraine, which was attacked by Russia.

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte rejected the Ukrainian demands at the summit, which for the first time in 26 years was held in Berlin. Ukraine had entry prospects; however, NATO members currently lack unanimity on this issue. NATO alone decides who becomes a member. "There is total clarity on that within the alliance," Rutte said.
If Russia attacked NATO, would Germany be prepared?
Merz: Denying Ukraine NATO membership in 2008 'was a mistake'

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz advocated for Ukraine to receive security guarantees similar to what NATO members have, in the instance of a possible ceasefire. In retrospect, it was clear "what a mistake it was not to follow the American suggestion back in 2008 at the NATO summit in Bucharest to admit Ukraine as a member," Merz said at a joint press conference following a meeting with Rutte.

Whether or not a NATO entry for Ukraine could be part of negotiations with Russia is another question, according to Rutte. He approved of current US efforts to bring about peace talks, and how Europe was closely consulting with Ukraine and the US for a unified position. "But it is also to test now whether Putin is willing to play ball, and then these issues might come up again."

The Russian invasion of Ukraine has led to NATO arming itself on a massive scale. Members have committed to raising their countries' defense spending to 5% of their gross domestic product (GDP) by 2035.

Rutte warned that all the allies needed a credible path to get there, "and ideally, they get there sooner than 2035." In addition, he said weapons production among member states needed to further increase because "right now, demand still far exceeds the supply."
Why Germany's military ambitions face a battle at home
Germany's military budget has had a massive increase

The contribution by Germany's Bundeswehr armed forces to NATO was explained by Carsten Breuer, Germany's highest-ranking soldier. For example, the massive increase in military spending: "Our defense budget has tripled since 2021. The goal is to achieve the 5% target, which was set at the summit in The Hague, well before 2035." In the coming year, Germany's defense budget has risen to more than €139 billion ($151 billion).

The Bundeswehr was further developing into a "constantly modernized, effective and innovative army, Breuer said. Also, a much larger one than before. "To reach our current capability goals we are expanding the Bundeswehr to a total of 460,000 soldiers by the mid-2030s," the German chief of defense said. Of those, 200,000 are to be reservists. "This is like walking a tightrope because we must find the right balance between growth and operational readiness."

Following his speech, Breuer answered questions from the delegates who showed keen interest in the developments. The discussion was a preview of Breuer's new post: He has been voted in as the new chair of the NATO Military Committee and will move to the alliance's headquarters in Brussels mid-next year. Then he will become the principal military advisor to NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte. "I take this election as a sign of recognition that Germany has now accepted its responsibility as well as its role in security policy," Breuer said.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: More than 300 Russians killed as Moscow props up Mali’s junta, leaked data reveals
articles.summary:
Records list 349 deaths in three years in Mali and also shed light on Russia’s military activity elsewhere in Africa

When the attack on Kidal began before dawn on 25 April this year, the…
articles.byline: Pjotr Sauer, Michael Goodier, Harriet Agerholm and Philip McMahon

blocks.text: When the attack on Kidal began before dawn on 25 April this year, the Russian fighters were caught off guard. Within the first hour, checkpoints on the outskirts of the remote desert city nestled among the rocky hills of northern Mali had fallen to the insurgents, who pushed towards the police station where fierce fighting erupted.

“Everything was happening at once. Explosions were going off all around us, people were shouting,” recalled a former member of Russia’s Africa Corps who was stationed in Mali at the time and spoke on condition of anonymity. “Nobody knew where the enemy was coming from.”

The Kremlin-controlled forces and their Malian allies were facing a coordinated surprise assault by the al-Qaida-linked JNIM and the Tuareg-led Azawad Liberation Front (FLA), whose fighters used suicide car bombs and drones to break through the city’s defences.

blocks.caption: The view from a helicopter flying over a convoy of tankers heading towards Mali’s capital, Bamako, in May 2026, posted on the X account of the Africa Corps. Photograph: Africa Corps/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Leaked Russian state records suggest the losses were heavy that day. Death certificates of Russian fighters killed in Mali, held by Rosstat, Russia’s state statistics agency, were obtained by the hacker groups Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow and analysed by the Guardian.

The records show that 43 Russians died in Mali on 25 April, including six in Kidal and one in nearby Aguelhok. Others were recorded as dying in the capital, Bamako, and in Gao, where rebels shot down a Russian military helicopter that day.

By the following morning, the Russians had abandoned Kidal, which Russian mercenaries had helped capture in November 2023 and which Moscow had since held up as a showcase of its growing influence in Africa.
In all, the records list 349 Russian deaths in Mali between September 2023 and September 2026, most of which the Guardian was able to link to known battles with rebel groups.

blocks.caption: A billboard in Bamako carrying birthday wishes for Vladimir Putin, October 2024. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The figures offer a previously unseen glimpse into the human cost of Moscow’s efforts to prop up Mali’s military junta, in what has become Russia’s largest military deployment in Africa.
Two western officials who have travelled to Mali and were shown the data said the death toll was higher than previously estimated.
“That’s over 10% of Russia’s forces killed in action,” said one of the officials, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to comment publicly.
Moscow does not publish its losses in Africa, and its foreign ministry did not respond to a request for comment.

The Wagner private military group, led by the warlord Yevgeny Prigozhin, first arrived in Mali in late 2021, a year after a military coup had toppled President Ibrahim Boubacar Keïta. French forces were ordered to leave the country as relations with the junta deteriorated, bringing an end to France’s decade-long counter-terrorism operation and leaving Russia as the regime’s main foreign protector.

blocks.caption: Three Russian mercenaries operating in northern Mali, January 2022 Photograph: French army/AP

blocks.text: Wagner handed over its operations in Mali to the Africa Corps in June 2025, two years after Prigozhin led a failed mutiny on Moscow that discredited the group in the eyes of the Kremlin. By that summer, British intelligence estimated that about 2,000 Africa Corps personnel were deployed in the country.

The Africa Corps, closely overseen by Russian military intelligence, currently provides backing to several African governments in return for payment or lucrative contracts granting access to natural resources.

Despite the Russian presence, Mali’s security situation has continued to deteriorate. In late July 2024, Russian and Malian forces fought Tuareg separatists for several days near Tinzaouaten, on the Algerian border.
Wagner at the time issued a rare statement admitting losses, including the death of a commander, but gave no figure. Estimates from Russian sources ranged from about 20 to more than 80 dead.

blocks.caption: Graves of Wagner fighters in a cemetery near the village of Bakinskaya, in Russia’s Krasnodar region, January 2023. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: The Rosstat records list 70 Russians who died on 27 July 2024, all but one of them in the Kidal region. The figures make the battle of Tinzaouaten the deadliest single day for Russian forces in Africa since Wagner mercenaries first deployed to the continent in 2017.

The toll in Mali may have been driven up by Ukraine, which has extended its war against Russia to the Sahel. Kyiv has been assisting Tuareg rebels there, according to two people with knowledge of the operations. CNN has reported that about 15 Ukrainian specialists were deployed to Mali to help local rebel forces fighting Russian troops.

The records are probably an undercount. Registration often lags, and no Russian deaths in Mali are recorded for March 2026 although at least three Africa Corps fighters were reported killed in an ambush near Nampala that month.

The leaked data also sheds light on Russia’s military activity elsewhere in Africa. Central African Republic, where Wagner fighters guard the president, Faustin-Archange Touadéra, accounts for 30 deaths. While not all could be linked to known incidents, three men died on the night drones struck Wagner camps in Kaga-Bandoro in December 2023.

In Libya, where Russian forces back the eastern commander Khalifa Haftar and use his airbases as a supply route to their deployments in the Sahel, some of the recorded deaths were probably linked to a helicopter crash at the Maaten al-Sarra base in February 2026. On Sunday, Ukrainian drones sunk a Russian warship off the coast of Libya; it is unclear whether there were any casualties.

blocks.caption: Supporters of Niger’s ruling junta hold up a Russian flag in Niamey, August 2023.  Photograph: Sam Mednick/AP

blocks.text: In Niger, where Russia’s Africa Corps moved in after the military junta expelled French and US troops, a Russian fighter died two days after Islamic State militants attacked Niamey airport in January, a previously unreported casualty.

Moscow has in recent months stepped up its effort to show it is back in control in Mali. On 6 October, Malian troops and the Africa Corps recaptured Kidal after what the army called an air and ground campaign.

A report this month by the US-based Conflict Insights Group (CIG) found that the Africa Corps had sharply increased its use of drones in Mali, including Lancet suicide drones, amid an intensifying air campaign.

The group wrote that the drone campaign had also targeted civilians, boostering support for the rebels. “Civilian deaths in the intensified air campaign, which the Africa Corps leads, are likely to aid insurgent recruitment,” it said.

blocks.caption: Vladimir Putin and the Malian junta leader, Assimi Goita, at the Kremlin in June 2025. Photograph: Pavel Bednyakov/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: A western diplomat who works in the region said the attacks in late April had punctured the image of Russian military invincibility that Moscow and the junta had cultivated among Malians.
“Russia still wields considerable influence in Mali, but patience with its military performance is wearing thin.”

articles.title: World Chess Championship 2026 Game 1: Gukesh Dommaraju v Javokhir Sindarov – live
articles.summary:
• Youngest title match in chess history starts Tuesday

  • Sindarov, Gukesh open with Berlin defense of Ruy Lopez

blocks.text: Everything you need to know about the World Chess Championship

India’s Gukesh Dommaraju is defending the world chess championship against fast-rising Uzbek grandmaster Javokhir Sindarov in the youngest title match in the competition’s 140-year history. The best-of-14-games contest is scheduled to take place from 24 November to 12 December at the Fondation Martin Bodmer outside Geneva, with an overall prize fund of $2.5m (£1.9m).

items: Game 1 starts at 3pm in Geneva, 2pm in London, 9am in New York and 7.30pm in India
Sindarov will have the white pieces for Game 1 and make the first move
Gukesh and Sindarov are both 20 years old, making this the youngest matchup in world championship’s 140-year history
Read the Guardian’s comprehensive watch guide for the Gukesh v Sindarov showdown
Go move by move through 22 of the most famous games in world championship history

blocks.text: Key events

items: 1h agoGame 1 is under way!
2h agoHow do Gukesh and Sindarov match up?
2h agoThe format
2h agoPreamble
3h agoEverything you need to know about the World Chess Championship

blocks.text: And finally Gukesh makes his move! After a think of more than 15 minutes, the world champion has opted for 13 ... Bd7, bringing his last minor piece into play. The bishop also shields the black king from a potential check along the d-file, giving Gukesh greater flexibility in repositioning his king and coordinating his rooks. He’s more than 35 minutes behind the challenger on time, though.
Gukesh is in another deep think as Javokhir leaves the board for the nearby lounge chair inside the cramped playing hall.

“Now I understand what Javokhir was playing for,” English grandmaster David Howell says on the Chess.com broadcast. “I would have expected this opening from two older players, not maybe two 20-year-olds. But now I understand he’s trying to bait Gukesh. He’s trying to tempt him into some line where he has a deep, deep idea. Yeah, it’s very provocative.”

blocks.caption: Sindarov looks on as Gukesh ponders his response to 13 Ne4. Photograph: Chess.com

blocks.text: Gukesh has developed his dark-squared bishop and Sindarov has centralized his queenside knight (12 ... Be7 13 Ne4). The pace of play has slowed considerably as the players begin to grapple with the strategic subtleties of the Berlin. Both Stockfish and the Sesse supercomputer assess the position as dead even (0.00).

blocks.caption: Gukesh studies the position during Tuesday’s opening game of the world chess championship. Photograph: Denis Balibouse/Reuters

blocks.text: An email from the always welcome Gary Naylor, who sees parallels between the world chess championship and another of Europe’s great endurance events:

double quotation markGiven the location, the schedule, the fact that each leader has a team supporting him and, more than anything, the stamina required, this feels like the Tour de France. I suppose players have the ability to make stages – games – hard or easy by their strategies too. Any sign of lycra?

No lycra to report, Gary, but there’s certainly something to the analogy. The ability to conserve energy over a three-week campaign, knowing when to attack and when to settle for a quiet day, is an underrated component of world championship matchplay.
Gukesh has been mulling his response to 12 Be3 for more than 10 minutes, after spending about eight minutes on his previous move.

“He still knows the position, but he is taking time to make sure he makes the right moves,” Russian grandmaster Peter Svidler says on the official Fide broadcast. “But Gukesh is already down almost 18 minutes on the clock. Considering he’s playing one of the most topical openings of the past 25 years, that’s some time expenditure.”
Gukesh has brought his knight to g6, putting pressure on the advanced white pawn on e5, and Sindarov has continued his development by bringing his bishop into play (11 ... Ng6 12 Be3).

Gukesh has returned his king to its original square and rerouted his knight (9 Rd1+ Ke8 10 Nc3 Ne7 11 h3). Sindarov’s last move prevents black’s light-squared bishop from coming to g4 and pinning the knight on f3, while giving his own king some breathing room.

“I think it’s important to highlight for our viewers that black is not playing for a draw,” the Hungarian grandmaster Judit Polgár says on Chess.com’s broadcast. “Black is just deciding to go into an endgame or a middlegame without queens, where it seems like only white has a slight edge. Black has doubled pawns on c6 and c7, black has the bishop pair, but basically black can go b6, develop the pieces properly.”

blocks.caption: The position after 10 Nc3. Photograph: Fide

blocks.text: We’re heading straight into the famous Berlin endgame (4 O-O Nxe4 5 d4 Nd6 6 Bxc6 dxc6 7 dxe5 Nf5 8 Qxd8+ Kxd8). The queens are off the board after only eight moves, leaving white with a kingside pawn majority and black with the bishop pair but doubled c-pawns and a king that has forfeited the right to castle.

Don’t mistake the early exchange of queens for a lack of ambition. The resulting position is deceptively rich in strategic possibilities and has been the subject of decades of analysis at the highest level. Gukesh has continued with 9 Rd1+, and both players are still moving quickly.
Game 1 is under way!
The players have shaken hands and we’re off! We have a Berlin defense of the Ruy Lopez (1 e4 e5 2 Nf3 Nc6 3 Bb5 Nf6), one of the most thoroughly analyzed openings in modern chess.

The Berlin famously helped Vladimir Kramnik dethrone Garry Kasparov in their 2000 world title match in London and has been a staple of elite chess ever since, earning a reputation as one of black’s most reliable weapons against 1 e4.

We’re eight minutes to the scheduled first move, but American grandmaster Maurice Ashley has started with his introduction of the players to the playing hall. Gukesh enters first and takes his seat behind the black pieces. Sindarov, playing as white after Sunday’s drawing of lots, enters second.

blocks.caption: Fide president Timur Turlov makes the ceremonial first move for white in Tuesday’s opening game of the world chess championship between Javokhir Sindarov and Gukesh Dommaraju near Geneva. Photograph: Denis Balibouse/Reuters

blocks.text: If you’re looking for some pre-match reading, the Guardian spoke exclusively with Javokhir Sindarov on Sunday about his meteoric rise, his love of Lionel Messi, his plans to play GTA VI once the match is over and why chess’s happy warrior believes there’s more to life than the game. A taste:

double quotation mark“I’m the guy who can’t play games just for fun,” Sindarov tells the Guardian less than 48 hours before Tuesday’s world championship opener in Geneva, smiling at the absurdity of it. “If I play something, I always try to learn, trying to become better.” That means poring over Counter-Strike tactics and watching YouTube tutorials before joining in with his mates. There is, it appears, no such thing as a casual game in Sindarov’s world, much less a friendly. “I always like to beat my friends,” he says. “I watch some video lessons and then come and beat them after some tournaments. I think the best thing is to beat your friends in some game.” It is a revealing admission from a young man who has acquired a reputation for being uncommonly relaxed at the chess board. While many of the world’s elite players seem to carry the weight of every position on their shoulders – the viral clip of Sergey Karjakin agonizing for 25 minutes over a move during the 2016 world title match remains a cult classic in chess circles – Sindarov frequently gives off the impression of someone who is simply enjoying himself. The easygoing mien of the sport’s happy warrior is a quality that has caught his opponent’s attention. “One thing I learned from Sindarov is that he seems to be so happy while playing chess,” Gukesh Dommaraju, the reigning world champion, said in an interview published last week.

We’ve gone through the 140-year history of the world championship and chosen 22 of the most memorable games. You can go move by move through each of them here. It’s the perfect timesuck in the final run-up to today’s first move.

double quotation markFrom the middle of the 16th century, there have come down to us the names of chess players who have been widely regarded as the strongest of their time. The earliest of these was the Spanish priest Ruy López de Segura, after whom one of the most popular openings of modern times is named. Others who followed include the Calabrese Gioachino Greco, François-André Danican Philidor, Louis-Charles Mahé de La Bourdonnais, Alexander McDonnell, Howard Staunton, Adolf Anderssen, Mikhail Chigorin and Paul Morphy, each of whom are lionized for their contributions to the development of theory and strategy as well as their dominance over their board during their respective eras. But not until Wilhelm Steinitz and Johannes Zukertort sat down in a small room at 80 Fifth Avenue in New York City on the afternoon of 11 January 1886 did a formal competition to determine the best player on the planet come to pass. Their first-to-10-wins encounter was held in three US cities over the next 78 days for a prize fund of $4,000. Since then, the world chess championship has provided the stage for countless unforgettable contests showcasing the precision, imagination and brilliance of the royal game at the highest level.

The legitimacy of the world championship, of course, remains a subject of lively debate. The absence of Magnus Carlsen continues to cast a long shadow over the sport’s showcase event. The 35-year-old Norwegian has held the world No 1 ranking for more than 15 consecutive years and was widely regarded as the game’s strongest player even before he defeated Vishy Anand for the world title in 2013. He only strengthened his claim as the greatest player of any era in 2021, when he crushed Ian Nepomniachtchi in Dubai in his fourth successful defense of the crown.

But Carlsen declined to defend his title for a fifth time in 2023, citing a lack of motivation to endure the months-long grind of preparation that championship matches demand. Only twice before had the chain of succession that stretches back to Wilhelm Steinitz in 1886 been broken: when Alexander Alekhine died as champion in 1946 and when Bobby Fischer forfeited the title in 1975.

blocks.caption: Norway’s Magnus Carlsen has held the world No 1 ranking for more than 15 consecutive years. Photograph: Yu Chun Christopher Wong/Eurasia Sport Images/Getty Images

blocks.text: Ding Liren went on to defeat Nepomniachtchi for the vacant title before losing it to Gukesh Dommaraju in Singapore the following year. Now Gukesh faces Sindarov in a match between two 20-year-olds ranked No 26 and No 4 in the world respectively, while the planet’s top-ranked player remains on the sidelines – at a time when his No 1 ranking is looking more vulnerable than any time in anyone’s memory. The generational stakes are undeniable, but the question that has dogged the championship since Carlsen walked away remains unresolved: can the winner truly claim to be the best chess player in the world?
How do Gukesh and Sindarov match up?

For two elite players born in the same general part of the world barely six months apart, their competitive history is remarkably sparse: just three encounters in classical chess. Sindarov holds a 2½-½ advantage with two wins and one draw in their lifetime head-to-head, which dates back to their first encounter as tweens at the Moscow Open in 2018. Their most recent meeting happened in January at the prestigious Tata Steel tournament in Wijk aan Zee, where a tense positional struggle gave way to a wild, time-scrambled endgame before the pair settled for a draw after 78 moves. Sindarov also holds a 2-1 edge in their three rapid and blitz contests this year.
Allow content provided by a third party?

This article includes content hosted on lichess.org. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

Gukesh’s form has largely gone off the rails since reaching the summit 23 months ago in Singapore. After making it to No 3 in the world with a peak rating of 2794, the Indian suffered a prolonged run of disappointing results, including a joint-last finish at March’s Prague Chess Festival and last-place showings at Norway Chess and the Chennai Grand Masters. He subsequently withdrew from the classical portion of the Grand Chess Tour and had tumbled to No 32 in the rankings by September, when his live rating briefly dipped below the 2700 barrier for the first time in four years, although his performances improved at that month’s Chess Olympiad.

Many of the world’s top grandmasters have expressed deep pessimism about Gukesh’s chances in Geneva due to his lengthy slump and Sindarov’s sustained upward tick. So too have the bookmakers, who have installed the Uzbek as a clear frontrunner at roughly 1-3 odds despite Gukesh being the champion. Carlsen has described Sindarov as “a pretty significant favorite”, citing the Indian’s tendency to take excessive risks. “His evaluations are way too optimistic,” the world No 1 said recently. “That makes him take way more chances than he should. I think especially now his confidence hasn’t been too high, he just tries to do a little bit too much.”

Yet one factor in Gukesh’s favor is his firsthand experience in the cauldron of a world championship match, where the intense psychological and physical rigors of facing the same opponent for weeks on end can be as punishing as the chess itself. Caruana, the world No 3 and former world title challenger who pushed Carlsen to the brink in 2018, has cautioned against writing off the champion despite his struggles. “The kind of ability he had – or has, whatever you want to say – it doesn’t disappear overnight,” Caruana said in September. “So, in my opinion, it can reverse at any moment.”

blocks.caption: Javokhir Sindarov, left, and Gukesh Dommaraju stand on the podium during Sunday’s world chess championship opening ceremony at the United Nations’ European headquarters in Geneva. Photograph: Salvatore Di Nolfi/EPA

blocks.text: The format

Here’s a review of the format for the world championship match. Gukesh and Sindarov will play up to 14 classical games with each player awarded one point for a win and a half-point for a draw. Whoever reaches seven and a half points first will be declared the champion (and no dead rubbers will be played).

The time control for each game is 120 minutes per side for the first 40 moves, then 30 minutes for the remainder of the game, with a 30-second increment per move starting with move 41. That means games can stretch beyond seven hours, testing both players’ concentration and endurance. Players are not permitted to agree to a draw before black’s 40th move, a rule designed to discourage short, uneventful games. A draw claim before then is only allowed in the case of threefold repetition or stalemate, subject to approval by the chief arbiter or deputy arbiter.

If the score is level after 14 games, a series of tiebreaks will be played on 12 December, starting with four rapid games at 15 minutes per player plus 10 seconds per move. If still tied, the players will contest two games at 10 minutes plus five seconds, followed if necessary by two blitz games at three minutes plus two seconds. Further single blitz games will be played until a winner emerges. Three of the past five world championship matches have been deadlocked after the classical portion and required tiebreaks: 2016, 2018 and 2023.
The complete official regulations can be found here.

blocks.caption: Gukesh Dommaraju speaks with chess presenter Charlize van Zyl during Sunday’s media day at the United Nations’ European headquarters in Geneva. Photograph: Michał Walusza/Fide

blocks.text: Preamble

Hello and welcome to Geneva for day one of the World Chess Championship. Over the next three weeks, India’s defending champion Gukesh Dommaraju and Javokhir Sindarov of Uzbekistan will compete in a scheduled best-of-14-games match for the sport’s most prestigious title and a share of a $2.5m prize fund. The setting is the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, an affluent suburb overlooking Lake Geneva, where the two 20-year-olds will make history as the youngest pairing ever to contest a world championship match in the competition’s 140-year history.

Gukesh became the youngest undisputed world chess champion in history when he defeated China’s Ding Liren in Singapore in December 2024, aged just 18, shattering the record held by Garry Kasparov, who was 22 when he dethroned Anatoly Karpov in 1985. An aggressive player known for creating sharp, tactically complex positions aimed at unsettling opponents, the Chennai-born grandmaster has struggled badly for form since winning the crown, sliding from a career-high No 3 to No 26 in the world rankings and raising questions over his chances of retaining the title in his first defense.

blocks.caption: A tram bearing promotional artwork for the world chess championship in Geneva. Photograph: Maurizio Giuliani/Fide

blocks.text: Sindarov, meanwhile, has emerged as one of the most formidable talents of a new generation of Uzbek grandmasters. Born in Tashkent, he became a grandmaster at 12 years and 10 months, the second-youngest in history at the time, and secured his place in Geneva by winning the eight-man Candidates tournament earlier this year. A fearless, resourceful player in a rich vein of form, he enters his first world championship match ranked fourth in the world, up from No 25 last year and a remarkable 22 places above the reigning champion, and with a favorable head-to-head record against Gukesh in classical chess.

We’re roughly 80 minutes away from the ceremonial opening moves. Fide president Timur Turlov will do the honors for white, with five-time world champion and Fide deputy president Viswanathan Anand moving for black. Plenty more to come between now and then.

articles.title: Gaza issues meningitis epidemic alert after steep rise in cases
articles.summary:
Health ministry records 272 new infections in October, more than eight times the normal monthly rate

Gaza’s health ministry has issued an epidemic alert after a sharp rise in meningitis…

blocks.text: Gaza’s health ministry has issued an epidemic alert after a sharp rise in meningitis infections, with more than 270 new cases reported in October.
Dr Nidal Ghoneim, a senior official at the ministry, said the spread of the disease posed a threat to the lives of hundreds of thousands of people, including children.

Health organisations attribute the rise in infections to the destruction of infrastructure, overcrowded shelters and the contamination of drinking water with sewage – a crisis made worse by winter flooding and restrictions on humanitarian aid. Much of Gaza’s drinking water previously came from desalination plants and three Israeli-controlled pipelines, which were cut off at the start of the war and have only partially reopened.

Ghoneim told a news conference that 272 meningitis infections had been reported in the territory in October, more than eight times the normal monthly rate of 30 to 50 cases. Fifteen Palestinians have died of meningitis since the beginning of this year, he said.

blocks.caption: A doctor examines a child suffering from meningitis at al-Rantisi children’s hospital in Gaza City. Photograph: Omar Ashtawy/HL/Getty Images

blocks.text: “We hold the [Israeli] occupation fully and directly responsible for the epidemic outbreak due to its prevention of the entry of maintenance spare parts, sterilisation materials and fuel,” the health ministry said.

The UN’s humanitarian agency (Ocha) had previously reported 413 suspected cases of meningitis in Gaza between 27 September and 31 October, including 294 viral and 119 bacterial cases. About 68% were recorded in Gaza City.
Ocha said the increase in cases could be attributed to crowded tents and schools, the deterioration of shelter and sanitation conditions and exposure to unsafe water.
Gaza’s water crisis is severe. Before the war, 80% of the territory’s supply came from an aquifer that is now contaminated by seawater and wastewater, making it unfit for human consumption.

For many, this means a stark choice between drinking an extra cup of water or saving it to wash their hands and prevent disease. Acute diarrhoea is among the leading causes of illness in the territory. About 15,000 cubic metres a day of untreated waste seeps into the groundwater from soak-away pits, particularly in the informal camps in al-Mawasi.
The World Health Organization said in September that microbial contamination in water samples had risen from less than 6% in January to nearly 20% in August.

In addition to disease outbreaks and shortages of drinking water and basic necessities, Palestinians continue to face attacks and ceasefire violations by the Israeli military, which has intensified its strikes in recent days.

Soldiers crossed into Hamas-controlled central Gaza last Wednesday in the first ground operation across the “yellow line” boundary since a fragile ceasefire was agreed in October last year, forcing dozens of displaced Palestinians to flee their tents.
Four people were killed and seven wounded in Gaza over the past 24 hours, according to the health ministry, bringing the death toll since the ceasefire took effect to 1,679.
More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and more than 176,000 wounded since the beginning of the war in October 2023, according to Gaza’s health authorities.

articles.title: The Nvidia case is just the latest episode of Trump disregarding intelligence
articles.summary:
Trump’s reaction to sensitive information that contradicts his worldview mirrors his conduct towards war with Iran

Donald Trump’s unwillingness to heed warnings of suspected Chinese…

blocks.text: Donald Trump’s unwillingness to heed warnings of suspected Chinese penetration of the tech giant Nvidia follows a pattern of the US president ignoring sensitive intelligence that contradicts his world view.

Trump disregarded repeated information that the company’s co-founder, Jensen Huang, was having an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy that threatened to undermine Washington’s geo-strategically vital goal of pipping China for global supremacy in the artificial intelligence race.

The woman, Alice Huang – no blood relation of Jensen – was also responsible for buying $4.8bn worth of Nvidia’s highly sensitive AI chips in her capacity as head of a Singapore-based technology company, Megaspeed. The chips were then diverted to China, despite US export restrictions forbidding such sales to a country Washington regards as a key strategic adversary.

The president was inactive even after Marco Rubio, the secretary of state and national security – and one of the administration’s renowned “China hawks” – repackaged the intelligence into a classified report last May warning of the geopolitical risks posed by the relationship.

“It’s clear that the White House was warned, had adequate opportunities to take action against what was an emerging and then eventually very clear chip diversion network that was emerging under Megaspeed and other Southeast Asian offshore data farms – and it just failed to act,” said Julia Curlee, a former Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) officer who specialized in the Middle East and China and also worked on the White House national security council during Trump’s first presidency.
“It’s the latest episode of the president ignoring or not believing the intelligence that’s being provided to him.”
Despite the intelligence concerns raised by his conduct, Huang was reinstated as Nvidia’s chief executive on Monday following pressure from the White House and the company’s shareholders.

Trump’s behaviour over the Nvidia affairs mirrors his conduct towards the war with Iran, Curlee argues, where he pressed ahead with military actions despite being forewarned of potential complications.

Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran contradicted advice that the country’s Islamic regime had the resilience to withstand attempts to topple it and was likely to retaliate by closing the strait of Hormuz – predictions that were subsequently borne out.

Trump’s dismissal of intelligence warnings in both cases recalls his comments at a 2018 summit with Vladimir Putin when he openly sided the Russian president over US intelligence agencies, who had assessed that Russia had interfered in the 2016 presidential election.

His indifference to intelligence work and the professionals who perform it appears to surpass that of previous administrations, even those who were accused of deliberately politicizing the practice – an accusation leveled at George W Bush following the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

“There are other administrations that have ignored or or tried to politicize intelligence but I think the Trump administration stands alone in how little it seems to regard the intelligence analysis prepared to help the president make decisions,” said Curlee.

“The best example of this is the run-up to the war in Iran, where the administration just truly shut out the warnings which have been there and were provided for many years about what the Iranians would do in the case of a war.”

Trump’s administration has also fired agents for providing intelligence assessments at odds with the president’s own statements. Last year, Lt Gen Jeffrey Kruse, the head of the defense intelligence agency, was dismissed over a report that contradicted Trump’s claim that Iran’s nuclear sites had been “obliterated” by US strikes carried out in June 2025.

“What makes them really different from, say, the Bush administration, is that even that administration did not publicly fire officers when they didn’t provide information the president wanted to hear,” said Curlee, who also served on the White House national security council under Trump and Joe Biden.
“I feel pretty strongly that the fault of the Iran war lies at this refusal to listen to the intelligence community.”

Curlee said the Chinese acquisition of the Nvidia chips compared in strategic significance to the case of Julius and Ethel Rosenberg, a US couple who were executed after being convicted of passing on atomic secrets to the Soviet Union in the early years of the cold war. That made official indifference to the intelligence discovery all the more remarkable, she argued.

“This is a technology at the heart of the strategic competition with our primary competitor in the world, and at an industrial scale, they managed to divert chips from our leading hardware company,” she said.

“It’s a terrible thing that’s occurred and we can’t undo that. But uncovering it and stopping it was done at least over a year ago. If the policymaker then refuses to do their to do their job, there’s nothing the intelligence community can do about that.”
The administration’s stance has drawn further scrutiny by deciding not to provide a “defensive briefing” to Jensen Huang about the discovery.

“Before public accusations and scandals, it used to be accepted practice for someone to pull the American target aside for a man-to-man chat – to tell him to think with the head between his shoulders,” said Fulton Armstrong, a former CIA analyst specializing in Latin America who also has experience in Taiwan.

“The chat might even include discussion of feeding the foreigner some disinformation. It seems that four years of Trump first presidency, four years of do-nothingism with Biden, and now almost two years of Trump II have so deeply changed the intel community that practical solutions are no longer allowed.”
No explanation has been provided for the failure to warn Huang – thus allowing him to continue his relationship with Alice Huang. He was also allowed to maintain his already close access to Trump.

Curlee said it was a “policy decision [rather than] an intelligence decision.” She added “It is to me a very unusual suspect decision to let something like this go on for as long as it apparently did, without at minimum protecting this US citizen, who is the object of of a Chinese spy operation.”

Fevered speculation has swirled over whether Alice Huang may have been part of a “honey trap” operation set by China’s intelligence services to lure Jensen Huang into a close business relationship that would entice him into vast amounts of Nvidia’s coveted chips to a company which would them to pass them to China, subverting American law.

China’s sprawling Ministry of State Security [MSS] is believed to use the technique, which most western intelligence agencies publicly insist they do not use, on the grounds that is unethical and potentially counterproductive, because it often depends on blackmail.

But analysts doubt that it occurred in this instance. Alice Huang, they suggest, could have disclosed the relationship to Chinese agents after it began because she was legally obliged to do so under China’s catch-all intelligence law, which legally obliges the country’s citizens to “cooperate” with security services on matters defined as “national security”. That term has a much broader definition under China’s laws than in most western countries, and can cover commercial and economic development issues.
Frank Montoya, a retired Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) agent who specialized on China, said a straightforward “honey trap” was unlikely.

“I don’t think that it was it was mapped out specifically where the MSS officer said we’re going to find this person and we’re going to set her up for business and then target her against against the CEO of [Nvidia],” he said.

“There was a confluence of opportunities. She’s very ambitious, very smart and she has this idea, and doesn’t necessarily brings it to the MSS, but is talking to somebody else. She has connections in the party, and she’s talking to somebody else, and then somebody else talks to the MSS and says, ‘hey, let’s see if we can take advantage of that’.”

He added: “This was a multi-billion dollar purchase [of Nvidia chips]. There’s no way the MSS alone can fund that. They’re going to need somebody higher up [in the Chinese communist party] to not only approve that but to provide the money when the deal is made.”
The operation, Montoya said, bore the hallmarks of the Chinese espionage approach, which he described as “whole of government” and lacking the “clandestinity” of traditional spy craft.

Alice Huang would have drawn the attention of US intelligence agencies through Megaspeed’s mass purchase of Nvidia chips, and because it rented out services from its Singapore data centers to Chinese AI companies, Curlew argues.

The intimate nature of her relationship with Jensen Huang, and her links to Chinese intelligence is thought to have been discovered through surveillance of her phone, almost certainly carried out by the National Security Agency.

Trump has dismissed the case’s importance, saying he does not believe US national security was threatened and telling Fox News: “We spy on China. They spy on us.” He later told reporters that he raised the matter only briefly when he met China’s president, Xi Jinping, at last week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) gathering Shenzhen.
It is an attitude Curlee lamented as disdainful of intelligence as a whole.

“We are spending tens of billions of dollars and people put their lives in jeopardy to collect information at great personal risk so that our leaders have decision-advantage, the ability to anticipate crises around the corner and can respond to foreign threats,” she said. “If the president can’t be bothered to listen to his intelligence community then what is what is the point of it all?”

articles.title: Watch: Moment troops raid home and capture Mexican drug lord
articles.summary: Newly-released bodycam footage shows the moment troops detained 'El Chapo Isidro', who had managed to evade capture for years.

blocks.text: Newly-released bodycam footage shows the moment troops entered a house and detained a Mexican drug lord who had managed to evade capture for years.
The video shows armed personnel entering via a garage and finding Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, also known as 'El Chapo Isidro', who was on the FBI's most wanted list.
Seven suspects were killed in last Friday's operation, as were four members of the Mexican army who were travelling to reinforce security in Guasave, Mexico's defence secretariat said.
The arrest of Meza Flores in the northern Sinaloa state sparked a wave of unrest, which led to eight alleged drug cartel members being detained for their involvement in the retaliatory violence.

articles.title: Leader of India’s Cockroach movement says he was stopped from boarding flight to UK
articles.summary:
Saurav Das was due to give talks at UK universities on protest movement but says ‘coward government’ prevented him flying

A leader of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement has said he was…

blocks.text: A leader of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement has said he was prevented from leaving Delhi to fly to the UK to give talks on the viral group’s protests.

Saurav Das, 27, has been at the forefront of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), which has amassed millions of social media followers since its launch in May. Das, who was due to fly out early on Tuesday, said immigration officials told him at the airport that his passport had been flagged.
The incident comes a month after he was detained for defying a security crackdown in Delhi during protests demanding the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner.

“This coward government did not allow me to board my flight to London where I was invited by prestigious universities like Oxford, Cambridge, LSE (London School of Economics), Edinburgh to deliver talks on the Cockroach movement,” Das said in a social media post late on Monday. “Indian students put their heart and soul to organise the events but this anti-intellectual government was scared of me going to these prestigious institutions.”
Das was due to speak at the Oxford Union society on 1 December.
CJP-organised protests in July over alleged examination irregularities forced the education minister to resign, marking a rare climbdown by the government of Narendra Modi.

Critics say human rights and press freedoms have declined since Modi came to power in 2014. Earlier this month, India barred more than 100 foreign speakers from attending a democracy summit organised by the opposition Congress party. Those denied visas included a Norwegian journalist who had previously questioned Modi about press freedom.

In 2022, authorities prevented Sanna Irshad Mattoo, an award-winning photographer from India-administered Kashmir, from flying to the US to collect her Pulitzer prize.

articles.title: After 80 years in Oxford, Naga ancestors are finally going home
articles.summary:
A campaign securing the landmark return to India of ancestral remains taken during British colonial rule has opened a wider conversation about restitution

The lacerating legacy of…

blocks.text: The lacerating legacy of colonialism survives in many spaces, particularly in museum collections and private holdings across the western world. And it’s not just limited to inanimate artefacts or cultural objects.
For almost 80 years, human remains were displayed on crowded glass shelves at Pitt Rivers Museum at Oxford University, one of the world’s most celebrated institutions.

Many of them were, in fact, skeletal remains taken from Nagaland brought to the museum by two British colonial administrators, John Henry Hutton and James Philip Mills between 1910 and 1940. Now, after six years of consultations, negotiations and a concerted effort to build consensus across Naga communities, 39 skeletal remains are finally coming home. In early November, the museum handed custodianship to a Naga delegation of leaders and scholars. The repatriated remains include those of two children, a woman and a village chief.

“This is the first such repatriation of human remains to India,” Dolly Kikon, a Naga anthropologist and professor at the University of California, Santa Cruz, told me. She had contacted the Pitt Rivers Museum in 2020 after reading in the Guardian that the museum was removing human remains from public display following an ethical review, setting the repatriation process in motion. In a statement, the museum’s director, Laura Van Broekhoven, acknowledged that it has been a “long journey”, adding that “hope is possible as we work towards reconciliation and healing”.

blocks.caption: Members of the Naga delegation in Oxford, where the university transferred custodianship. Photograph: FNR RRaD Pictures

blocks.text: The review was part of a broader reassessment of the museum’s display practices and how it presented human remains from communities across the world. Among its most contentious displays were the shrunken heads known as tsantsa, from the Shuar people in South America. Pitt Rivers – one of the world’s leading anthropology and ethnography museums – has acknowledged that its display reinforced racist stereotypes about the culture. The Naga remains were displayed alongside artefacts and human remains from a number of communities, including from Nigeria and Papua New Guinea.

Naga academics have challenged the perception that the remains were exclusively associated with the practice of headhunting. While Naga warriors traditionally collected the heads of enemies killed in raids, the anthropologists say that British collectors acquired Naga human remains under duress during colonial expeditions.

For the Naga community, that was just the beginning of a long journey. India, unlike countries such as Australia, Canada and the US, has no national laws for the repatriation of Indigenous ancestral remains, says Kikon. “We had to ensure the process was community-led, in the absence of a policy and make sure the focus remained on healing and reconciliation. It was all unprecedented.”

The Forum for Naga Reconciliation, a collective working toward peace and reconciliation among Naga Indigenous communities, facilitated the repatriation, and a voluntary research group, Recover, Restore and Decolonise (RRaD), was formed to build wider community awareness. Its volunteers travelled to urban centres and villages, talking with students, elders and intergenerational audiences about the human remains kept at the museum and what the community wanted to do with them.

The museum still has around 178 objects that contain, or may contain, human hair. It also has 6,500 Naga objects, including clothing items, weapons, vessels and musical instruments, many from Mills and Hutton, while some items, like weapons, were bought from auction houses. “The Pitt Rivers Museum has one of the largest collections of Naga objects, artefacts and human remains in the world. What we have focused on for now is the skeletal remains, but this is only a first step in thinking more broadly about these collections,” said Arkotong Longkumer, a professor of anthropology and modern Asia at Edinburgh University.

The question of restitution of Indian artefacts and cultural heritage items has long occupied a prominent place in public discourse. At its heart is the Koh-i-noor diamond, which passed through Mughal, Persian and Afghan hands before Britain wrested it from the 10-year-old king, Maharaja Duleep Singh. Today, it is part of the British crown jewels, a symbol of the plunder of the empire and, for many in India, a theft that continues to rankle. Last year, an Indian parliamentary committee recommended establishing a dedicated heritage recovery taskforce to pursue the return of cultural objects held abroad, particularly those taken during the colonial period.

In the case of the human remains, the question is about the right to honour the ancestors and give them a dignified resting place. “How we imagine a shared future depends on how we understand our history. We have to look back and make sense of the past in order to think about the kind of future we want to create,” Longkumer told me.
“The Naga repatriation addresses a very deep colonial violence,” Kikon says. “It is about the dehumanisation where the remains of human beings were stored in museums and exhibited as exotic objects.”

The return prompted Kikon to reflect on the contradiction between the longstanding reverence for Oxford University by Indians, many of whom have aspired to study there, and the institution’s history of exhibiting the remains of their ancestors. “Repatriation is not just about bringing back bones. It was about starting a process of deep introspection,” she says. “Ultimately, it leaves us with a greater responsibility to reflect on how we live our lives.”
The remains will be buried at Naga Solidarity Park in Kohima, the capital of Nagaland.
What else we’re reading about

blocks.caption: A courtroom sketch of Nikhil Gupta in New York in 2024. Photograph: Jane Rosenberg/Reuters

blocks.text: Crime | A federal judge in New York sentenced Indian national Nikhil Gupta to almost 20 years in prison for an assassination plot against the Khalistan separatist leader Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, an American citizen. The prosecutors argued that Gupta had been directed by an Indian government employee, a charge that India denies.

Politics | In a new report, Human Rights Watch argued that India’s democratic institutions have been systematically hollowed out under the Modi government, which has used state agencies to target critics, undermined parliamentary oversight and promoted Hindu majoritarianism. Based on dozens of interviews, and drawing from news reports, HRW describes these actions as part of a broader authoritarian move to concentrate executive power.

Arts | The second edition of the India Biennale, organised by the Ministry of Culture, begins in Delhi on 4 December. Highlights include photographer Dayanita Singh’s work on show at Humayun’s Tomb and artist Paresh Maity and fashion designer Ritu Beri’s installation at Qutub Minar.
after newsletter promotion
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste

blocks.caption: Barefoot College brings solar-powered lighting to rural areas. Photograph: Rebecca Conway/Getty Images

blocks.text: Writer Gayatri Rangachari Shah, a founding member of the Women Leadership Circle, recommends an inspiring model of rural development. “If there is an institution that captures an alternative vision of India, it’s the Barefoot College in Rajasthan. Set up by Sanjit ‘Bunker’ Roy in 1972, it has spent more than five decades putting rural communities at the centre of their own development. Its Solar Mamas programme has enabled women of all ages who had never been to school to learn to make and install solar lights. Its other initiatives include digital learning centres for young women, night schools for those working during the day, menstrual-friendly toilets in government schools, rainwater harvesting, waste management and recycling.
Roy died on 10 November but he passed on his work to a younger team.”
Count it

blocks.caption: The National Chambal Sanctuary is one of the areas where wildlife clearances were granted. Photograph: Hira Punjabi/Alamy

blocks.text: India’s top wildlife body approved the clearance of ecologically sensitive land and wildlife corridors covering an area of at least 99,000 hectares (244,530 acres) – an area about a third larger than Singapore – between 2014 and 2026, an analysis by Article 14 concluded. Defence projects, mining and irrigation were the top sectors for which the board granted clearances at the expense of forests and wildlife habitats, according to the investigation by Prakriti Srivastava and Prerna Singh Bindra.
Vibe check

blocks.caption: GTA VI has brought Disco Jazz to new audiences. Photograph: YouTube

blocks.text: Grand Theft Auto VI, billed as the biggest cultural event of the year, has smashed sales records. It has also helped propel a little-known 1982 Indian disco track to global fandom. Aaj Shanibar by the Bengali singer Rupa Biswas features on Worldwide FM, one of the radio stations in the game.

The song was part of an album called Disco Jazz that Biswas recorded during a visit to her brother in Canada. The album never made a splash and faded into obscurity, but years later her son discovered the track had found a following in DJ sets and was reissued by the US label Numero Group. Now, with GTA VI, the song has reached a generation who were not even born when the original was released 44 years ago.

articles.title: Myanmar has been found guilty of genocide. Should Israel be worried? – podcast
articles.summary: The international court of justice has for the first time ruled that a state has committed genocide. Yasmin Ullah explains what it means for the Rohingya people, while…
articles.byline: Presented by Annie Kelly with Kaamil Ahmed, produced by George McDonagh, Harriet Mogie and Rudi Zygadlo

blocks.text: For seven years, Yasmin Ullah had been part of the delegation arguing that Myanmar had committed genocide – one of the gravest human rights crimes – against Rohingya Muslims.

The genocide has directly affected Yasmin and her family. Last week she was in court to hear the international court of justice’s landmark verdict against Myanmar. “I was really kind of pinching myself. It felt like we were all able to breathe again,” she tells Annie Kelly.

The verdict could have far-reaching consequences – especially for Israel, which is also facing a genocide case at the ICJ. The Guardian journalist Kaamil Ahmed explains how the case unfolded and what could happen next.

articles.title: Ukraine confirms it used naval drones to strike two Russian ships off Libya
articles.summary:
Ukraine’s security service says seven drones were launched from mothership in operation that sank Merkury warship

Ukraine has confirmed it deployed naval drones in

blocks.text: Ukraine has confirmed it deployed naval drones in strikes on two Russian vessels off Libya on Sunday, including one that sank the corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest vessels.
Ukraine’s security service, the SBU, said seven domestically made naval drones were launched from a mothership in the operation, which Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as “exemplary”.
“We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia’s aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons,” the Ukrainian president added.

Zelenskyy released video footage, filmed by an approaching drone, showing the drones as they smashed into the side of the warship at its berth in the Benghazi naval base, triggering huge explosions that lit up the night sky.

In its own statement, the SBU said: “The defence forces of Ukraine have once again demonstrated that the Russian military fleet and its logistics networks have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea.”
Zelenskyy said the other vessel hit on Sunday, the dry cargo ship MV Angara, was being used by Russia to transport weapons.

The operation, conducted 1,500 miles (2,400km) from the frontline in Ukraine, was the latest daring long-range assault by Kyiv’s forces. Last week Ukraine hitthe Kerch bridge - a key supply line to Russian-occupied Crimea – and the Russian Baltic sea port of Kaliningrad.
Residents in Benghazi heard loud explosions and saw flames at the naval base early on Sunday. Civil defence units rushed to the site and extinguished the fire, authorities in eastern Libya said.

The Merkury had docked to refuel and take on supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, the statement said without providing details about the vessel or its cargo.

Vladimir Putin had taken a personal interest in the ship. In 2019 he toured the St Petersburg yard where it was being built and backed naming it after a tsarist-era brig celebrated for fighting off two Turkish warships in the Black Sea in 1829.

At the 2023 Navy Day parade, the Russian president singled it out among 30 new vessels as evidence that Russia was “consistently building up the power of its fleet”. He hailed its St George flag as “a sign of the inviolability of our naval traditions” and said it was “gratifying” that the brig’s name had been revived.
Russian state media also talked up the ship. The news agency Tass called it the “newest missile corvette”, while the channel TV Tsentr claimed its stealth technology made it “invisible to radar”.

Divided Libya has emerged in recent years as a proxy battlefield. Moscow has long supported the breakaway government in Benghazi of Khalifa Haftar in its efforts use eastern Libya as a staging post for its military presence in north Africa and the Sahel.

More recently there have been reports of increasing Ukrainian operations. In April, the Associated Press reported that Ukrainian drone specialists had been operating at military sites in Misrata, Tripoli and Zawiya in Libya’s west. In September Libyan authorities denied reports by CNN that it allowed Ukraine to use a military base in the to launch drones against vessels from Russia’s “shadow fleet” in the Mediterranean.
The rival UN-recognised government in Tripoli said in a statement it was alarmed by “risks posed by involving civilian ports and facilities in activities linked to external conflicts”.

There was no immediate comment from Russia about the strikes. The UN mission in Libya (UNSMIL), however, expressed “serious concern” over the attacks, calling for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”. It said on X: “Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts.”

Ukraine prides itself on its military industry, particularly its progress in drone technology, which it has extensively developed since Russia invaded more than four and a half years ago. It has repeatedly touted the effectiveness of its domestically produced drones, including naval drones deployed throughout the war to hit Russian ships and infrastructure in the Black Sea.

In 2024, the Ukrainian general staff announced it had destroyed the Russian landing ship Cesar Kunikov with naval drones off the coast of Ukraine’s peninsula of Crimea, which was annexed by Russia in 2014.

Ukraine has also claimed to have attacked Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet – believed to carry Russian oil to circumvent sanctions – including in the Mediterranean last December. In March, a Russian liquefied natural gas carrier sank off the Libyan coast following an attack that Putin blamed on Ukraine.
Additional reporting by Pjotr Sauer

articles.title: Ukraine shares video of strikes on Russian ships off Libya
articles.summary: President Zelensky said a Russia warship was sunk, with a Russian cargo ship also hit.

blocks.text: Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky has shared footage on social media which he says shows strikes on Russian vessels off the coast of Libya on Sunday.
A Russian warship was sunk by Ukrainian drones and the attack also hit a second vessel, a cargo ship which was being used to transport weapons, Zelensky said.
Footage verified by the BBC shows a ship ablaze at Benghazi's port.

The local health ministry said it had received injured people from a commercial ship that was targeted off the coast. It is not clear whether this is the same vessel as the one Ukraine has claimed responsibility for.
Following the strikes, the Kremlin warned of an "escalation of tensions in the region", but declined to comment directly on the attacks in Libya.
